News.title: Moment brave builders confront samurai sword-wielding thug and fight him off with spirit level – as attacker, 32, jailed
News.content:
Next

THIS is the shocking moment brave builders take on a samurai sword-wielding thug, armed only with a spirit level.

Aaron Messenbird, 32, approached a group of people hanging around a van and threatened them while swinging the blade about, in Milton Keynes on July 30 at around 9.05pm.



He also “raised the weapon in a threatening manner,” the police said.

During a struggle, Messenbird’s victim sustained injuries to his hands, including a damaged tendon requiring specialist treatment, as well as injuries to his ribs.



Two builders then intervened, one holding a spirit level, causing Messenbird to flee the scene.

Messenbird was later spotted walking along Silbury Boulevard while still armed with the sword.

He was arrested on August 5 and charged the next day.

Investigating officer PC Jordan Buchanan-Kay, of the Central Milton Keynes Neighbourhood Policing Team, said: “This was a violent and unprovoked incident in which Messenbird threatened members of the public with a potentially lethal weapon before assaulting a man who had stepped in to protect others.



“The victim suffered painful injuries, including damage to a tendon in his hand, as a result of Messenbird’s actions.

“I would also like to acknowledge the bravery of the members of the public who intervened and helped prevent this incident from becoming far more serious.

“Their actions undoubtedly contributed to protecting others from harm.

“However, we would always urge people not to put themselves in danger when confronted with somebody carrying a weapon.

“The safest course of action is to move to a place of safety and call 999 immediately, providing as much information as possible to help officers respond quickly.



“I am pleased that Messenbird has been given a custodial sentence and hope this outcome provides reassurance to the victims and the wider community that violent offending involving weapons will not be tolerated.”

Messenbird, of Milton Keynes, was sentenced to 12 months’ imprisonment at Aylesbury Crown Court on October 14.

He pleaded guilty to threatening a person with a bladed article, possession of a bladed article in a public place and assault occasioning actual bodily harm (ABH).

News.title: Migrants let off paying visa fees more than 76,000 times since Labour came to power
News.content:
Next

MIGRANTS have been let off paying visa charges more than 76,000 times since Labour took office – costing taxpayers up to £300million.

Home Office officials waived the fees for applicants who said they could not afford them while asking to stay in Britain on human rights grounds under the controversial ECHR.



Each waiver is now worth up to £3,994 per adult, covering the £1,407 application fee and a £2,587 NHS surcharge for 30 months of leave.

Applicants must show they are destitute, that paying would leave them unable to afford food or housing, or that it would harm a child’s wellbeing.



The waivers were brought in after a string of human rights court rulings found it unlawful to charge people for human rights applications they could not afford.

A record 33,737 people applied to be let off in the first three months of this year, more than double the 13,669 who asked at the end of 2023.

Another 33,393 joined the queue between April and June, the second highest quarter on record.

Stats show officials are now struggling to keep up with the surge in applications, with 50,257 of those applications still waiting for a decision.

Just 478 of the 33,737 requests made in the first three months of the year were dealt with inside the Home Office’s 20-working-day target.

If the backlog is approved at the current rate, the bill since Labour came to power will climb to close to £390million by the end of this year.



Official figures show 70,916 waivers were handed out in Labour’s first 18 months alone, up 57 per cent on the 45,101 in the final 18 months of the last Conservative government.

Applications began soaring in early 2024, when the health surcharge jumped from £624 to £1,035 a year.

Waivers are open to partners and parents on the 10-year family route, people who have built a private life in the UK, and failed asylum seekers later given leave on human rights grounds.

Small boat migrants and those granted asylum are already not required to pay a visa surcharge.

Those on the 10-year route must reapply every 30 months, so the same migrant can be let off up to four times before they can apply for settled status.



A further 2,353 waivers went to families applying to join relatives from abroad in Labour’s first 18 months.

Nigerians, Indians and Pakistanis top the nationalities granted extensions on the family and private life route since July 2024, with 21,220, 19,402 and 16,679 grants respectively.

But the Home Office does not publish which nationalities are most likely to receive the waivers.

The Government was asked to comment on the figures.

News.title: Musk ‘ordered Starshield blackout’ that left Ukraine defenceless against Putin’s attacks – after tech titan blamed Trump
News.content:
Next

ELON Musk pulled the plug on the military-grade Starlink service that blindsided Kyiv leaving it defenceless to Putin’s attacks, US officials said.

The world’s richest man ordered the slowdown after expressing anger at recent Ukrainian strikes on Russian diesel hubs and rising fuel prices.



He capped the speeds at which Ukrainian hardware could stay connected to the satellite-based network, according to the Wall Street Journal.

The move essentially rendered offensive and interceptor drones useless as the Kremlin unleashed missile barrages on Kyiv and other major cities.



It had been suggested that Donald Trump ordered the slowdown after the US president expressed anger at Volodymyr Zelensky.

Musk also blamed Trump for throttling the service, writing on X: “Starshield systems are owned and controlled by the US government.



“Any limits on speed or usage are decided by the US military and ultimately POTUS,” an acronym for the president of the United States.

The tech titan and Trump reportedly discussed the decision in a private call while the president was campaigning last week, two sources told the WSJ.



One claimed that their discussion took place prior to the slowdown being implemented.

Zelensky’s complaints that Ukrainians would die if the unrestrictive service wasn’t restored led to confusion over who ordered the directive.

He said: “It’s painful when President Trump chooses one side, not our side.



“I think his advisers are wrong. I don’t know who is pushing him. Not to the right side, this is not the right side of history.”

Some US officials claimed that Musk acted unilaterally, although one said that he talked to multiple senior White House officials, including Trump, before introducing the cap.

The outage struck without warning on Tuesday night, as Russian forces unleashed a deadly salvo of ballistic missiles on Ukraine’s energy infrastructure.

Power was cut off from 600,000 people in Kyiv after 39 ballistic missiles, 120 drones, and a record number of Zircon hypersonic missiles rained down on the Ukrainian capital.

It highlighted Musk’s influence over the brutal four-and-a-half year conflict, with Starlink providing a lifeline to Ukrainian troops.



The decision also came after several statements by the Trump administration that Kyiv perceived as hostile to Ukraine, leading officials to suspect US involvement.

Trump accused Kyiv of “seriously hurting the world diesel markets” by continuing to launch strikes on Russian oil refineries.

He also blocked numerous sanctions against the Kremlin on Friday and struck a diesel deal with Vladimir Putin earlier this month.



Zelensky in turn blasted Trump for “rewarding” the Russian tyrant and said he felt “betrayed” by the White House.

With air defence systems operating at reduced speeds, more missile and drone barrages have been able to hit Ukraine.

A drone attack on a park near Kharkiv yesterday killed six people, including a toddler and an 11-year-old girl.

Zelensky blasted the “pure atrocity” of the indiscriminate strike, which hit a park as families played with their children.

He said: “Sadly, two women and a baby who was in a buggy were killed,” alongside blurred images of the infant victim slumped in her pram.



RECOMMENDED STORIES

Zelensky continued: “These are horrific photos, but behind them are shattered lives and the truth about this war. Lives must be protected. Ukraine needs air defence.

“I am grateful to everyone who supports Ukraine under these circumstances and helps us shoot down ‘shaheds,’ shoot down missiles, and stop Russian assaults.”

News.title: Jeremy Clarkson’s pal urges Andy Burnham to scrap family farm tax as he blasts ‘clueless’ Whitehall officials
News.content:
FARM PLEA Jeremy Clarkson’s pal urges Andy Burnham to scrap family farm tax as he blasts ‘clueless’ Whitehall officials







Next

ANDY Burnham has been urged to reverse the family farms tax and ignore out-of-touch civil servants who are “clueless” about rural life.

A top farmer and Jeremy Clarkson pal has slammed urban Whitehall pen-pushers for unleashing an inheritance raid that will backfire into higher food costs.



Olly Harrison told The Sun: “They’ve gone to university, they’ve studied Politics, and now they work in London, and they’ve never stepped foot on a farm or have an understanding of where the food comes from or what motivates an industry.”

Mr Harrison is also a high-profile social media personality, who promotes the countryside on his Olly Blogs YouTube channel which has 150,000 subscribers British farms were exempt from inheritance tax until ex-Chancellor Rachel Reeves said they would be subject to a 20 per cent levy on land and assets worth £1million.



But a major backlash from rural Britain led to the threshold being raised to £2.5million in December 2025 or £5million for married couples.

The 45-year-old, from Merseyside added: “At the moment, I think a lot of it’s to do with the civil servants.



“It doesn’t matter who it is that is the frontman of the band doing the singing.

“It’s the people in the back that write their words, isn’t it? That seems to be the problem.

He added: “They don’t understand that it can be a 12-to-24-month process to produce food on our own shores.”

The PM is under increasing pressure to scrap the family farm tax altogether to rebuild relations with the countryside.



Close-ally of Burnham David Blunkett also called the tax raid “a mistake” and urged the Prime Minister to use his position and listen to rural people more.

News.title: Britain is broke & bills are soaring but when it comes to funding accommodation for boat migrants the sky’s the limit
News.content:
2-tier Britain







Next

BRITAIN is broke, bills are soaring and ministers have been ordered to tighten belts ahead of next week’s brutal Budget.

Yet when it comes to funding accommodation for illegal boat migrants, the sky’s the limit.`



Landlords are being offered lucrative, publicly-funded contracts well in excess of the market value to evict tenants so asylum seekers can move in.

What a disgraceful way to treat people when money is tight and there are 1.3million families on the waiting list for social housing.



One Home Office contractor offered £4,500 a month for a three-bedroom flat in South London — more than double the £1,790 put up by the local Labour council.

Last year the Government spent nearly £4.2billion on accommodation and support for asylum seekers and boat migrants.



Paying over the odds to jump the housing queue clobbers Brits twice, leaving taxpayers to foot the bill while families, students and women fleeing domestic violence are priced out of a home — or even kicked out of one.

If Chancellor John Healey wants to tighten belts, he should start by cutting the blank cheques for illegal migrants and put struggling British families first.

Down periscope

IT’S bad enough that the Royal Navy is running out of warships — but soon we’ll have no captains left to sail them.

Not a single submarine commander passed the intense training course required for taking charge of the nuclear weapons deterrent.



On the surface it’s almost as bleak, with only a handful completing the test to steer our fleet of frigates, destroyers and patrol vessels.

The only thing preventing a skipper crisis is the fact that half of Britain’s warships are either stuck in port or in line to be scrapped.

The vanishing fleet — and crew — yet again lays bare the scandalous budget cuts crippling our entire military and leaving the UK vulnerable to attack.

But instead of finding ways to boost defence spending, Andy Burnham is busy issuing new guidelines about car parking and loud music on trains.

Popular as those crackdowns may be, they are small fry compared with the threats that imperil our nation.



The PM must wake up and rebuild the Navy before we’re all sunk.

Jobs at stake

LABOUR’S betting taxes are still impacting Britain’s high streets a year on, with the firm behind Paddy Power, Betfair and Sky Bet now laying off 1,400 workers.

If the Chancellor increases levies on fruit machines in his Budget, experts warn it could cost a further 16,000 jobs.

Don’t gamble with people’s livelihoods, Mr Healey.

News.title: Mad Labour is trying to borrow its way out of debt and pulling us deeper into trouble – they need to get a grip urgently
News.content:
Next

THE Labour Government is doing the equivalent of taking out credit cards to pay the interest on Britain’s existing loans. It’s madness.

Any family or business in this position would know they were sinking, that every attempt to borrow their way out of trouble was pulling them deeper. But Andy Burnham and John Healey just don’t get it.



We have to start living within our means.

It is the only way Britain will be able to fund our Armed Forces, bring down taxes and get our economy growing so that everyone can feel richer again.



Labour aren’t interested.

Since they entered government, they have increased borrowing by £170billion. Britain’s national debt is now higher than at any point since the 1960s.



We’ve heard nothing from the PM and his Chancellor about cutting spending and getting the deficit down.

Instead, they’re planning a “nothing to see here” Budget next week that tries to do as little as possible in the hope that no one notices.

Britain cannot afford to do as little as possible. We need to get an urgent grip on the public finances.

The Conservatives are the only party that understand we must cut spending and start cutting the deficit.



That’s why we have found more than £70billion in savings the government could start making today.

Under our Golden Economic Rule, half of those savings would go to reducing the deficit. Because the Conservatives believe in handing a stronger economy to the next generation.

With the other half, we would create a stronger economy and a stronger country.



Defence is the first duty of any government.

It is unconscionable that after almost two-and-a-half years of Labour, the Armed Forces still don’t know how much money they are getting from the Government.

Keir Starmer and Rachel Reeves sat on their hands for two years, and now Andy Burnham has kicked the decision into next autumn.

John Healey actually resigned as Defence Secretary because he said that failing to meet a defence spending target of three per cent of GDP would put our country and our troops at risk. He was right.

But sadly, we have a Prime Minister who believes that “national security can’t come at the expense of social security”.



So, we are paying hundreds of thousands of young people with anxiety and ADHD to sit at home on benefits, instead of giving our Armed Forces the backing they desperately need.

The second part of creating a stronger country and a stronger economy is making sure you keep more of what you earn.

Next week’s Budget will be Labour’s third since the general election.

At the first, they put up taxes by £40billion. At the second, they put up taxes again by £26billion.



Since the election, unemployment has skyrocketed, with 350,000 more people unemployed, while graduates are finding it harder than ever to get a job and vacancies are at their lowest level in 12 years.

Politicians today are spending money they don’t have and leaving young people to pay the bill. No wonder they are angry.

They can’t get jobs and we are saddling them with more and more debt.

Raising taxes just kills growth. Businesses close, people lose their jobs and the country gets poorer.



But Labour keep dreaming up new taxes because, as their own Welfare Secretary once said, at every meeting he has with Labour MPs, they ask: “Who can we tax in order to pay benefits to others?”

A country cannot tax its way to prosperity. It has never worked before, and Labour’s two-and-a-half years in government are proof it doesn’t work now.

These problems didn’t start under Labour, but they have got much, much worse since they came in.

By contrast, the Conservatives are now under new management and, with my Shadow Chancellor Andrew Griffith and new Economic Team, we are showing we have learnt from our mistakes and we are setting things right.

So here’s my opening offer: cut National Insurance for under-25s to get young people back into work.



Cut Business Rates for shops on the high street to revitalise our town centres and bring back good local jobs.

Scrap Labour’s Family Farms Tax and Family Business Taxes so that farmers and families who have built up businesses over generations aren’t penalised when they hand them to their children.

And scrap Stamp Duty and Inheritance Tax, because only the Conservatives understand the importance of home ownership and will make sure that, whether it’s getting on the housing ladder or keeping a home in the family, people aren’t taxed for doing the right thing.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

Cut spending. Cut the deficit. Fund our defence. Cut taxes.

That is how we live within our means.

News.title: Brits face ‘overwhelming’ boom in rat populations across UK – as pest controllers warn they ‘can’t keep up’
News.content:
RAT-PID EXPANSION Brits face ‘overwhelming’ boom in rat populations across UK – as pest controllers warn they ‘can’t keep up’







Next

RATS are surging in numbers across UK households – and pest controllers have warned they “can’t keep up”.

The furry rodents have been overwhelming cities across the country as some areas have noticed a 25 per cent increase in populations.



Pest control experts have noticed a significant increase in the pests, as the winter may only bring more.

Lee Stewart, of Pest Proof London, told The Telegraph: “We are noticing that it’s significantly worse – we can’t keep up, quite frankly. And as it gets to winter, it’s overwhelming.”



He warned the milder weather over coming months risks extending their breeding period, and therefore encourages reproduction.

Stewart also added the rodents are fertile from six weeks, allowing for rampant multiplying.



During this year’s scorching summer, many rats may have had to travel further to find water.

This would lead them to homes and businesses – and as the weather turns cool again, they’ll be looking for shelter.

Many rat networks operate in drains, with one camera recording 54 rodents over one night in a manhole in London, according to Stewart.

This comes after monster rats were found feasting in a rubbish bin in Essex.



The 16-inch beasts are the largest Brit pest experts have ever seen.

Paul Claydon, the owner of Fast Track Pest Control in Essex, has described business as being “exceptionally busy” this year due to the rats, with some reaching 40 centimetres long.

“Normally, rat call-outs start to ease off through the summer, but this year the volume has stayed really high.

“I’m seeing levels of rat work in summer that I’d usually associate with the peak winter periods,” he continued.

According to Claydon, the rodents are managing to reach such an enormous size for a number of reasons, such as milder winters improving food availability and survival rates for the creatures.



The size of the rats is also said to be provoked by the changing waste collection schedules in lots of different areas, with some councils moving to fortnightly pick-ups instead of weekly.

Overflowing bins then become the perfect food source for rats, who feast on food waste, takeaway leftovers, and fly-tipped boxes.

Rats can pose significant health and safety risks by carrying diseases, contaminating food and water, covering surfaces with waste and causing building damage by chewing through cables.

News.title: Fears Royal Navy could run out of captains after record low numbers passed their ships’ ‘driving tests’
News.content:
Next

THE Royal Navy could run out of captains after record low numbers passed their ships’ “driving tests”.

Not a single submarine commander passed the legendary Perisher course last year.



Only three were selected to attempt it, with two failing at the simulator stage.

Surface ships fared little better with less than ten officers passing the command qualification known as CQ2.



The Navy needs 35 passes a year to sustain its sea commands.

Sources say the only reason the shortage has not affected operations is because so many ships have been scrapped or stuck in port for repairs.

Labour have axed nine warships since coming to power in 2024, with three more facing the chop.

Only three Navy officers have qualified to command submarines since 2024 — all on foreign courses.

Sources claimed the low pass rate was down to “chronic lack of sea time” and low morale.

Former Perisher instructor Ryan Ramsey said: “You can do what you want in a simulator and no one is going to die.”



A source added: “Sea command is less appealing than it was. Thirty years ago you’d get your destroyer, it would be working, and you’d be off doing cool stuff. Now, a lot of the time the ship is alongside.”

The Navy said: “We continue to generate the high-quality leaders we need for operational commitments.”

News.title: Idaho mum who claimed twins died from vaccinations could face firing squad execution
News.content:
Idaho mum who claimed twins died from vaccinations could face firing squad execution

Prosecutors are seeking the death penalty for Andrea Shaw over the deaths of her 18-month-old twins, Dallas and Tyson. She denies murdering the children and is due to stand trial in January

View 2 Images Shaw appeared on a podcast days after losing her twins (Image: Ada County Sheriff's Office)

A mum accused of murdering her toddler twins could face execution in a US state that has not put a prisoner to death for 14 years and has recently made firing squads the primary execution method.

‌



‌



Andrea Shaw, 23, pleaded not guilty to two counts of first-degree murder after her daughter Dallas and son Tyson were found dead in the bed they shared. The children were just 18 months old when they died at their home in Payette, Idaho, on May 1, 2025.

‌



Prosecutors alleged Shaw smothered the twins, though she claims their deaths were linked to vaccinations. Now, months after her arrest, prosecutors have confirmed they will seek the death penalty.

‌



To see more of the stories you love from The Mirror and to find them easily in Google then make us your preferred source. Free and easy-to-do, just click on the link here to find more from The Mirror at the top of your feed.

View 2 Images Shaw and her husband appeared on a podcast produced by Children's Health Defence, an anti-vaccine organisation (Image: CHD TV/ Youtube)

‌



Robert F Kennedy's granddaughter Kyle dies aged 42 six years after spinal cord injury left her paralysed READ MORE :

The decision was outlined in a court filing on Friday, ahead of her trial scheduled for January. Her lawyer Joe Filicetti rejected the prosecution’s case, saying: “There is no chance that a jury is going to find this case beyond a reasonable doubt.”

Idaho has not executed a prisoner since 2012, meaning Shaw could potentially become the first person put to death there since then. However, she has not been convicted or sentenced, and other prisoners remain on the state’s death row.

‌



The state recently made firing squads its primary execution method in July. That followed an abandoned attempt to execute convicted murderer Thomas Creech by lethal injection in 2024, when officials failed to establish a suitable vein.

In a separate filing on Monday, prosecutors argued that the allegations against Shaw met the conditions required to pursue capital punishment. They alleged she showed “exceptional depravity” and “utter disregard for human life”, according to court documents reported by the New York Times.

‌



For a death sentence to be imposed, a jury would have to find her guilty and determine beyond a reasonable doubt that at least one statutory aggravating factor had been proved. Shaw was arrested in June, more than a year after the twins’ deaths. Days after losing them, she appeared alongside her husband Nathaniel on a podcast produced by Children’s Health Defense, an anti-vaccine organisation.

During the interview, she claimed the children became unwell after receiving hepatitis A, DTaP and flu vaccinations. She said: “They were okay. They took a nap when we got home. For the rest of the evening it was business as usual.”

‌



Shaw claimed the twins became lethargic the next day, developed diarrhoea and had a blue tinge around their lips. She said they were taken to hospital and later discharged. She said they were discharged after a few days, but she later found them dead at home.

She previously said: “They looked as if they had gone in their sleep. I flipped over Tyson to try and shake him awake, then I immediately grabbed my phone to dial 911. Then I flipped Dallas over and found her the same way.”

‌



Payette County prosecutor Mike Duke previously rejected her account of vaccine-related deaths, telling the court: “This is not a vaccine case.” The prosecutor disputed her explanation, saying a forensic pathologist had excluded vaccinations as the cause of death.

According to his court filing, the autopsies identified pulmonary vascular congestion - a build-up of blood and fluid within the lungs’ vessels. Investigators had also excluded heat and carbon monoxide poisoning. Mike alleged Shaw changed her account during the investigation and argued that smothering was “the only reasonable explanation for why both would die at the same time.”

Article continues below

Her defence team disputed the suffocation allegations and indicated it would continue arguing that the twins suffered vaccine injuries. Shaw remained in custody in Payette County while awaiting the trial scheduled in January.

News.title: Man charged with murder of Alisha Samuels, 26, in Manchester as police issue update
News.content:
Man charged with murder of Alisha Samuels, 26, in Manchester as police issue update

Alisha Samuels, 26, was found with fatal stab wounds in the Newton Heath area of Manchester after locals reported hearing a disturbance outside in the early hours

View 2 Images Alisha Samuels was 26 (Image: MEN Media)

A 26-year-old man has been charged with the murder of Alisha Samuels at a home in Manchester.

Alisha, also 26, died after she was found with fatal stab wounds in Newton Heath on Thursday.

Lawrence Johnson of Dorking Avenue, Manchester has now been charged with her murder and also the attempted murder of a man. Both incidents were allegedly in Dorking Avenue.

Detective Chief Inspector Justin Bryant, of Greater Manchester Policer, said: "We are continuing to work on establishing the full circumstances of Alisha’s tragic death and to provide Alisha's family with some answers.

"We have now charged a man, but our investigation is not over. I'd like to thank those that have called and supported our investigation thus far, your reports are always taken seriously and prove vital to our work. I urge others who may have information, no matter how small, to please come forward."

View 2 Images Heartbroken friends have paid tribute to Alisha Samuels (Image: @alishasamuels2/TikTok)

Emergency services were called to Dorking Avenue at around 2am after neighbours reported hearing "screaming and shouting" outside.

Devastated friends have shared tributes to Alisha online. "How is this real life? How am I going to live without speaking to you every day with all of my problems?" Aimee Quinn wrote on Facebook. "I can’t believe I'm never going to hear your daft one liners or belly laugh with you again, nor more holidays and all the plans we had to travel the world together.

"You were more of a sister to me than a friend, a good listener and beautiful inside and out. I love you forever and a day my gorgeous girl."

Article continues below

Another pal wrote: "Oh Alisha, from the minute I met you, I knew you were special. I loved you from the start. You were one of the kindest, funniest people I’ve ever met and I’ll always be grateful I got to know you."

News.title: Furious Trump blasts reporter at White House press conference - 'I'm not playing'
News.content:
Furious Trump blasts reporter at White House press conference - 'I'm not playing'

Donald Trump has furiously snapped at a reporter while taking questions at the White House, telling them: 'You had better be careful!'

View Image Donald Trump snapped at a reporter at the White House (Image: Sky News)

US President Donald Trump has responded furiously to a question at a White House press conference, warning a UK reporter "I don't know who the hell you are, but you better be careful."

‌



‌



The tense exchange came as the US President took questions in the Oval Office after launching a new $25million incentive programme aimed at encouraging people to report suspected fraud against the federal government.

‌



Trump had been discussing the war in Ukraine and his administration's past support for Kyiv when he suddenly turned his attention to someone among the assembled media.

‌



He snapped: "Hey, I'm not playing. I don't know who the hell you are, but you better be careful. Go ahead."

Content cannot be displayed without consent

"Go ahead," he added as he turned to another question.

‌



The reporter was Andrew Feinberg, The Independent's White House correspondent, according to Raw Story.

Mr Feinberg responded to the exchange on X moments later, writing: "I had told him exactly who I was not five minutes before this exchange."

‌



Mediaite reported that Mr Feinberg had identified himself to the President earlier in the event when he questioned the administration about its new fraud whistleblower scheme.

The journalist challenged the proposed 1% commission for whistleblowers, pointing to the False Claims Act, which he said had been on the books since 1863 and could allow whistleblowers to receive between 10% and 25%.

‌



Mr Trump defended the proposal, saying: "Because it's a lot of money. And because when they did that, that's a certain type of crime. But nobody ever thought that you could have stolen $2 trillion or whatever the ultimate number is going to be.

Content cannot be displayed without consent

‌



"And at 1%, people will make millions and millions of dollars for turning in what actually is a somewhat routine crime of, you know, of millions of millions. But we're talking about we're talking about billions and actually probably trillions of dollars."

Mr Vance also challenged Mr Feinberg over the question, calling it "fundamentally dishonest".

‌



He said: "First of all, I think that's a fundamentally dishonest question because over 99% of the fraud that we're finding in the federal government isn't covered by the False Claims Act.

"What the president is saying is he wants all fraud to be the sort of thing where if you find it, if you uncover it, you find evidence and allow us to undo the money, you should be able to benefit, not just the very narrow slice that's covered by the False Claims Act."

Article continues below

Mr Trump then asked: "Who are you?", prompting Mr Feinberg to identify himself and his media outlet.

News.title: Heartbreaking tribute to 'caring' grandmother 'murdered' in her Manchester home as cops issue update
News.content:
Heartbreaking tribute to 'caring' grandmother 'murdered' in her Manchester home as cops issue update

Yvonne Kemp has been named as the woman found dead at a property in Moss Side, Manchester, with her family paying tribute to the grandma "who was loved by all who knew her"

View 2 Images Yvonne Kemp (r) and her partner Tom Grant (Image: MEN)

A woman found dead at her home in Manchester sparking a murder investigation was a "much loved" grandma says her family.

Emergency services rushed to the Moss Side area following reports of a disturbance at a property on Crondall Street just before 1.30pm on Monday.

A 26-year-old woman has been arrested on suspicion of murder and has been detained under the Mental Health Act.

In a heartfelt tribute to Yvonne, her family said: “Yvonne was a much-loved mum, Nana, sister and auntie, known for her caring heart, strength and kindness.

“She was the kind of person who would do anything for anyone, always putting others before herself. She leaves behind a family who love her dearly and memories that will be cherished forever.

“Yvonne will be deeply missed and forever loved by all who knew her.“

View 2 Images A police cordon was put in place in Moss Side (Image: Jason Roberts /Manchester Evening News)

Along with the tribute, the family have shared a photo of Yvonne and her beloved partner, Tom Grant, reported the Manchester Evening News.

A statement from Greater Manchester Police read: "Officers were called to a disturbance at an address on Crondall Street, Manchester shortly before 1.30pm on Monday 19 October 2026.

"Emergency services attended and sadly found the body of a woman. A 26-year-old woman has been arrested on suspicion of murder and has been detained under the Mental Health Act."

Detective Chief Inspector Louise Edwards from GMP's Major Incident Team previously said: “We understand an incident of this nature will cause concern however we would like to reassure the public that we believe this is an isolated incident and there is no wider threat to the community.

“We would ask that people stay away from the scene and we’d like to thank the local community for their patience whilst officers undertake their work.

Article continues below

“If you have any information in relation to this incident, please get in touch via the reporting function on our website, Live Chat or by calling 101 quoting log 1631 of 19.10.26. Alternatively you can speak to Crimestoppers anonymously on 0800 555 111.”

News.title: Ebola virus confirmed in new country as epidemic behind 4,600 deaths spreads
News.content:
Ebola virus confirmed in new country as epidemic behind 4,600 deaths spreads

The Ebola outbreak in the Democratic Republic of the Congo has now led to confirmed cases in four other countries with the latest being Nigeria

View 2 Images Ebola has been found in Nigeria (Image: Getty Images/Science Photo Library RF)

The Democratic Republic of the Congo's fast moving Ebola outbreak has now led to a confirmed case in a fifth country - as the death toll from the epidemic rises to more than 4,600.

‌



‌



Nigeria confirmed an Ebola case in its capital, Abuja, today (Tuesday) after a patient who arrived from Uganda tested positive for the virus, the country's Health Ministry said.

‌



The patient was admitted to a private hospital in Abuja before being diagnosed with Ebola. Health Minister Muhammad Pate said authorities had begun tracing 44 people identified as contacts of the patient.

‌



Authorities in the DRC have confirmed 9,552 cases, according to latest figures, with 4,602 patients dying.

View 2 Images Isolation facilities have been created to receive any Ebola patients in Kenya

‌



RAF Eurofighter Typhoon suddenly declares mid-air emergency near Manchester READ MORE :

Kenya has had nine cases with one death and Uganda 20 with two while one case has been identified in France. Uganda was later declared free of the virus.

Ebola symptoms include bleeding from ears, eyes, nose or mouth. According to the NHS other symptoms include being sick, diarrhoea and tummy pain, a skin rash, yellowing of the skin and eyes and muscle pain.

‌



"We see pockets of Ebola generally going down, but unfortunately geographically it's spreading out," World Health Organization Regional Director for Africa Mohamed Yakub Janabi told The Associated Press in an interview in Beni, eastern Congo, on Friday, prior to the news from Nigeria.

Janabi said one of the biggest challenges has been convincing those who are infected to seek medical assistance, adding that some deaths occur in the community outside of health centres.

Article continues below

The spread of the DRC outbreak, caused by the rare Bundibugyo virus for which there is no approved vaccine or treatment, is fuelled by mass population movements, rebel violence, mistrust and poor working conditions of front-line workers.

It has now reached an eighth province in the country’s north, authorities said on Sunday.

News.title: Andy Burnham praises Daily Mirror awards, says 'best bit of Britain is the people'
News.content:
Andy Burnham praises Daily Mirror awards, says 'best bit of Britain is the people'

Following Monday's Pride of Britain Awards, our inspirational winners were invited to celebrate at a special reception at the Prime Minister’s Downing Street home today

Andy Burnham says having a safe space to open us is "critical infrastructure"

Andy Burnham will be running the Great North Run next year for Pride of Britain winners Andy’s Man Club. The founders of the pioneering men’s suicide prevention charity were among the Pride of Britain Award winners invited to celebrate at a special reception at the Prime Minister’s Downing Street home today.

‌



‌



After presenting the charity’s founders, Elaine Roberts and her son-in-law Luke Ambler, with a Special Recognition award on stage at London’s Grosvenor House Hotel on Monday night, at the amazing Daily Mirror Pride of Britain Awards in partnership with P&O Cruises, Mr Burnham said: “Forget celebrities, the real stars were on the stage.”

‌



Describing the array of extraordinary winners as “down to earth, full of humour” he continued: “The best bit of Britain is the people. If we get Britain pulling together, in the same direction, we'll be unstoppable.”

‌



View 6 Images Our amazing Pride of Britain winners outside No10, with Prime Minister Andy Burnham (Image: Jonathan Buckmasterr)

A massive fan of Andy’s Man Club, he told The Mirror: “I have followed their progress over many years and I do feel a real connection with them - and not just because my name is Andy.

“To present them with an award last night was brilliant. And to say to Elaine and Luke, ‘you've changed so many lives, saved lives, in the name of the son and brother-in-law that you lost’ - it's just an amazing thing for people to do.

‌



“When I was in the Wakefield by-election and Andy's Man Club was going on in the back room, I popped in. I'm a huge supporter of what they do. I would go so far as to say it's critical infrastructure in any community to have a place like that and services like that.”

Andy’s Man Club is a simple, barrier-free space for men to have “a brew and a chat”. Launched by Elaine and Luke, after her son, Andy, took his own life in 2016, aged just 23, his devastated family had no idea that he had been struggling so much.

‌



View 6 Images Justice Minister Jake Richards, Luke Ambler, Elaine Roberts, Andy Burnham, Alfie and Lisa (Image: Lauren Hurley / No10 Downing Street)

But they soon discovered that male suicide is the biggest killer of UK men under 50. Luke said: “The Prime Minister told us that he’s running the Great North Run next year for Andy’s Man Club and it’s a real wow moment for us. Who better to have on board than the leader of the country?”

‌



Andy’s Man Club started as one group meeting with just nine men in Halifax, West Yorkshire, and has now - ten years later - expanded into more than 360 community groups across England, Scotland and Wales, alongside online sessions

Mr Burnham said: “The debate about mental health has changed in this country about a decade ago, with people being more open, but there was still a real lack of places to go and support. And the statutory services couldn't find a way of providing what many people were looking for.

‌



“Andy’s Man Club is a place in the community to open up with people who were in a similar position and talk in a way without judgment or stigma or anything like that.

View 6 Images The Prime Minister with Child of Courage winner Zac Howells (Image: Jonathan Buckmasterr)

‌



“Having been to some of the sessions, it's quite humbling to see men of all ages of different backgrounds, some in tracksuits, some in hi-vis, some in work suits, just sitting down together and talking. It's quite a thing.”

The charity even had an impact on Pride of Britain Special Recognition winner Esther Ghey, who while collecting her own award, told the audience on Monday night how - following the tragic murder of their daughter, Brianna - Andy’s Man Club helped her father Peter Spooner, who turned to them for support.

‌



She and the other Pride of Britain winners were given a hero’s welcome by Mr Burnham and his wife Marie-France van Heel, who praised their bravery. Esther, who has tirelessly campaigned for stricter online safety regulations, smartphone restrictions for minors, and improved youth mental health support, said Brianna would be proud.

Of her award, she said: “This is for Brianna. I like to think she’d be proud of us. I like to think of her looking down on us.”

‌



View 6 Images Andy Burnham with Dr Asif Hasan and Dr Eli Prior (Image: Jonathan Buckmasterr)

Pioneering heart surgeon Asif Hasan spent 36 years saving Britain’s sickest children, and was honoured with a Lifetime Achievement award. He told the Mirror: “As a 12 year old boy, growing up in Pakistan, I never imagined for one moment that I'd be meeting the Prime Minister. It’s a real privilege to be here.

‌



“The walls have so many stories. I love the history. As I walked up the stairs I took my time and looked at all the photographs.” Mr Hasan has performed over 400 transplants and was surprised on stage at the Pride of Britain Awards by 19 of the young people he saved.

Meanwhile, Child of Courage winner, Kirsty Waugh, 12, who has raised nearly £250,000 for research after being diagnosed with a benign brain tumour, aged 10, told The Mirror she was “totally starstruck” meeting the Prime Minister.

‌



She said: “I’m so excited to be here. Andy is great, it’s funny meeting him and realising he is a real person. This building is amazing, everything from the pictures to the chandeliers, it’s like being inside the TV - and the staff keep coming round with canapes and I can’t refuse. I’m full to the brim and I don’t want to go home. I do like being in the spotlight so maybe I could be Prime Minister one day.”

View 6 Images The PM with Esther Ghey, Ellen Roome and Ian Russell (Image: Jonathan Buckmasterr)

‌



Elsewhere, fellow Child of Courage winner Zac Howells took home a very special memento of his day at Downing Street, as he got the Prime Minister to sign his scrapbook. “Dear Zac, You are the pride of Wales and the pride of Britain,” Mr Burnham wrote, signing his name at the bottom.

Zac, 13, who won his award for steering his mum’s car to safety when she passed out at the wheel last year, said: “I’m going to keep it in my bedroom with my Pride of Britain award. I can’t believe I’m at No10. I’m going back to school tomorrow with quite a story.”

‌



Angela Rayner, Secretary of State for Housing, Communities and Local Government, spoke with the brave little lad and his mum, Nicola Crump. She said: “We’re in good hands if the next generation is anything like Zac.”

Calling Pride of Britain “a tonic,” she continued: “Pride of Britain is honouring people who do extraordinary things every single day. It gives a big dose of hope. It reminds us too what our communities are about. Often we hear challenging stories about division, anti-social behaviour. But hearing these stories and seeing what people are able to overcome, it's what we all need to hear sometimes.”

‌



View 6 Images Child of Courage winner Kirsty Waugh with Marie-France van Heel, wife of PM Andy Burnham (Image: Jonathan Buckmasterr)

And Mr Burnham agreed. He said: “These guys are the epitome of hope. They filled the room with hope last night and they fill the country when it's broadcast on ITV. They give you hope in tough times.

‌



“What it shows though, is the British public have not changed. They're still as brilliant as they ever were, and this country is full of people who will make a sacrifice in a heartbeat, even if it puts themselves at risk, or will turn private grief to public good. That's who we are.

“Every year, Pride of Britain reminds you of that, and that's why it's such an incredible thing.”

Article continues below

*Don’t miss The Daily Mirror Pride of Britain Awards on Thursday 22 October at 8pm on ITV1 and ITVX.

News.title: Revolut and Lloyds down: Google Cloud outage hits banks as cards 'declined'
News.content:
Major apps and websites, including those of banks Revolut, Halifax and Lloyds, were hit by disruption today amid a Google Cloud outage in western Europe

A Google Cloud outage has disrupted a range of online services across the UK, leaving Revolut customers unable to make payments for hours.

The apps and websites of Revolut, HSBC, Rightmove, Royal Mail and Lloyds Banking Group brands Lloyds Bank, Bank of Scotland and Halifax, among other companies, experienced issues on Tuesday morning, according to outage-tracking website Downdetector.

Revolut appeared to be down for thousands of customers, with many taking to social media to complain that their cards were being declined and they could not access their accounts through the app or website.

Google Cloud said the outage in its western Europe region was caused by a "power event", which had been "mitigated" by lunchtime on Tuesday. The companies mentioned have yet to confirm that their service disruptions were linked to the outage.

News.title: Tommy Robinson trial hears messages sent to journalist left him fearing 'vigilante attack'
News.content:
Tommy Robinson trial hears messages sent to journalist left him fearing 'vigilante attack'

Journalist Jacob Dirnhuber has told a court how he feared for his safety and stayed in a hotel with his partner and dog after allegedly receiving messages from Tommy Robinson's X account

View 2 Images Tommy Robinson is on trial for allegedly harassing journalists (Image: Jeff Moore/Press Association)

A journalist says he was left fearing a "vigilante attack" after receiving messages from Tommy Robinson's X account, a court has heard.

‌



‌



Robinson, whose real name is Stephen Yaxley-Lennon, is on trial for allegedly harassing journalists Jacob Dirnhuber and Andrew Young, causing them to worry for their safety in August 2024, after they worked on a story about him while he was on holiday in Cyprus.

‌



The 43-year-old activist, who founded the English Defence League, entered not guilty pleas to two charges of harassment causing fear of violence in July last year.

‌



Mr Dirnhuber, an editor at the Daily Mail, told Southwark Crown Court how he, along with his partner and their dog, decided to leave their home after Robinson's X account allegedly shared images of him and messaged him photographs of an unknown woman.

The court was told that on the evening of August 6, 2024, Mr Dirnhuber received direct messages via X from Robinson’s X account, which said: "Your bosses need to contact me, Jacob."

View 2 Images A court sketch of Robinson (Image: Elizabeth Cook/the Press Association)

‌



In a witness statement read out in court by prosecutor Ben Holt, Mr Dirnhuber said: "Attached to this message was an image of a woman by an open window." He added: "I do not know who the woman in the image is, or where the image was taken."

Later that evening, the journalist took the decision to stay in a hotel, he said. "Nothing quite like this has ever happened to me," his statement continued. "To my knowledge, I have never been tracked down to an address."

‌



On the impact of what allegedly happened he said: “It made me scared to go out in public, it made me scared to go to my own house, it made me feel guilty about how it had affected my loved ones. Even now, when I step out my front door, I’m aware I’m at risk of a vigilante attack.”

Mr Dirnhuber claimed he felt he would be looking over his shoulder "for a long time” saying: “I have the knowledge that Tommy Robinson knows my address and my last name is very identifiable. I feel vulnerable. I feel I will be looking over my shoulder for a long time.”

‌



Robinson is accused of making a telephone call on August 5, 2024, in which he allegedly told Mr Young he would visit his house, saying: “I’m coming to get you.”

An image from Mr Young’s ring doorbell camera was shown to the jury which captured a grey Audi that had been parked outside his house shortly before he returned from Cyprus.

‌



His statement read: “The driveway and path to our front door is quite overgrown, so there is really only one spot on the road which has a view all the way to our front door.”

Mr Young added: “I was worried and concerned, I felt that my family was under threat and I was fearful of what might happen next.”

‌



Mr Young alleged Robinson became “increasingly menacing” after he called his personal number.

His statement read: “I told him repeatedly that I didn’t want to engage with him and he should direct any matters to the Daily Mail legal department. His tone became increasingly menacing raising his voice, swearing and shouting.

‌



“I kept telling him the same thing which only seemed to make him more angry.”

Mr Young said Robinson “kept screaming at me” as he told him he had been researching his family.

‌



“I told him several times that I regarded what he was saying as threatening behaviour and that I would be reporting it,” the statement said.

“He said that he would be coming round to my house to see me and that I would have to move house.”

‌



The court previously heard Robinson used “bully-boy, intimidatory tactics” to frighten the journalists with a series of posts and direct messages on social media platform X.

The court heard the activist told police his hotel in Cyprus was "overrun with news crews" following stories published in the Daily Mail and MailOnline.

Article continues below

The trial, expected to last five days, continues.

News.title: Two men re-arrested on suspicion of assisting Iran intelligence after RAF Fairford incident
News.content:
Two men have been re-arrested after an incident near RAF Fairford last month, counter-terrorism police have said.

A 24-year-old UK national, and a 25-year-old dual UK-Iranian national, are being held on suspicion of assisting a foreign intelligence service under Section 3 of the National Security Act 2023, with police saying the investigation relates to Iran.

Police had been alerted to three suspicious vehicles near the US airbase in Gloucestershire in the early hours of 27 September - a major incident was subsequently declared and dozens of homes evacuated.

Seven men in total have been arrested as part of the counter-terror police investigation.

Gloucestershire Police said it had received a call about "three suspicious vehicles" travelling towards RAF Fairford at 00:45 BST on 27 September.

A bomb disposal team was deployed to the village to examine a number of vehicles.

Petrol was found in three vans near the airbase and five men were arrested.

They had been initially arrested on suspicion of committing offences under the Explosives Act and then further arrested on suspicion of preparation of a terrorist act.

Police later said they did not find "improvised explosive devices".

The re-arrests announced on Tuesday relate to a 24-year-old man who was initially arrested on 27 September near the base and a 25-year-old who was arrested on suspicion of preparation of terrorist acts days later on 1 October in the borough of Westminster.

The other five men - who also include a 22-year-old British national arrested in Westminster on 6 October - remain on police bail.

The head of National Counter Terrorism Policing, Assistant Commissioner Laurence Taylor said: "This is very much a live investigation, and our evidence gathering continues, but at this time our position remains the same; we consider it highly likely that there is Iranian state involvement.

"Our investigators are continuing to examine what that level of involvement was and the ambition behind it."

The officer added that national security investigations can take time to progress due to their sensitive nature.

"Our specialist teams have been working tirelessly to interrogate the many lines of enquiry involved in this hugely complex investigation," he said.

Days after the incident, Prime Minister Andy Burnham told the BBC there were "strong indications" Iran had played a part in the incident.

He did not provide further details at the time.

Iran has previously denied any involvement.

RAF Fairford has been used as a forward operating location by the US Air Force (USAF) for decades.

In recent months, the US has flown B-1 and B-52 bombers from the base to the Middle East, after the UK approved a request for Fairford to be used for defensive strikes against Iran.

In the week after the incident, it emerged that the US had pulled its bombers out of the base and returned them to America.

US President Donald Trump said the aircraft were removed due to "some threats" to the base without giving specific details.

Vice-President JD Vance said it was done out of an "abundance of caution".

News.title: Government failings allowed Covid 'to spread like wildfire' in care homes, inquiry finds
News.content:
Government failures in care settings created an environment that allowed Covid to spread like wildfire, an official inquiry has said.

The sixth report from the Covid inquiry said the care sector appeared to be "something of an afterthought" in the early stages of the pandemic and there was no "protective ring" put around homes as claimed by ministers at the time.

There were more than 43,000 recorded deaths involving Covid in care homes between March 2020 and July 2022.

The 287-page report also highlighted shortages of PPE for carers and criticised the way hospital patients were discharged into care homes.

It said limits on visits caused enormous harm to residents and their loved ones, though it blamed this on care homes themselves.

Around 1.5 million adults were either living in care homes or receiving support in their own homes when Covid hit.

Action to protect them came too late, causing devastating consequences, the inquiry said.

Chair Baroness Hallet said a lack of testing, PPE and pre-pandemic planning combined with policy decisions early on "created an environment in which the virus could spread like wildfire".

"At the critical early stages of the pandemic, not enough was done to protect those living and working in care homes," she said.

"The overriding focus of the UK government and devolved administrations was on protecting hospitals."

News.title: BBC Three, BBC Scotland and Radio 4 Extra broadcast channels to close
News.content:
BBC Three, which is aimed at young audiences and launched hits such as Fleabag, Normal People and Gavin & Stacey, previously moved online in 2016, but was reinstated as a TV channel in 2022.

BBC Scotland launched as a channel in 2019, broadcasting a variety of Scottish programming including news, sport, documentaries and entertainment.

However, some of the shows that air on the two networks, such as Two Doors Down on BBC Scotland and Sort Your Life Out on BBC Three, are repeats of episodes originally broadcast on other more mainstream BBC channels.

Both networks currently only broadcast TV programming in the evenings, although BBC Scotland simulcasts BBC Radio Scotland during the rest of the day.

The BBC said that the network's nightly programme Reporting Scotland: News at Seven will not move to BBC iPlayer and will cease when the linear channel closes.

Audiences will continue to be served by BBC Scotland's wider news offering, including Reporting Scotland, The Sunday Show, Radio Scotland Breakfast, Debate Night and Scotcast, the corporation said.

While Radio 4 Extra does air some original programming, its schedule is predominantly made up of archive content, much of which is available on BBC Sounds.

Sir Peter Bazalgette, former chairman of ITV and production company Endemol, told BBC News: "This is a modest and pretty well-judged package.

"The essence of it is it protects the spending on content, it really cuts money in the distribution of programmes, and it really had to happen because the BBC has lost 30% of its revenue in 10 years."

But entertainment trade union Equity said Tuesday's announcement "does not signal a thriving BBC, and we are concerned about the UK's preeminent public service broadcaster's ability to meet its duties to the fullest".

Affected staff were told about the changes on Tuesday, although the proposed closure of BBC Scotland and BBC Three had been reported by some media outlets in recent weeks.

The BBC is aiming to cut between 1,800 and 2,000 jobs - almost one in 10 - in an attempt to save Â£500m over two years as it faces "significant financial pressures".

Around 550 job closures have already been announced in news, while more than 30 job cuts have so far been announced for BBC Sport.

The newly appointed director of BBC News, Rachel Jupp, announced on Tuesday that a further Â£5.5m of savings were being proposed, which would represent the closure of around 100 roles.

Meanwhile, several high-profile BBC TV series have been cancelled altogether in recent weeks.

RuPaul's Drag Race UK, Blankety Blank, Celebrity Mastermind, Live at the Apollo, Football Focus, Ski Sunday and Radio 4âs The World Tonight and You & Yours are among the programmes the BBC has dropped so far.

News.title: King praises Strait of Hormuz peace efforts at glittering banquet
News.content:
The US and Israel launched wide-ranging strikes on Iran in February, killing the country's supreme leader and sparking the ongoing Iran war.

The Strait of Hormuz, one of the world's most vital shipping lanes, has been effectively closed since then.

King Charles, Queen Camilla, Prince William and Catherine and Princess Anne were among the royals on duty at Windsor for the state visit.

It was the first state banquet for Prime Minister Andy Burnham, who was seated next to the Omani academic and novelist, Jokha Alharthi.

It was a table laden with elaborate candelabra and polished decorations, with five glasses per setting, and even the surface of the salt had an imprint of the cypher of King Charles.

The hot summer meant a bumper crop of pomegranates in the Windsor Castle gardens, and the fruits were placed on the table alongside the floral decorations.

The King's speech, delivered to 160 guests in English with some quotes in Arabic, expressed his approval that his son Prince William had worked on an expedition project alongside the Sultan's son.

"There can be few happier symbols of success than a living relationship being passed from one generation to the next," said the King.

News.title: Elon Musk says Tesla-SpaceX merger would be a 'good idea'
News.content:
Elon Musk has said he likes the idea of a merger of Tesla and SpaceX, two of his most notable companies, and it is under active consideration.

"Do I think it would be a good idea? Yes," Musk said during a call with financial analysts over the quarterly business results of SpaceX on Tuesday.

While Musk noted the certainty of such a merger should not be assumed, and it would need shareholders' support, he said special committees within both companies have been formed to consider it.

"The special committees have not reached agreement on terms of any transaction and there's no guarantee that they will," Musk added. "But I do think there is a lot of merit to merging and a lot to be gained."

With Tesla valued roughly $1.5 trillion and and SpaceX valued at $2 trillion, a combination of the two companies would mark one of the largest mergers in history.

Musk is not included in either of the special committees considering the move, he said, because he is a "conflicted party" as the chief executive of Tesla and of SpaceX.

Even commenting on the possibility of a merger between the two companies, Musk compared to being like "tap dancing through a minefield".

Musk added a merger would ultimately be decided by shareholders. At least 50% of Tesla's shareholders would need to approve the merger, which Musk described as "quite a high hurdle to achieve".
