Sports.title: Former world boxing champion cleared of petrol station assault
Sports.content:
Two-time IBF super-featherweight champion Joe Cordina has been cleared of assaulting a man he punched outside a petrol station; a district judge found Cordina, 34, not guilty of assault

Joe Cordina: Former boxing world champion cleared of assaulting man he punched outside petrol station

Joe Cordina has been cleared of assaulting a man he punched outside a petrol station

Former boxing world champion Joe Cordina has been cleared of assaulting a man he punched outside a petrol station.

A district judge found Cordina, 34, not guilty of assault by beating against Jamie O'Brien, 33, following a trial at Cardiff Magistrates' Court.

The court heard Cordina had been filling up his Land Rover at Pentwyn service station in Cardiff in February when he noticed O'Brien staring at him.

Cordina, a two-time IBF super-featherweight champion, approached O'Brien - who was sitting on the pavement near the station exit - believing he was a fan.

Judge Charlotte Murphy described how O'Brien then "shoulder barged him to the chest and chin", in what she found was a "deliberate assault" on Cordina.

She highlighted that the attack had taken place just two weeks after Cordina had been told by police that there was a threat to his life.

In her ruling, the judge said: "I am satisfied that the defendant believed it was necessary to use force to defend himself.

"I am further satisfied that a single, measured, controlled punch was proportionate in the circumstances.

"It is very easy to consider the defendant's response by considering the CCTV in slow motion, however the defendant had a split second to consider his response to the shoulder barge."

The judge said she accepted Cordina's evidence that he had repeatedly pushed O'Brien "while on the floor to keep him away from him".

"In my view, it was necessary and the force used was proportionate in the circumstances," she added.

"I reject any suggestion that the defendant was retaliating in any way.

"This is a person who has lived in the public eye for many years and has interacted with the public on a daily basis.

"For all of those reasons, the crown has not proved to the criminal standard. I therefore find the defendant not guilty and dismiss the charge."

The judge had previously ruled there was no case to answer in relation to the second charge of assault.

CCTV footage played to the court showed O'Brien pushing Cordina with his shoulder, before Cordina punched him.

O'Brien, from Pentwyn, previously pleaded guilty to a charge of assault by beating.

Police began to investigate the incident after footage was circulated online. The judge ruled on Tuesday there was no evidence that O'Brien knew the person who was filming.

She added that Cordina had approached O'Brien "in good faith", believing he was a fan.

During the trial, Cordina said he initially thought O'Brien wanted a photograph and described how he was accustomed to being recognised four or five times a day.

He told the court he had acted in self-defence because he felt threatened after O'Brien assaulted him.

"He had his hands in his pockets, I don't know what people carry on them these days," Cordina said.

After the case, Cordina's lawyer Nadeem Majid issued a statement to the media.

He said: "Today's verdict is a huge relief for Joe and everybody who is close to him.

"He has always maintained he is innocent throughout this.

"On behalf of Joe, I'd like to thank his family, his friends, his loyal fans, his legal team for their unwavering support through what's clearly been a very difficult time.

"Joe would now like to concentrate on his family and in particular his boxing. We'd all like to see him on the bill in December. Thank you all very much."

Sports.title: Doué and Vitinha burn bright as brittle Barcelona come unstuck against PSG
Sports.content:
Fire, noise, fury, a sense of empty energy. And across town, a football match too.

Do any of these randomly pitched autumnal Champions League fixtures mean anything? Probably not when you’re Paris Saint-Germain and Barcelona, and the only game in town is risk-free TV income and a semi-guaranteed place in the knockout stuff.

But this was still a dazzling occasion at the Parc des Princes as the champions of France and Spain played out a light, open, frictionless, exhibition-style game of football. PSG finished 4-2 winners, having been pegged back to 2-2 at one stage. But this was also a game where the score almost didn’t seem to matter at times, and where the only really hard message was the frailty of the Barcelona backline and PSG’s thrilling attacking energy in these midweek A-games.

“Debris! Debris! DEBRIS!” the insanely loud announcer screamed into his mic before kick-off, what appeared to be a poor-taste tribute to the current state of the nation’s capital, although it may also have been “du bruit”.

In the hours leading up to this game France’s interior minister had specifically ruled out postponing the whole thing due to the ongoing state of civil unrest, the kind of statement that is no doubt intended to sound reassuring, but which also generates its own kind of whiplash.

Paris is burning. Paris is always burning. No, but Paris really is burning this time. The main site of the violence of the last few days is three miles east of the Parc, which lurks by the ring road in one of Paris’s slightly négligé inner quarters, rising up like a vast concrete alien doughnut in between the townhouses.

On matchday it required a degree of cognitive dissonance to take in these two opposing spectacles. On one hand the piles of charred bikes and the mass looting which has, in reassuringly Parisian style, seemed to focus on elite high-fashion brands. Chanel will rue the day.

View image in fullscreen Désiré Doué strikes to give PSG the lead in the first half. Photograph: Julien de Rosa/AFP/Getty Images

And in the middle of this Paris also hosted this glittering treat of a football match, stuffed with so many throwaway little delicacies, like an elite artisan patisserie. Before kick-off there were leaping tongues of flame, a laser show spectacular, and an awe-inspiringly vast tifo at one end showing a ghoulish PSG serial killer type attacking the Barcelona badge with his blood-soaked chainsaw. The message here seemed to be: we are confident. We believe in our process. And we will hack you to death.

This was a high-grade, disarmingly open game at the start. For Hansi Flick’s Barcelona it represented a genuine test of method, an elite team that plays with a studied disregard for some of the tenets of positional defensive play. We will press forward and trust what lies behind. We will also give up on the basic idea of marking from the kick-off, as it turned out.

With one minute gone PSG should have scored. A quick passing move from right to left put Khvicha Kvaratskhelia in space. His shot pinged off a post and back to an offside Ousmane Dembélé, who shinned wide of an open goal.

There was a fury to PSG in those opening minutes, the front players finding angles and free channels. Pedri and Marc Bernal in central midfield took a while to settle for Barça. Bernal is pure La Masia, a baby-faced 19-year-old Catalan, misleadingly so, as he also has the physique of a rugby union flanker. And Pedri is of course the kind of footballer who glides through these occasions, so casual you half expect to look down and notice he’s playing in flip-flops and holding a Calippo.

Before long Barcelona were making chances of their own, Dani Olmo setting off on a couple of surging deep runs, Anthony Gordon almost getting on the end of a cutback.

View image in fullscreen Xavi Espart scores his first Champions League goal to equalise for Barcelona at 1-1. Photograph: David Ramos/Uefa/Getty Images

João Cancelo was booked with 16 minutes gone for a lunge on Désiré Doué, a disastrous state of affairs for any full-back faced with this nightmare of feints and fast-twitch feet. And two minutes later Dembélé was off, injured chasing the ball, replaced by Ferran Torres. Maybe he should play a bit more, get match fit.

Still the game just zinged from end to end. Raphinha had a close-range shot blocked by Matvey Safonov after a nice pass from Gordon. PSG had three shots blocked or saved in the space of six seconds on 28 minutes, Joan García saving brilliantly low down.

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to Football Daily Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

And on 37 minutes PSG deservedly took the lead. The goal was in keeping with the game, expertly hi-tech but also oddly easy and open. Lamine Yamal tried a clever chipped clearance. João Neves claimed the ball back. It fell to Doué, and he was able to jink inside, feel the space around him, and shoot low inside the post.

PSG were bossing this by now, Kvaratskhelia running up and down the gears on the left. By the break Barcelona were hanging on, overrun in midfield and straining to contain PSG on the flanks.

The start of the second half was more of the same: mobile, relentless, high grade product, lovely attacking interchanges, large spaces in the Barcelona backline. Doué forced another fine close-range save, played in by Vitinha.

View image in fullscreen Vitinha fires in from the edge of the box as PSG retake the lead late on. Photograph: Dave Winter/Shutterstock

On 54 minutes Barcelona equalised. Xavi Espart got it, galloping through the left side of the PSG defence and smashing a shot into the net off the hands of Safonov. The PA announcer gave the goal to Lamine Yamal, because, well, great branding. But it was Espart’s first in Europe, the second of his career. He’s 19, hyper-versatile, another Catalan youth-team player.

Before long Barça had made a triple substitution. One of those entering the field was Rodri. Would this see order restored? For a while it did feel as though Rodri was the only grown-up on the pitch, as Barcelona did started to dominate possession and territory.

But PSG always have tools to hurt you. Doué sliced open the right hand side again and crossed for Fabián Ruiz to hit the post from six yards out. From the corner Lucas Hernandez was given space to leap and produce a wonderful finish, thumped off the meaty part of the forehead high into the top corner.

Six minutes later it was 2-2. This was a strange goal, scored by Lamine Yamal after a wonderful run in from the right and a lofted near-post finish that in the moment either looked like a mistake from Safonov or a moment of pure invention.

And two minutes after that it was 3-2 to PSG as the game just kept on running to its own speed. It was another brilliant goal, this time a controlled first time shot from Vitinha, seizing on a bouncing ball near the edge of the box. Fabián Ruiz added a fourth four minutes from the end as PSG just kept coming.

Sports.title: Mac Allister double sparks Liverpool’s thrilling comeback win against Villarreal
Sports.content:
Andoni Iraola and Iñigo Pérez parked their long and close friendship in the buildup to the Champions League duel between two old Athletic Bilbao teammates. They will have a humdinger of a contest to dissect when communications are restored. Liverpool, driven by Alexis Mac Allister and ignited by Rio Ngumoha, recovered from two goals down against Villarreal to maintain their 100% record in the competition in emphatic style.

Mac Allister struck twice as Liverpool fought back from a tepid start to record a third successive win in all competitions. They were given a scare when Tani Oluwaseyi volleyed in a late third for Villarreal but were well deserving of their latest impressive result.

The regular phone calls between Iraola and Pérez had eased off as their first competitive confrontation as coaches approached. Iraola could have advised his close friend to bring a coat had they kept in touch. It had rained incessantly in Liverpool all day yet the Villarreal head coach opted for a short-sleeved polo shirt on the touchline. A brave move, although he would have been warmed by his team’s potent start against a much-changed host.

Liverpool’s expensive attacking trio of Florian Wirtz, Alexander Isak and Bradley Barcola were all on the bench as Iraola made six changes to the side that beat Brentford on Saturday. A fourth game in 10 days explained the omissions of Wirtz and Barcola, who had featured heavily in the previous three, while Isak’s workload was being carefully managed after his recent thigh injury. The rotation resulted in a second successive Champions League start for Trey Nyoni and Ryan Gravenberch shifting forward into Wirtz’s number ten role.

View image in fullscreen Alexis Mac Allister heads home to score Liverpool’s opening goal. Photograph: Allstar Picture Library Ltd/Ed Sykes/Apl/Sportsphoto

Iraola’s rejigged team did not have time to find their rhythm before falling behind. An error-strewn start by Van Dijk was responsible, and also in keeping with a ponderous opening half hour from Liverpool in which Villarreal passed their way around Anfield with style and precious little resistance.

The Liverpool captain presented Georges Mikautadze with an opportunity as early as the second minute when he misjudged a long clearance out of defence by Renato Veiga. Van Dijk’s poor touch almost released the Georgia international striker through on goal but Jérémy Jacquet was across quickly to close off that route. Van Dijk’s second slip followed moments later, and this time there was no reprieve. The defender attempted to head another Veiga long ball back into the safe arms of Alisson. He found Mikautadze instead and Villarreal’s number nine pounced expertly, controlling well before rolling the ball under the Liverpool keeper. There were apologies all round from Van Dijk.

Villarreal doubled their lead with a goal that encapsulated the start made by both teams – the visitors passing their way through Liverpool’s midfield and picking holes in their high defensive line, with the home side slow to react. Pape Gueye, Alberto Moleiro and Nathan Saliba all combined to send their rampaging left back, Sergi Cardona, clear of the Liverpool backline. Played onside by Kostas Tsimikas, the full-back beat Alisson with a finish a striker would have been happy with.

Cardona’s defending was much less impressive as Liverpool, stung more by their own performance than the groans of the Anfield crowd, clawed their way back into the contest before half-time. The recovery commenced when Mac Allister rose superbly to meet a Tsimikas corner and flicked an unstoppable header into the unguarded side of Peter Gulacsi’s goal. The former Liverpool keeper could only stand and admire the midfielder’s header, while asking where a Villarreal challenge was.

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to Football Daily Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

View image in fullscreen Ronald Araújo heads home Liverpool’s second goal in first-half stoppage time. Photograph: Jason Cairnduff/Action Images/Reuters

Villarreal had bigger questions to answer when their once comfortable lead vanished entirely with the final kick of the first half. The visitors had dealt with another corner from Tsimikas when Rio Ngumoha gathered possession and clipped a cross towards the far post. Cardona checked his surroundings, then inexplicably let the ball bounce behind him. And right into the spot where Ronald Araújo was lurking. The on-loan defender headed home for the second successive week in the Champions League and celebrated with a mass pile-on with fans in the Anfield Road Stand.

Araújo failed to appear for the second half as Iraola introduced Wirtz and moved Gravenberch once again, this time to right back. The Liverpool head coach must have been sorely tempted to shake things up more, such was the paucity of his team’s first half display, but his half-time switch and demands sufficed. Liverpool improved vastly after the restart with Ngumoha and Wirtz a constant threat. Pérez’s substitutions were less impactful and the former Newcastle forward Ayoze Pérez was the object of his ire on several occasions.

Ngumoha took the acclaim of the Kop after creating Mac Allister’s second of the night with a sparkling run down the right. It was some one-two that brought Liverpool the lead. Mac Allister floated a pass out to the 18-year-old winger, whose first touch brought the ball under control and took him away from Cardona in the same movement. He then left the substitute Juan Foyth in his wake before pulling back a pass from the byline for the incoming midfielder to smash a shot in off the underside of Gulacsi’s crossbar.

Wirtz completed the comeback, continuing his own recent improvement, after Tsimikas and Cody Gakpo had combined to create space for the playmaker inside the area. The Germany international drilled a clinical left-foot finish inside the Villarreal keeper’s far corner.

Sports.title: Foden hat-trick helps Manchester City cut through noise and crush AEK Athens
Sports.content:
Enzo Maresca has called for Manchester City to make their own noise on the pitch to drown out the cacophony surrounding them but maybe a quiet night at the Etihad Stadium was what they needed all along. AEK Athens were easily dispatched in a businesslike manner, as Phil Foden announced his return to form with a hat-trick to get City’s Champions League campaign back on track after being pummelled by Paris Saint-Germain.

The match was uneven throughout as Foden shone on the wing and later down the middle, with goals from Elliot Anderson and Rayan Cherki helping to ease City to victory in front of half-full stands. Stavros Pilios’s consolation was more a reward for the boisterous fans in yellow and black than for the overall efforts of the visitors.

Enzo Maresca took the calculated risk of eight changes from the win over Ipswich, although that did mean a return to the starting lineup for Enzo Fernández and Elliot Anderson while Erling Haaland was left on the bench. His replacement, with senior options lacking, was the 17-year-old academy graduate, Floyd Samba, whose only other senior football came in a Carabao Cup win against Norwich, when he scored twice on debut.

The game had not captured the imagination with the stands having huge gaps of blue, which is understandable amid the constant churn of fixtures for City and the cost of following the club. AEK was seen by many fans as a game that could be missed, in expectation of a simple victory over a team lacking global superstars. The visiting supporters were far more animated, filling a corner of the ground over three tiers where they created a party from two hours before kick-off.

Inspiration was required from those on the pitch with the home faithful subdued, which was provided by Fernández clipping a free-kick on to the bar and Anderson following up to whack the rebound into an empty net in the 12th minute. The celebrations lacked enthusiasm, acknowledged with a nod of approval.

View image in fullscreen Elliot Anderson fires Manchester City ahead from close range. Photograph: Scott Heppell/Reuters

AEK had no desire to capitulate and created some promising moves without ever threatening the City box, lacking quality when it mattered most. The Greek side had half of the possession in the opening quarter but the hosts, although not at their best, turned on the style when required, going from static to full steam in seconds to create chances.

The Champions League debutant Allan was City’s most entertaining offering, providing direct running and skill on the left wing. The Brazilian was a menace and almost marked his second home appearance with a goal but his vicious shot clipped the bar and flew into the stands. With seven matches in 21 days for City, games like this gave an opportunity for fringe players to impress and Allan was eager to make his mark.

City were able to take control, passing the ball around with ease and holding AEK at arm’s length, while Foden and Rayan Cherki tried to work their fleet-footed magic in tight spaces. Eventually the calmness in the final third was rewarded when Foden finished after neat work on the right from Rico Lewis, as the two academy products combined. The full-back has struggled for minutes in recent times and almost left the club 16 months ago but showed he can provide something as an attacking threat from defence.

With City comfortable, complacency kicked in and Abdukodir Khusanov reflected the crowd by drifting off, giving Zini the chance to turn him and slip a pass into Stavros Pilios who thrashed the ball across Gianluigi Donnarumma. The AEK fans erupted, while their counterparts pondered how City had been dragged back into a fight, having previously been impenetrable.

Natural order was restored by Cherki, a neat trick inside the box and a precise shot into the corner did the rest. It was an occasion for the maverick Frenchman to be a leader, making the difference in critical moments and he offered up evidence of his capabilities with the finish, creating breathing space in the process.

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to Football Daily Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

View image in fullscreen Rayan Cherki restores Manchester City’s two-goal advantage. Photograph: Martin Rickett/PA

If the plan was to test life without Haaland, the loss of Antoine Semenyo to injury for eight weeks created a problem for Maresca. Samba’s deployment ranked somewhere between plan C and D but the teenager was an adept decoy, allowing the more experienced around him to show off their repertoire. Samba acquitted himself well but whether he is a suitable replacement for the Norwegian will remain unknown until City face more competitive opposition.

City were starting to showboat as AEK realised resistance was futile. Cherki knocked it long for Lewis to control into the path of Foden, who provided a sublime first-time finish into the top corner from the edge of the box. The exceptional goals were racking up on what felt like an otherwise mundane night.

On a positive night for City’s academy, Ryan McAidoo came off the bench to send in a perfect cross for Foden to complete his treble with a striker’s instinct, earning the biggest cheer of the night. Foden scored his first goal since mid-December at the weekend but the confidence is clearly flooding back to a player who has spent too long watching on from the sidelines, especially considering the talent he possesses.

Sports.title: Carrick insists Manchester United board back him after Ten Hag points to ‘toxic culture’
Sports.content:
Michael Carrick believes Manchester United’s board continue to back him, although the manager admits he must start winning matches to keep his job. Carrick also denied there is a toxic culture at the club, after Erik ten Hag’s claim there had been when he was manager.

Carrick’s side travel to Como on Wednesday for their third Champions League game, aiming for a third victory of the season in all competitions. Sunday’s 1-1 draw at Leeds left United 13th in the Premier League, having won only once.

Their only other success was last month’s 4-0 home win against Sabah, of Azerbaijan, in the Champions League. Carrick was asked on Tuesday if he feels backed by the executive.

“Yeah – why wouldn’t I?” said the 45-year-old. “I’m in this position, I have a really good relationship with everybody at the club. We’ve got to win games of football and that’s what we’re striving to do.”

Despite the poor results Carrick has not sought reassurance from the hierarchy. “Certainly not. I don’t need any reassurance,” he said. “It’s pretty clear. I know the role, my responsibilities. I know we’ve got to win ­football games for everything to flow and ­everything to fall into place.”

Ten Hag was Carrick’s predecessor from April 2022 to October 2024. During his tenure the Dutchman claimed that the executive did not support him regarding some disciplinary ­matters. In early 2024 Jim ­Ratcliffe, who had recently become the largest ­single minority stakeholder, assumed control of the football department.

View image in fullscreen Erik ten Hag and Cristiano Ronaldo in 2022. ‘He let the team down, and he let me down,’ the former Manchester United manager said. Photograph: Ed Sykes/Action Images/Reuters

“They are continuing the toxic culture, they fuel it, they give power to the players,” Ten Hag told the Athletic, referring to his time in charge.

Ten Hag claimed that Cristiano Ronaldo “let the team down” ­when the Dutchman was managing United. The ­forward’s second spell at the club featured him walking out twice.

“He let the team down and he let me down, because we planned with him,” said Ten Hag. He also questioned ­Ronaldo’s commitment, saying that after United were beaten 4-0 at Brentford in the second game of his tenure, the ­Portuguese refused to complete a run in training.

“I confronted him with this,” Ten Hag said. “Many times I say: ‘Ronnie, everyone wants to work for you to bring you in the right position, but if you can’t bring yourself in the box, you can’t score.”

Carrick, who became interim manager in January and was appointed permanently in May, was asked if he has encountered toxicity at United. “No, I haven’t. The players, the staff, they’ve given us everything that they could give,” he said. “I couldn’t be happier with the togetherness.”

Ten Hag led United to the FA Cup in 2024, but claimed the owners then failed to meet promises made during talks that led to him agreeing a contract extension.

He said: “They promised me ­loyalty, they promised me backing, they promised communication, that we get aligned. We spoke about the issues. But the promises, they didn’t keep. “I said: ‘No selling Scott ­McTominay.’ And in the end they sold him. I got, of course, very embarrassed and disappointed.”

Carrick was asked if Ten Hag’s comments about the leadership raised any red flags. In answering he mentioned Jason Wilcox, the director of football, and the chief executive, Omar Berrada.

“Not for me, that’s Erik’s opinion, it’s totally wrong for me to comment or get involved, it’s nothing to do with me at that stage. We’re pretty stable. There’s certain conversations we have that we’re really clear with, with Jason with Omar, the owners, and to the players. It’s really important we’re all pulling in the same direction.”

Carrick will be without nine players for Como: Leny Yoro is ­suspended and Ayden Heaven is ill, while Luke Shaw, Lisandro Martínez, Kobbie Mainoo, Marcus Rashford, Benjamin Sesko, Patrick Dorgu and Manuel Ugarte are injured.

The absence of five frontline defenders (Yoro, Shaw, Heaven, Martínez and Dorgu) will force Carrick to field an unfamiliar backline that may include Matthijs de Ligt, who has not played since last November due to a back problem. An appearance for the 19-year-old left-back, Harry Amass, is also being considered.

There is a severe weather warning for lightning and rain in Como on Wednesday that may affect the 5.45pm kick-off.

Sports.title: Arsenal’s David Raya hits back at ‘boring’ label as Arteta defends side’s style of play
Sports.content:
David Raya says he does not care if rival supporters call Arsenal “boring” as his manager, Mikel Arteta, insisted that critics of the team’s style were only a “very small minority”.

Arsenal made it 10 wins out of 11 in all competitions for the season when they beat Nottingham Forest 1-0 at the City Ground on Sunday. But it was a day when Noni Madueke’s late goal papered over a flat and one-paced performance. Arteta admitted his players had to be better in attacking terms and the discussion over how they are able to get the job done has tracked them to Germany where they face Bayern Munich in the Champions League on Wednesday night.

Raya sought to cut through the external noise when he was asked whether the criticism irritated him and his teammates. “No it doesn’t,” the goalkeeper said. “People have their own opinions. We have our own opinion. At the end of the day, we have lost one game in 11 this season and if you call that boring or irritating … I don’t know what to say. We enjoy playing football. We enjoy going out there every single day to win football matches and that’s the most important thing.”

Arteta is focused on the glamour tie against Bayern, who will be without the suspended Michael Olise and might not have their manager, Vincent Kompany, in the dugout. He has been laid low by a viral infection that has also affected his legs. Arteta’s attitude to those who throw stones in Arsenal’s direction is that there will always be gripes about every club.

“If you analyse all the top teams in England and I go: ‘OK, what are they talking about?’ They all have a list [of things about them],” he said. “None of us are perfect and thank God that we are not perfect and we can still improve, even though we have won the amount of games we have done because otherwise the next day, what do you do? You just expect to be better than the opponent and that’s it. Especially in the Premier League, we know that is very far from the reality.”

Arteta sought to introduce a note of levity. “I don’t have that impression [about there being a debate over Arsenal’s style] because I heard it was incredible,” he said. “Because we scored so many goals, we have more possession, more shots, different players participating, no goals from set pieces … so the story is completely different to last year. I think we are talking about a very small minority and the other ones they know they have enjoyed a lot the way we have played and dominated games this year. We have proven that, so that’s my opinion.”

Arteta knows that Bayern will bring the game to Arsenal; perhaps it will be a relief not to face low-block opponents and it might allow his team to be more expansive.

“We know the kind of game that we’re going to play,” he said. “Both teams are very clear on that and we experienced that at the Emirates [last season, when Arsenal won 3-1]. It’s going to be a very similar one in many moments. A low block demands a different kind of game to a high block, to a team that is constantly putting the ball in the last line. But still on Sunday, I think we could have done things better and that’s in our hands. We need to recognise that openly, as well.”

Arteta is never short of intensity or motivation and he went back to last season’s Champions League final defeat by Paris Saint-Germain on penalties to illustrate how wildly the fire burns inside of him.

“I tried [to get over it] but I haven’t managed to,” he said. “I tried for many weeks during the summer but when I see the ball, the scenes, I hear the music, I want it so badly. We know that we have to go step by step but I think that fire is within the team and all of us individually. We know what we had to go through – not being champions of Europe by a penalty. So, let’s try again.”

View image in fullscreen Vincent Kompany may not be in the dugout due to a viral infection. Photograph: Marcel Engelbrecht/firo sportphoto/Getty Images

Raya remembered how Arsenal had only 28% of the ball against PSG but he feels they are better equipped to enjoy greater control against the elite. “I think so,” he said. “You have to see that in perspective, as well. It was our first Champions League final in so many years, we score in the fifth minute and you sit back a little bit knowing how good they are offensively. We didn’t want to give anything away. It is different now. You can see the way we play. You can see different type of ways of playing that we have. We are more prepared this year than last year.”

Kompany is touch and go to make the game. He was unable to attend Bayern’s training session on Tuesday while he ceded the responsibility of the pre-match press conference to his assistant, Aaron Danks.

Kompany had struggled through the 6-1 home win over RB ­Leipzig in the Bundesliga on Saturday – after which the club’s sporting director, Max Eberl, addressed the media instead of him. There have been reports in Germany that Kompany needed to lie down on his sofa at home after the Leipzig game and that the infection had affected an existing hip problem which meant he could hardly walk.

“It has affected his legs at times,” Danks said. “He’s felt some pain in his legs. I’m not sure about the reports about him lying down on the couch. I think we can all have a lie down on the couch after a game. It’s just a virus. The doctors and experts know way more than I do. The most important thing we have encouraged is that he rests; he takes the time he needs – however long that may be.

“Unfortunately, I can’t give you any more – whether that’s tomorrow or whether that’s two or three days’ time. I don’t know.We just take it day by day and see how he is. Getting Vince to rest is a challenge. You know him as a person. He’s a real leader. He works hard.”

Danks will take charge of the team against Arsenal if Kompany cannot make it, just as he did last season during the epic Champions League semi-final, first leg against PSG when Kompany was suspended. PSG won 5-4 at the Parc des Princes that night before progressing 6-5 on aggregate.

Birmingham-born Danks, who briefly took caretaker charge of Aston Villa in 2022 and has coached at various clubs including Anderlecht and Middlesbrough, said he would be in communication with Kompany “in some shape or form” if the manager was not able to come to the stadium.

Sports.title: How Brazil’s election result could shape women’s football in the country
Sports.content:
The day before the first round of Brazilian elections, the Estádio do Morumbi hosted the second leg of the Brazilian Women’s Championship final, in which São Paulo drew 1-1 with Corinthians to win 3-2 on aggregate and secure the Brasileirão Women’s title.

It had been an incredible final but after the game the goalkeeper Carlinha used an interview to appeal to her fans: “Never again Bolsonaro in power,” she shouted to a record-breaking TV audience of 23 million people.

Having lost her grandmother during the Covid-19 pandemic, Carlinha recalls the challenges faced by hundreds of thousands of Brazilian families when the far-right president Jair Bolsonaro spread fake information about the virus while ignoring public appeals for the government to buy and distribute vaccinations. More than 700,000 Brazilians died during the pandemic. Now his son, Flávio, is standing against the 80-year-old incumbent leftwing president, Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva.

“I didn’t just think of [my grandmother] when I gave that interview, I think about her and miss her every single day,” Carlinha tells Moving the Goalposts. “I felt relieved after talking about my personal opinion in such an important moment of Brazilian democracy. I’m a journalism student and I know the impact if the right wins the elections.”

Carlinha is one of several female football players who have used social media and their visibility to speak up before and during the presidential election, which will come to an end on Sunday with a second-round vote. The father of the Bolsonaro dynasty is currently under “humanitarian house arrest”, serving a 27-year sentence for a coup attempt.

Carlinha’s club and international teammate, Tayla Carolina, went viral the weekend after discussing her family’s background and how public policies implemented during Lula’s government were important for her mother and grandmother, who have worked as cleaners throughout their lives and have since passed. “I’m from a very humble family, I’m a Black woman. I’ve studied in public schools and used the national healthcare system … my mum, dona Dora, worked for over a decade for someone who never paid her labour rights … and she worked until she couldn’t walk any more due to the cancer that took her from us. She never saw me play because she never had the time, she never rested,” she wrote. Her story resonates with many Brazilians who fought for shorter working weeks, approved earlier this week in congress.

View image in fullscreen The Brazil international Tayla Carolina has expressed her support for Lula’s policies. Photograph: Aude Alcover/Icon Sport/Getty Images

Tayla elaborates her point: “I’m from a country where most of the people are poor but the country is not seen as poor. It shows there are huge inequalities, which come from exploitation. Years have passed and there’s still a lot of inequality and I come from it … as a public figure, and someone who has lived similar lives to the majority of Brazilians, I feel the responsibility to speak up.”

The player organisation Fifpro has just released a new study showing that nearly half of female football players think of early retirement owing to the psychological and financial pressures of the women’s game (800 professional players took part). With the Women’s World Cup being staged in Brazil next year both Carlinha and Tayla feel the election will have a huge impact on the game going forward.

“There is one side that makes it quite clear how they feel about women’s rights,” says Carlinha, referring to, among other things, politicians such as Eduarda Campopiano, one of the most voted members of the São Paulo Assembly, who calls herself an “enemy of feminists” and has said she does not believe in femicide – that women and girls can be killed because they are women. Tayla also feels the need for policies to support the women’s game at a crucial moment. “We still need government incentives, so it may not be immediate, but the game will be affected, positively or negatively, depending on how the elections go.”

Lula approved the World Cup law in June 2026, which regulates many aspects of the tournament, including how ministries, the Brazilian FA (CBF), state federations and clubs will commit to developing a legacy and supporting the women’s game in the country. The legacy plan, divided into four strands, proposes supporting access and permanence of girls and women in football, developing and professionalising the game, fighting gender- and racial-based discrimination, and enhancing the economic and cultural aspects of women’s football in Brazil. The commitment to the tournament is stated in Lula’s government plan. Bolsonaro’s proposals for women’s sport do not mention the World Cup; instead, he proposes “ensuring that women’s categories, from youth to elite, are played by athletes of the female sex, protecting women and tournaments from ideological agendas”.

Brazilian football, men’s and women’s, has been heavily politicised for decades, and the rise of social media has led to an increase in players publicly supporting their political candidates. In the men’s game, the far right is often championed by the Santos and Brazil forward Neymar, who has showed support for the Bolsonaro family on many occasions. Tottenham’s Richarlison, meanwhile, is positioned on the left and this week accused Flávio Bolsonaro of “taking possession” of an island he says he bought a few years back.

The country’s female players do not have the same number of followers on social media and cannot influence a big audience in the same way as the men. However, it is true that the result of the election is likely to have more of an impact on the women’s game than on the men’s.

View image in fullscreen Brazilian students and activists march in downtown Rio de Janeiro to support Lula and protest against the far-right candidate, Flávio Bolsonaro. Photograph: Ellan Lustosa/ZUMA Press Wire/Shutterstock

Kely Nascimento, the daughter of late football legend Pelé and founder and executive director of the Nascimento Foundation, says: “Female players, female athletes, they don’t have the protection of wealth. What feeds the brilliance of Brazilian football are the players, and they mostly come from communities, favelas and other places that are going to be hugely affected by these elections. Women are more affected by all this, right?”

Carlinha, who played in one of the two recent friendlies against Argentina, says playing for the national team at home is “one of the best feelings ever”. At both stadiums, in Porto Alegre and Recife, the crowd predominantly chanted in support of Lula, which could be heard over the TV commentary during the broadcast.

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Weekly Sign up to Moving the Goalposts No topic is too small or too big for us to cover as we deliver a twice-weekly roundup of the wonderful world of women’s football Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

The politicisation of women’s football is not new, as Brazilian women’s football historian and author Aira Bonfim explains. “This is a hundred-year-old history, because we have episodes of women playing football in Brazil since 1915, and the women’s game reveals different perspectives of gender inequalities, racial inequalities, class, territory, which will affect the progress of the women’s game,” she says. “By knowing women’s football history, we can look at episodes which are equally as political, such as the ban on the women’s game [between 1941 and 1979], the persecution of women, and lies that were told so that female players would give up on it.”

One of the pieces of history that she has uncovered in her research became a short film, which debuted earlier this month at the Rio Film Festival, The House of Dona Carlota, produced by Mymama Entertainment and directed by Lili Fialho and Bruna Linzmeyer, which tells the story of a woman who was arrested and persecuted because she led a women’s football team, Primavera Atlético Clube.

It shows women’s football as a space of socialisation, sport and resistance to the Estado Novo dictatorship in the late 1930s and early 1940s. The women’s game was banned in Brazil for decades, and the World Cup in 2027 is where many hope its renewed development will be consolidated.

“What’s at risk [in this election] is a waste of all of the human investments in building social legacy plans. There is also the risk of dismantling all political communication that has been done to support [the World Cup] through the ministries, cities and state governments. If you elect someone who did not make any commitments towards it, who did not commit to the World Cup or what it represents to women, it can be a huge loss,” Bonfim says. “Just the fact that during Jair Bolsonaro’s government he removed the status of the ministry of sports reveals how he feels about the sector.”

The hosting of a Women’s World Cup is key in developing public policies and attracting investment and support. As Nascimento says: “There are girls all over Brazil for whom football is not just their dream, but it’s also how they get out of very awful situations. And there are amazing people doing God’s work all over Brazil just to get girls to play, to be educated in another way … for some reason, Brazil just makes football magic, and that’s not gender-specific. And there’s an enormous Brazil that is being ignored and taken advantage of.”

There are many reasons for the international community to look closer at the second round of Brazil’s elections on Sunday, from how it can affect climate change, foreign policy and financial markets to many other issues. Women’s football, and all it represents, is one of them.

Sports.title: Football Daily | Kulusevski and Maddison return to form but are Tottenham also back?
Sports.content:
MAD FOR IT

As Tottenham edged to victory over Coventry, a familiar face among the post-match salutations. Could that be Dejan Kulusevski? For it was he, playing 526 days since his last Spurs appearance. Much has changed though still much stays the same. Ben Davies’s deflected late clincher catapulted Spurs up to … 16th. When Kulusevski last played on 11 May 2025, Tottenham were 17th, the position in which they finished both that season and in 2025-26.

So what has changed? Ange Postecoglou was tinned that summer despite winning the Flamin’ Bigger Vase. Thomas Frank was an appointment the soccer sensibles agreed was smart. A coach with impeccable credentials in improving players, willing to work in tandem with club suits, an ideal apex for an org chart. With lovely hair, too. Frank was sent packing in February, his popularity ratings plunging to depths unseen since Alan Sugar had the bright idea of appointing George Graham, who had paid his gardener to shape his lawn into the Arsenal crest. In football’s world of irrelevant but interesting (you sure? – Football Daily Ed) coincidences, the last time Spurs beat Coventry in the league, when Sergiy Rebrov’s goal completed a 3-0 stroll in 2001, the manager’s programme notes had been written by Gorgeous George, who the day previously had been the recipient of Sugar’s “you’re fired” flex.

Igor Tudor’s tenure resembled a slasher movie, an appointment on the nod from a sporting director, Fabio Paratici, who had already left. Classic Spurs. What could possibly go wrong? Everything, it turns out. Or close to, until Roberto De Zerbi was handed the keys and a control none of his predecessors commanded. The transfer spend has been heavy, and when Kulusevski arrived in the 87th minute on Monday, the game not yet won, he did so following an absence where Spurs signed 20 players either permanently or on loan, at a cost of £530m.



Scoring Spurs’ opening goal on Monday was James Maddison. Football’s king of the oche was absent for almost as long Kulusevski. Last season, as De Zerbi attempted to arrest the slide towards relegation, ‘Madders’ initially sat on the bench on a vibes-only basis and closed out the season with not much more than 30 minutes of play, and had little time to do Maddison things like his arcing beauty against his hometown club on Monday, which opened the scoring for Spurs.

Good feelings at last, following a sunshine break in Marbella where, according to De Zerbi, his players became less a squad than a family. “You have to play for your friend and your brother, not like 11 robot players on the pitch,” he cooed. With two of his stars back in tandem, De Zerbi’s enforcer intensity brought a first league win of the season, to help Tottenham off the bottom. “With them in the dressing room there is another atmosphere,” De Zerbi roared. Jam tomorrow? Glory, glory? Lads, it’s etc …

LIVE ON BIG WEBSITE

Join Scott Murray from 8pm BST for Liverpool 2-1 Villarreal in the Bigger Cup action while Simon Burnton is on clockwatch action to bring you updates from PSG 3-3 Barcelona, Manchester City 4-1 AEK Athens, and more.

QUOTE OF THE DAY

“People still call me a ‘party boy’. That stigma has been overused and has followed me since I retired from football. I’m not saying I didn’t enjoy myself as a player. You never hear that I didn’t turn up for training or wasn’t fit … now I’m not a kid trying to get into management for the first time. I’m a manager” – Dwight Yorke speaks to Morgan Ofori from his home in Dubai about his career ambitions, having been linked with the vacant Ghana job.

View image in fullscreen Dwight Yorke: ‘I’m straightforward. I don’t mess around, take shortcuts or do the job halfway.’ Photograph: Christopher Pike/The Guardian

double quotation mark Further to Peters and Lee [Monday’s Football Daily letters] another 70s example that occurred to me was the West Ham players Mervyn Day and Bill Green. They were both in the West Ham United team from 1976-78, and in Carlisle United’s greatest season 1974-75. When Green was still at Carlisle, he played against West Ham’s Day. So plenty of Green Day commentary opportunities there. Of course, the band hadn’t formed yet, but who knows, perhaps they thought of the band’s name whilst watching some old 70s football footage” – Bob Dunning.

Sports.title: Animal rights group urges Crystal Palace to retire bald eagle mascot
Sports.content:
A leading animal rights group has urged Crystal Palace to retire their American bald eagle mascot because, it says, the matchday experience can leave the bird “frightened, disoriented and panicked” and put spectators at risk.

In a letter to Palace’s chief executive, Sharon Lacey, People for the Ethical Treatment of Animals (Peta) called on the club to end Phoenix’s appearances at Selhurst Park and commit never to use a live animal mascot again.

Palace, known as the Eagles since 1973 after the then manager Malcolm Allison changed their nickname from the Glaziers, introduced a pre-match display from Kayla the Eagle in 2010. She died in 2020 after a decade’s service but Kayla’s replacement, Phoenix, made her debut before the game against West Ham in August 2024 at four months old, meeting supporters in the fanzone and being introduced at half-time with her handler.

Phoenix is based at the Eagle Heights Wildlife Foundation in Kent, and its website said at the time that she “had been carefully prepared for her prestigious role as Crystal Palace’s official live mascot since hatching”. Phoenix is not at every game but it is understood plans for her to make a maiden flight across the pitch before kick-off – a ritual Kayla for which was renowned – were abandoned at a match this season.

In the letter seen by the Guardian, Peta said bright lights, loud noises and boisterous crowds mean stadiums are “no place for animals” and potentially put animals and spectators at risk. It detailed incidents of eagles that have collided with walls or glass windows and a falcon that landed on a spectator’s head, embedding its talons in the man’s scalp. Peta also referred to an incident involving Kayla in 2015 when a Charlton fan was found guilty of trying to punch her during a League Cup tie marred by crowd trouble.

View image in fullscreen Kayla the eagle, who died in 2020, in flight before a Crystal Palace game in 2014. Photograph: Tom Jenkins/The Guardian

Dr Carys Bennett, Peta’s senior corporate projects manager, said: “Bald eagles are revered as symbols of freedom, yet Phoenix is being used as little more than a prop to entertain football fans. Crystal Palace already has a human mascot to energise supporters, so there’s no reason to drag a wild animal into a noisy, crowded stadium. Peta is urging the club to let Phoenix spread [her] wings and retire from matchday duties for good.”

Palace did not respond to Peta’s letter or to a follow-up request last week. They have been contacted for comment. The Guardian sent a number of questions to Eagles Heights to ask about Phoenix’s welfare and did not receive a reply.

Peta’s letter argued that eagles’ natural behaviours make the stadium environment unsuitable for them. In the wild, the birds can travel across vast territories and typically avoid close contact with humans. The organisation said even birds raised in captivity retain their natural instincts and may experience frustration and stress when unable to engage in natural behaviours.

Benfica’s home matches feature appearances from a bald eagle called Águia Vitória – a custom that the Portuguese club started in 2003 when their new Estádio da Luz opened.

Sports.title: Champions League: Liverpool fight back to beat Villarreal in seven-goal thriller, Phil Foden hits hat-trick for Man City against AEK Athens
Sports.content: After nearly seven years of being Man United's main man is the time drawing near when Bruno Fernandes will have to pass on that mantle? His display vs Leeds was a microcosm of his season, writes CHRIS WHEELER

Sports.title: The night Rio Ngumoha cemented his status as a future world-beater: Liverpool had a £400m attack at their disposal but it was the 17-year-old who shone brightest in chaotic comeback win, writes LEWIS STEELE
Sports.content:
They used to call it ‘Pep roulette’ at Manchester City, when Pep Guardiola would throw a surprise every weekend by changing up his front line to devastating effect. We don’t have such a snazzy phrase for Andoni Iraola – ‘AI Bingo’ or ‘Iraola tombola’ are the early drafts – but the Liverpool boss has an elite depth of attacking talent who, if they all fulfil their potential, can take this team to dreamy heights. With the best part of half a billion pounds worth of forwards not starting this victory against Villarreal, it was up to the supposed backup brigade to assert their authority and no one stood out more than the potential world-beater Rio Ngumoha. Still just 18, the three-time England cap will cost Liverpool a maximum fee of £6.8million after they poached him from Chelsea two years ago, but this teenage prodigy’s ceiling is as high as £125m Alexander Isak, £123m Bradley Barcola or £116m Florian Wirtz. Ngumoha has not found himself on the score-sheet again but he was the shining light of many in a thumping comeback win that could have unfolded very differently after an uncharacteristic and shoddy first half an hour. Alexis Mac Allister continued his fine season with a brace either side of Ronald Araujo’s header, with substitute Wirtz adding a fourth to put the game to bed. Liverpool beat Villarreal 4-3 in a chaotic Champions League encounter at Anfield on Tuesday Alexis Mac Allister was Liverpool's hero, scoring twice as the Reds came from behind to win But it was Rio Ngumoha's display that was most impressive as he showed all of his quality Liverpool 4-3 Villarreal: MATCH FACTS LIVERPOOL (4-2-3-1): Alisson 6; Araujo 7 (Wirtz 46, 7), Jacquet 6 (Gomez 74, 6), Van Dijk 5, Tsimikas 6; Nyoni 7 (McConnell 81), Mac Allister 8; Ngumoha 8 (Barcola 74, 6), Gravenberch 6; Gakpo 6; Koumas 6. Subs not used: Mamardashvili, Woodman, Kerkez, Isak, Chambers, Danns, Laffey. Booked: None. Scorers: Mac Allister 36, 65, Araujo 45+2, Wirtz 68. Manager: Andoni Iraola 7. VILLARREAL (4-2-3-1): Gulacsi 5; Mourino 5, Navarro 5, Veiga 6, Cardona 6; Saliba 7 (Oluwaseyi 46, 7), Gueye 6; Buchanan 5 (Freeman 60, 6), Comesana 6 (Moreno 78), Moleiro 6 (Foyth 54, 6); Mikautadze 7 (Perez 60, 6). Subs not used: Luiz Junior, Akhomach, Costa, Diatta, El Jmili, Gaitan, Macia. Booked: Moleiro, Mourino. Scorers: Mikautadze 4, Cardona 29, Oluwaseyi 87. Manager: Inigo Perez 7. Referee: Szymon Marciniak (Pol) 7. Attendance: not provided. Iraola will spend the coming days agonising over the slapdash first 30 minutes but will also know that, with his long list of attackers, the sky is the limit. Isak, Wirtz and Barcola all came on but it was Ngumoha, academy star Lewis Koumas and the returning Cody Gakpo who led the line as Liverpool turned this game on its head. This is not to mention Victor Munoz, described as a ‘F1 car on a pitch’ in these pages on Monday, and £79m Hugo Ekitike who is entering the final stages of a long recovery from a ruptured Achilles. Iraola locked horns with his former right-hand man, Inigo Perez, who was the No 2 during the Basque’s formative years at Rayo Vallecano. Perez, who sported a polo shirt and box-fresh white trainers – but notably braved the inclement Merseyside weather without a jacket – could not move to England when Iraola did because some wise cracks at the Home Office said he was not skilled enough for a work permit. The 38-year-old has made a mockery of that since, leading Rayo to the Conference League final after taking over from Iraola as head coach and now managing in the Champions League, where, for 45 minutes at least, his team played six-time European kings Liverpool off the park. Villarreal were magic, Liverpool tragic. The Reds were playing like a rabble who had met each other 10 minutes before kick-off and at the tempo of a charity match, while the yellow shirts of their Spanish visitors swarmed around them and exploited many gaping gaps. This was by far the worst half hour of the Iraola era, more worrying than the capitulation against Manchester City. At least that time they had the defence of going down to 10 men. This time they had no excuse, apprentice Perez was simply schooling master Iraola. Villarreal, nicknamed El Submarino Amarillo or The Yellow Submarine, were enjoying themselves in the land of the Beatles – whose song inspired that tag and is played before games at Estadio de la Ceramica. They were ahead after just four minutes. Virgil van Dijk made a honking error to head a long ball straight into the path of Georges Mikautadze, who could not believe his luck and scored. Van Dijk barely makes one wrong step, never mind a catastrophic mistake like this, and everyone at Anfield looked shell-shocked. That feeling strengthened when Nathan Saliba pulled a shot wide, then Mikautadze started showboating with kick-ups after 27 minutes. It was only 1-0 at this point but the Spaniards’ supremacy was as obvious as Liverpool’s tardiness. The 1,500 or so away fans and sea of vibrant yellow shirts were soon jumping for joy again on 29 minutes when Sergi Cardona sprung through a shoddy offside trap and waltzed through on goal to slot past a helpless Alisson for 2-0. Iraola was left scratching his head and probably regretting the six changes he made from the team that fought from behind to beat Brentford on Saturday. The attack was offering nothing and looked exactly what it was: a front four that had £400million worth of talent taken out of it. Bradley Barcola, Florian Wirtz and Alexander Isak sat on the bench, while Saturday’s energetic goal-scorer Victor Munoz was also missed and is nursing an injury suffered in the heat of battle at Brentford. Liverpool fought back after a dreadful first 30 minutes that saw Villarreal go 2-0 ahead Ronald Araujo scored his second goal in a week and celebrated by jumping into the stands Florian Wirtz (right) was also on the scoresheet to cap off a good few days for the German Out of nowhere, Liverpool found something and started the comeback, through a Mac Allister header. The Argentine may be small but is as good as most in the air and connected well with Kostas Tsimikas’s corner to score. Anfield found its voice and the Reds responded. Somehow, after the horror show of the first 35 minutes, they went into half-time level. Ngumoha made the goal with a fine ball that was headed home by Araujo for his second goal in a week after scoring at LASK. The Uruguayan loanee, here for the season from Barcelona, is quickly becoming a cult hero and is being affectionately referred to as ‘Big Ron’. He jumped into the Anfield Road End and made the night of one lucky lady, who received a bear hug. There was never any looking back from there, and Mac Allister put Liverpool ahead on 65 minutes after a dancing run from Ngumoha, before Wirtz came on and put gloss on the victory with a fine finish to continue an eye-catching week for the much-criticised German. Tani Oluwaseyi made it a nervy finish with an 87th-minute goal which highlighted Liverpool’s defensive issues – but Iraola knows his attackers are trending upwards and, after an uninspiring season, Liverpool once more possess a number of players who can win any game.
