World.title: US food importer sues Trump over 50 percent tariffs on Canadian goods
World.content:
A US food importer is suing US President Donald Trump over his 50 percent tariffs on Canadian goods, arguing he lacks the legal authority to impose sweeping tariffs without congressional approval.

Gellert Global Group, a New Jersey-based company that imports Canadian cheese, filed the lawsuit on Tuesday in the US Court of International Trade in New York.

The company says the tariffs are driving up its costs and disrupting its relationships with suppliers on both sides of the border. Between September 16 and October 11, Gellert had paid more than $520,000 in duties, according to the complaint.

“Gellert Global Group has spent generations building trusted relationships with suppliers, customers and partners across the food industry,” said Thomas Gellert, the company’s co-chief executive officer, in a press release. “These tariffs disrupt those relationships overnight and create costs and uncertainty that ripple through the entire supply chain.”

The lawsuit challenges Trump’s decision to use a Depression-era law to impose tariffs on a wide range of Canadian products, including dairy products, furniture, clothing and wine.

Trump first imposed the 50 percent tariffs over the summer, accusing Canada of discriminating against American-made cars, alcohol and dairy products. He expanded the measures in September, adding more products in response to Canadian retaliatory tariffs.

The lawsuit argues that the law doesn’t apply to the Canadian policies the Trump administration says are discriminatory, since two of them “arose in response to the president’s own tariffs, while the third involves Canadian dairy policy governed by the US-Mexico-Canada Agreement (USMCA)”.



It also questions why Canadian cheese is being taxed over disputes involving alcohol and cars.

“No president should have the power to pull a dormant statute off the shelf and use it to impose sweeping tariffs or import bans without the limits Congress required,” said Sara Albrecht, chairman and CEO of the Liberty Justice Center, a nonprofit legal organisation that filed the suit on Gellert’s behalf.

The White House did not immediately respond to a request for comment, according to the Reuters news agency.

At the centre of the case is Section 338 of the Smoot-Hawley Tariff Act of 1930, which allows the president to impose tariffs of up to 50 percent on imports from countries found to discriminate against American businesses.

The provision had never been used until Trump invoked it this year.

The lawsuit argues that newer laws passed by Congress since then, such as Section 301 of the Trade Act of 1974, require investigations, public comment and other safeguards that Gellert says the Trump administration has bypassed, and that these override Section 338.

“The administration cannot skip those protections by reaching for a 1930 statute that no president had ever used to impose a tariff,” said Jeffrey Schwab, the Liberty Justice Center’s senior counsel and director of litigation.

In addition, the lawsuit says that even if Trump is allowed to use the older law, he hasn’t met its requirements, including waiting 30 days before tariffs can be collected on new products added to the list.

The administration only waited seven days to start collecting tariffs on cheese in September, according to the lawsuit.

Gellert is asking the court to declare the tariffs illegal, stop them from being collected, and order refunds with interest for importers who have been impacted.

The lawsuit marks the fourth major legal challenge to Trump’s tariffs.

In February, the US Supreme Court struck down most of the tariffs he imposed in 2025, and a trade court later ruled against a temporary 10 percent global tariff. A separate challenge to tariffs imposed over alleged forced labour in international trade is still pending.

World.title: Why do the US midterms matter for Trump and Congress?
World.content:
Republicans and Democrats jockey for control of Congress, which will set course for Trump’s final two years in office.

Share Why do the US midterms matter for Trump and Congress? on social media

The United States midterms on November 3 are dominating national and international headlines.

The stakes of the election are high. The midterm race will determine which party controls the US Congress, and in turn, shape the direction of Trump’s final two years in office. It will also decide key state and local positions.

But notching big wins in the midterm election may not be enough to shake up the balance of power in Washington, DC.

To understand the implications of this year’s midterm election and what may come next, Al Jazeera has put together this simple primer.

Here’s why the US midterms matter at the federal level.

Battle for the US House of Representatives and US Senate

Midterm elections fall at the halfway point of a president’s term, meaning the executive office will not be on the ballot.

Front and centre will be the battle for control of Congress. Two chambers make up the US legislature: the House of Representatives and the Senate.

Because members of the House serve two-year terms, all 435 seats in the chamber are up for election on November 3. However, most races are already considered formalities, with a clear frontrunner.

That leaves only a handful of races — about 50 — to decide who will win the House majority.

While subject to change, nearly every reputable election prognosticator has predicted that Democrats will win control of the House, some by as many as 15 seats.

The Democrats have a slimmer chance of winning a majority in the Senate, however.

That chamber has only 100 seats. But because senators have staggered six-year terms, only 35 seats are up for election. Only about a dozen of those races are considered competitive.



Still, Democrats have seen their odds of seizing the Senate increase, as the number of competitive races has grown.

Left-wing candidates have made inroads in deep-red states like Texas and Kansas, creating more opportunities for the Democratic Party to claim a Senate majority this election cycle.

Because the US vice president breaks ties in the Senate, Democrats would need 51 seats to control the chamber.

What does party control mean?

Congress passes laws and approves federal budgets. But even if a party secures a majority in both chambers of Congress, it may not be enough to control the country’s legislative agenda.

Laws can pass by a simple majority in the House, but they typically need a supermajority of 60 votes in the Senate to overcome a process known as the filibuster. That process can allow a minority group to stall legislation indefinitely, barring a supermajority.

Therefore, unless a party wins more than 60 seats in the Senate, most legislation will still require at least some level of bipartisan support to pass.

Even if legislation passes both chambers, the president can veto any bill that comes across his desk. Overriding a presidential veto requires a two-thirds supermajority in both the House and the Senate.

Achieving the broad bipartisan support needed to overcome a presidential veto is exceedingly rare.

The last time it happened was in January 2021, during Trump’s first term. At the time, the US president had lost the 2020 election, and he saw his support from Republican lawmakers dissipate when he attempted to veto a defence spending bill.

Still, there are instances when bipartisan support overcomes presidential objections. A bill to increase the housing supply passed both the House and Senate with veto-proof majorities earlier this year, despite Trump’s stated opposition.

So what happens if Republicans maintain control of Congress?

Republicans currently hold two majorities in Congress, with 53 seats in the Senate and 218 in the House.

With Trump in the White House, that means the party has held a so-called government “trifecta” over the last two years, with three levers of power under its command.

The Republican majorities in Congress have helped Trump pass some of his signature legislation, including surging funding to Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) and cleaving back some forms of publicly funded healthcare as part of a sweeping 2025 tax bill.

But Republicans’ numbers have not been enough to pass Trump’s entire legislative wishlist. Notably, he has been unable to pass his signature federal voter identification law, dubbed the “SAVE America Act“, amid Democratic opposition.



There have also been a handful of issues where Republicans have defied Trump, particularly on tariffs. A few Republicans have also voted to assert congressional authority over the US-Israel war with Iran.

If the Republican Party maintains control of both the House and Senate in November’s race, its majorities could continue to help Trump’s legislative agenda. But there is an important caveat.

Lawmakers will be keeping an anxious eye on voter sentiment as the 2028 elections approach. With Trump unable to seek a third term, some Republicans may have more appetite to publicly oppose the lame-duck president during the next two years, in order to boost their election prospects.

If Republicans maintain control of the Senate but lose the House, they would still be able to help Trump confirm his nominees for key federal roles.

Hundreds of federal positions require approval from a simple majority in the Senate, including roles in the judiciary, including Supreme Court justices.

What if Democrats take control?

The party in control of Congress, with a few exceptions, can determine what legislation is brought to a vote and when.

But for Democrats, the most significant outcome of winning a majority in one or both chambers would be the ability to block Trump from legislating his agenda over the next two years.

That said, analysts expect a Democrat-led Congress to take a largely defensive stance, batting down Trump’s proposals.

Going on offence — and passing their own legislative agenda — will be far more difficult, even if the party wins a majority in both the House and Senate. Democrat-led laws would still face Trump’s veto power.

However, holding majorities would help Democratic members slip policy priorities into “need-to-pass” funding legislation. The spectre of a government shutdown could pressure Republicans to pass budget bills, even if they do not agree on all the terms.

Democrats can also bring topics to a vote to force congressional Republicans to oppose popular policies or simply take a public stance on divisive issues.

House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries has laid out a 100-day plan for if Democrats take control of the chamber. Topping the agenda are votes on Trump-backed healthcare funding cuts, asserting congressional authority over the US-Israel war with Iran and rolling back Trump’s tariff programme.

Those issues have split the Republican base and would pose thorny dilemmas for lawmakers already posturing for the 2028 vote.

Will Democrats impeach Trump?

As Trump rallies on behalf of Republicans in the run-up to November’s vote, he has repeatedly expressed concern that Democratic control of Congress could lead to one eventuality: his third impeachment.

Trump was already impeached twice during his first term. “If we don’t win, they’ll end up impeaching me,” he told a rally in Durant, Oklahoma, in early October.

If Democrats do take control of the House or the Senate, they will take over leadership of dozens of committees. Through those committees, they can launch investigations — with subpoena power — into an array of subjects.



Some Democrats have already said probing allegations of Trump family corruption will be a top priority.

House lawmakers can also introduce articles of impeachment and ultimately vote to impeach federal officials, including the president, with a simple majority.

However, the Senate would need to vote to convict the official with a two-thirds majority before they can be removed from office.

Perhaps more significantly, if Democrats win control of the Senate, they would be able to block the confirmation of Trump appointees in key roles during his final two years in office.

So what will change on the war with Iran and the economy?

A Democratic surge is likely to signal discontent with the Trump administration, but there will not be a swift, tangible change on many of the issues that have defined the election season.

For example, if Democrats secure both majorities in Congress, they could assert their leverage to seek to address affordability issues, drilling into topics like housing, healthcare and the cost of living.

But they can do little to immediately change the myriad factors that led to the high price of petrol and groceries. Any gains would most likely be hard-fought, slow-coming and incremental.

The same is true for the US-Israel war with Iran.

Under the US Constitution, only Congress can declare war, something it has not done since World War II. Presidents have long used various legal arguments to circumvent that constitutional requirement.

Most recently, the Trump administration argued that the US-Israel war with Iran did not require authorisation from Congress because the president has a duty to protect the American people.

Trump has also argued that the war has started and stopped several times, each time renewing the 60-day window he has to receive Congress’s authorisation.

To reassert Congress’s authority to declare war, Democrats could pass a legally binding “war powers resolution” to rein in Trump, but they would need two-thirds support to overcome the presidential veto.

Even if a resolution were able to overcome the veto, experts say it is unclear how the US judiciary would respond if Trump were to flout Congress’s will.

Still, Democrats could use control of Congress to attempt to stifle any funding for the war.

World.title: UK police re-arrest two men on suspicion of assisting Iran’s intelligence
World.content:
The duo was first arrested for a suspected link to an incident at a US-run airbase used for striking Iran during this year’s war.

Share UK police re-arrest two men on suspicion of assisting Iran’s intelligence on social media

Police in the United Kingdom have re-arrested two men on suspicion of assisting Iran’s intelligence service after an incident at a United States-run airbase in England last month.

Counter Terrorism Policing in the UK said the men, a 24-year-old British national and a 25-year-old dual British-Iranian national, were arrested under the National Security Act.

One of the suspects was first arrested on September 27, when the suspected plot against RAF Fairford took place. The airbase in Gloucestershire in western England has been used to launch strikes on Iran during this year’s war.

The second suspect was first arrested on October 1. Until Tuesday, the men had been released on bail pending more investigation.

Laurence Taylor, head of National Counter Terrorism Policing in the UK, said the investigation was “hugely complex” and that detectives were looking at “many lines of enquiry”.

“This is very much a live investigation,” Taylor said in a statement, adding: “We consider it highly likely that there is Iranian state involvement.”

“Our investigators are continuing to examine what that level of involvement was and the ambition behind it,” he added.

Major incident

British police declared a major incident in the area around RAF Fairford after a member of the public reported seeing three “suspicious” vans driving near the base.



Residents were forced to leave their homes as armed police officers and army bomb-disposal experts swarmed the rural area.

Police later said they had found a quantity of an accelerant – petrol – in three vans at the site, but no explosives.

The incident prompted the US to pull its bombers out of RAF Fairford, while British authorities blamed Iran.

British Prime Minister Andy Burnham said the apparent plot was “almost certainly” directed by Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC).

Not unique

Ken McCallum, the UK’s domestic intelligence spy chief, warned that Iran and Russia were expanding attacks against military bases in the UK, adding that the RAF Fairford incident was not unique.

In all, more than 50 people have been arrested over Iran-linked plots in the past year, McCallum said.

Iran has denied involvement, although it has previously said that it considers any base used to attack its territory a legitimate target.

Five other men in their 20s were arrested earlier then released on bail pending further investigation. No one has yet been charged.

World.title: EU revises Arctic strategy as pressure from Russia, US grows
World.content:
The new strategy shifts the bloc’s focus from long-term climate concerns to urgent security measures.

Share EU revises Arctic strategy as pressure from Russia, US grows on social media

The European Commission has unveiled a new Arctic strategy for the European Union that lists security and resilience first among four priorities, alongside climate change, economic prosperity and opportunities for Arctic communities.

The strategy calls for a new maritime security hub to help member states and partners share information and monitor maritime activity in the Arctic, the Commission said on Tuesday.

The hub would later expand to track shadow fleet vessels, detect illegal fishing and pollution, and improve search and rescue coordination.

The Commission also said the EU will work to expand European icebreaker capacity. Icebreakers are specialised vessels designed to navigate ice-covered waters by breaking up sea ice and maintaining safe shipping routes.

“The Arctic is one place where the tectonic plates of geopolitics are colliding,” European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen said, adding that sovereignty and territorial integrity can no longer be taken for granted.

EU foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas said Russia is expanding its military footprint in the high north, citing drone incursions, GPS jamming and cable sabotage, the AFP news agency reported.

Cutting reliance on Washington

Several measures appear aimed at reducing dependence on the United States. The Commission said the EU will back a strategic pan-Arctic fibre-optic telecommunications cable project linking Greenland directly to Europe. It is part of a wider plan that would also connect Canada, Japan and South Korea.



The EU will also provide secure satellite connectivity for government communications through the IRIS² constellation, a constellation AFP said is meant to rival US tech mogul Elon Musk’s Starlink.

The shift follows US President Donald Trump’s repeated demands to take control of Greenland, a Danish autonomous territory. Although his tone has softened this year, with a security deal signed with Greenland and Denmark, many in Europe remain wary, AFP said.

Member states press for action

The strategy follows last month’s meeting of leaders from 12 countries, including Germany, France, Finland and Denmark. Member states urged the EU to take a more strategic and proactive role, according to a joint statement.

Participants identified Russia as the largest threat while noting the ambitions of China and the US.

At the meeting, German Chancellor Friedrich Merz said the era of “high north, low attention” was over. Finnish Prime Minister Petteri Orpo called Russia the most significant long-term threat and said the EU must treat the Arctic as a strategic frontier.

The Commission reiterated the EU’s position remains that oil, coal and gas should stay in the ground, including in the Arctic.

To combat increasing climate concerns, the Commission pledged to “strengthen climate research, observation and monitoring to better understand these changes and support effective responses”, while working in tandem with the people who live and work in the Arctic.

World.title: Zelensky says US intelligence sharing 'works now' after talks with Trump envoy in Oslo
World.content:
Ukraine's President Volodymyr Zelensky has said US intelligence sharing on deadly Russian missile attacks "works now" after talks with President Donald Trump's special envoy Steve Witkoff.

The meeting in Oslo came after accusations by Kyiv that Washington was withholding key intelligence - a claim rejected as "scandalous" by US Secretary of State Marco Rubio.

Finnish President Alexander Stubb, who also took part in the talks, said "genuine progress" was made on proposals to achieve peace but gave no details and warned that patience would be needed.

Zelensky and his European allies said it was now up to Russia to respond to the proposals agreed in Oslo when Witkoff arrives in St Petersburg on Wednesday.

Witkoff was not present at the joint press conference after Tuesday's talks in the Norwegian capital. Trump's son-in-law Jared Kushner, another key envoy, took part in the meeting via video link.

A US official later described the talks as "very productive and constructive", saying there was a "strong alignment at the working level" among the US, Ukraine and Europe on "the next steps".

The official confirmed that Witkoff is due to meet President Vladimir Putin in Russia tomorrow to discuss the proposals and that Kushner will again participate virtually.

Putin is yet to publicly comment on the latest developments, but Foreign Minister Sergei Lavrov earlier said the Kremlin would listen to what Wiktoff would offer, while ruling out "any political concessions".

Relations between Ukraine and the US have soured in recent weeks to the extent that Trump has said it is time for Ukraine to get a new president, and most recently "for somebody else to negotiate on behalf of Ukraine".

Ahead of next month's US midterm elections, Trump has also sought to blame Ukraine's attacks on Russian oil refineries for fuel prices which have been rising since the start of the US-led war on Iran.

Speaking after Zelensky's news conference in Oslo, Trump again told reporters at the White House he wanted Kyiv to "make a deal". He said Russia would like to "get it done" and it was "time for Ukraine to end this war".

Putin launched a full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022, and Moscow currently controls about 20% of Ukrainian territory.

Russian drone attacks continued on Tuesday. Ukrainian officials said at least 10 people were killed - four in Kyiv and the capital region, another four in the eastern Donetsk region, and two in the central city of Dnipro.

World.title: Marseille braces for more unrest after protests give way to 'apocalyptic' disorder
World.content:
Thunder and lightning have boomed across Marseille following the weekend's mayhem, illuminating the cracked windows and boarded-up doors of hundreds of businesses that were smashed as protests gave way to disorder.

France's second city saw some of the worst violence as chaos gripped the country on Saturday. Local business leaders say more than 500 premises were damaged, and the majority looted.

A police union boss told the BBC that the weekend had been an "apocalyptic" hell for his colleagues. 118 officers were injured, representing more than a tenth of the national figure.

So far, 101 arrests have been made in the port city, a quarter of them children.

But by Monday, it was police who were most conspicuous on the city's streets, not protesters. For eight hours, demonstrations and gatherings were banned in an effort to avoid a third consecutive day of disorder.

World.title: Man charged with attack on Australia MP to face court
World.content:
A 43-year-old man has been charged after Australian MP Helen Haines was hit by a car in the state of Victoria on Monday.

The suspect will appear in court on Wednesday to face charges of dangerous driving causing serious injury, intentionally causing serious injury and the federal offence of causing harm to a public official.

Local media earlier named the alleged attacker as environmental activist Brendan Nugent. His father and his partner said they had been friends with Haines "for more than 20 years" and thanked residents and officers who helped her after the "shocking and horrific crime".

Haines remains in a critical condition after surgery and is reported to have lost one of her legs.

"Helen Haines is a deeply respected, valued and much loved member of our local community," Rod Nugent and his partner Christine Cunningham said in a statement.

"All of our love and all of our thoughts are with Helen and her family and friends."

They promised to assist Victoria Police "in any way we can".

Police say they will allege the incident was targeted.

Haines, 65, the independent member for Indi, is in a critical but stable condition after undergoing surgery at a Melbourne hospital.

World.title: Trump and Zelensky appear at loggerheads despite Oslo optimism
World.content:
The hug that Trump envoy Steve Witkoff offered Volodymyr Zelensky ahead of this afternoon's talks in Oslo is unlikely to have dispelled the Ukrainian leader's misgivings about the current direction of US policy towards his war-ravaged country.

Zelensky posted a video of the moment on social media, with the message "Ukraine is working for peace. I thank our partners for their support!"

But given everything that's happened this month, does the Ukrainian leader still regard Donald Trump as a partner?

The two men have never been close â that much is obvious â but have they now fallen out once and for all?

Both in rhetoric and actions, the past ten days have seen evidence of a rupture as deep as any in their fractious relationship.

Just listen to the way they talk about each other.

"Zelensky's not a good guy for us to deal with," Trump told Newsmax last week.

The verbal assault has continued this week.

"Zelensky doesn't know what he's talking about," Trump told a reporter on Monday when asked what he thought of the Ukrainian leader's suggestion that striking a diesel deal with Russia put the US on the wrong side of history.

Such personal attacks are typical of Trump's sledgehammer approach to diplomacy. It's hard to know when to take them seriously.

In June, he lashed out at Israel's prime minister, saying Benjamin Netanyahu "has no f**king judgement". Four months later, he endorsed Netanyahu enthusiastically, calling him a "great warrior prime minister".

"Trump can always do another U-turn," says Ian Bond of the Centre for European Reform. "But this does look bad."

World.title: 'Great result for Canada', says Carney as Alberta votes to reject separatism
World.content:
Prime Minister Mark Carney says an overwhelming vote by people in Alberta to remain part of Canada is a "great result" for the country.

Speaking to reporters as he walked into a cabinet meeting on Tuesday, Carney said he was "thrilled that Albertans have chosen unity" by rejecting a proposal to pursue separation through a binding referendum.

Preliminary results indicate more than two-thirds chose Canada over a push for independence for the province, according to Elections Alberta, external.

Monday's referendum was the result of a months-long campaign by separatists in the western Canadian province to get a public vote on the issue.

Provincial leader Danielle Smith welcomed the initial results, commenting: "Albertans have voted for a stronger Alberta in a united Canada."

Premier Smith herself opposed the separatist push but said the public will for a vote was undeniable, and many supporters of her own political party - United Conservative Party - were in the separatist camp.

Smith said she would address Albertans later on Tuesday on the path forward for the province.

In making the case for independence from Canada, many of the separatists said the oil-rich province's economic growth had been stifled by the environmental policies of Canada's central government in Ottawa.

But those who opposed a breakup - including Carney - called for Canada to present a united front in the face of external pressures, including an ongoing trade war with the United States.

"They've chosen to build together," Carney said. "They've chosen to continue to take care of each other, to move forward, to move forward together, with purpose, high ambition."

Carney added that he had spoken to Smith that morning and discussed "moving forward in the spirit of cooperative federalism, including on issues of immigration, other common priorities".

Over the past year, the prime minister has worked with Smith on a number of shared goals, including pushing for an oil pipeline to the Pacific coast.

World.title: Trump sued over Canadian tariffs in latest legal challenge
World.content:
US President Donald Trump is facing another legal challenge on tariffs after the group that successfully sued over his so-called "liberation day" import taxes filed a new lawsuit over the latest Canadian levies.

The White House imposed a 50% levy on some $20bn of Canadian goods after trade talks between the US and Canada broke down in August.

The Liberty Justice Center filed a suit on behalf of US food business Gellert Global Group, urging the US Court of International Trade to find the levies unlawful and to order refunds with interest for affected importers.

The lawsuit argues the White House exceeded its authority in imposing the tariffs and caused "immediate harm to American businesses".

The White House has been contacted for comment.

Gellert Global Group is a third-generation family business that is paying 50% tariffs on cheese exported from Canada. The New Jersey-based firm is also facing retaliatory tariffs from Canada on American-made cheese it sells north of the border.

Co-chief executive Thomas Gellert said the firm had spent generations building relationships with suppliers and customers in the food industry.

"These tariffs disrupt those relationships overnight and create costs and uncertainty that ripple through the entire supply chain," he said on Tuesday.

The Liberty Justice Center is challenging the administration's use of Section 338 of the 1930 Tariff Act to hit Canadian goods from wine to dairy products and hockey sticks.

That section of the nearly 100-year-old Act is aimed at protecting US business against foreign discrimination, but the legal group is arguing that it does not allow the executive branch "to impose sweeping tariffs or import restrictions whenever a trade dispute arises".

World.title: North Korea publishes photos of Kim Jong Un - why do rumours of his death keep coming back?
World.content:
Kim Jong Un has appeared in North Korean state media looking remarkably healthy for a man rumoured to have died from a brain haemorrhage.

Photographs published by state newspaper Rodong Sinmun show the 42-year-old dictator touring what the paper said was a clothing and footwear exhibition with his daughter.

The images emerged hours after a Chinese dissident who lives in the US claimed, without evidence, that Kim had been taken to a hospital in Beijing in a coma and had died.

For those who watch North Korea closely, this kind of rumour has become almost routine.

In one of the world's most secretive states, facts are often difficult to verify, creating fertile ground for speculation.

This latest claim originated with Wanjun Xie, who identifies himself as chairman of the Chinese Democratic Party, a group banned by Chinese authorities. He has previously circulated unverified claims, including speculation about the death of Chinese leader Xi Jinping.

Xie alleged that Kim suffered a severe brain haemorrhage and was transferred to Beijing because North Korea lacked the medical facilities to treat him.

He claimed Kim later died and that his body had been secretly returned to North Korea, with the regime concealing his death.

Yet the photographs tell a different story.

Kim is seen examining displays, accompanied by Kim Ju Ae and his usual entourage of officials.

While there is no way to know exactly when the images were taken, there are other reasons to doubt the claim.

World.title: Swimmer, 65, killed in shark attack off South Africa's east coast
World.content:
A South African woman has been killed in a shark attack off the country's east coast, in what is the first recorded such fatality this year.

Janine Lochrenberg was swimming off a beach in KuGompo City (formerly East London) on Tuesday morning when she was attacked.

Witnesses said the 65-year-old was bitten in two places and died before she was brought to shore.

Shark attacks are rare in South Africa, with about 10 fatal ones since 2012, according to the Florida Museum's International Shark Attack File.

Lochrenberg was out on a daily morning swim with her local open water swimming club when she was attacked at around 08:00 (06:00 GMT). Fellow swimmers brought her to shore, but it's believed she died before they could get her out of the water.

She was bitten on her thigh and her upper arm, one of her fellow swimmers told the BBC. They also said she had been wearing a magnetic shark repellent band on her ankle at the time.

Lochrenberg's sister Margot said she was holding her sister's head as they brought her to shore but believed she bled out in the water.

She told the BBC that her sister had "loved the water so much" despite knowing there was an "elevated shark presence in East London".

"She'd made peace with that. She had a deep affinity with the water and was a remarkable person," she said.

Barbara Briceland, Lochrenberg's partner, told the BBC the retired medical physicist was a good swimmer, who often swam far out into the breakers, and described her as very brave.

"She was highly intelligent, lots of fun, kind, in a quietish way, thoughtful, well-loved with a love of life."

Briceland added they were looking forward to retirement and were about to leave for a three-week road trip together.

Orient Beach, where the attack took place, has been closed alongside another nearby beach, authorities confirmed.

World.title: Ebola: 44 identified contacts to stay isolated for three weeks – Minister
World.content:
The 44 people identified as contacts of Nigeria’s confirmed Ebola patient will remain in isolation for at least three weeks.

The Coordinating Minister of Health and Social Welfare, Muhammad Pate, disclosed this Tuesday evening during an NTA interview, shortly after the ministry announced Nigeria’s first confirmed Ebola case in the Federal Capital Territory (FCT).

Mr Pate said authorities are currently treating the case as an imported infection and not community transmission.

“At this moment, we are treating it as an imported case, not community transmission,” he said, adding that the situation could change if the virus begins to spread beyond the known contacts.

He said the 44 contacts, including healthcare workers, patients, caregivers and travel contacts, are being isolated at a designated facility in Abuja. At the same time, public health teams determine who may have been infected.

“They remain in communication with their families by phone and other ways, but not physical contact, until we clarify who is infected and who is not,” he said.

Travel manifest obtained

The minister said Nigeria had been conducting risk-based surveillance at points of entry for the past five months through the Nigeria Centre for Disease Control and Prevention (NCDC) and Port Health Services.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

He said the aviation industry had also been an important partner in the surveillance effort.

According to Mr Pate, authorities obtained the infected passenger’s travel manifest, which is helping them identify people who may have been exposed.

He said the patient was asymptomatic when she entered Nigeria and developed symptoms after arriving in the country.

“This makes it less likely that the travel itself exposed folks at risk,” Mr Pate said, while noting that authorities were still investigating the circumstances surrounding her entry into Nigeria.

The patient, an unidentified woman who recently arrived in Nigeria on an international flight from Uganda, is currently in isolation and receiving medical care at a private hospital in the FCT.

Symptoms

Mr Pate urged Nigerians and health workers to watch for symptoms including fever, headache, nausea, vomiting, body aches, and severe muscle pain.

He said the Ebola variant involved in the current outbreak is different from the Sudan and Zaire variants, adding that bleeding could occur but is less prominent than with some other Ebola variants.

The case comes amid an ongoing regional outbreak of Bundibugyo Ebola virus, which the NCDC has been monitoring since the outbreak was reported in the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC).

The minister also stressed the importance of travel history when assessing suspected cases, particularly among people who have recently travelled to eastern Africa.

He said the Abuja patient had no confirmed travel to the DRC, so authorities presumed she was likely infected in Uganda.

“We presume it is likely that it was picked up in Uganda,” he said, stressing the complexity of tracing the source of infectious diseases.

Regional outbreak continues

The Nigerian case comes amid an ongoing Ebola outbreak in the DRC, where the disease has spread across several provinces.

WHO reported more than 8,700 confirmed cases and more than 4,200 deaths in the DRC as of 6 October, with transmission continuing across dozens of health zones. The outbreak is caused by the Bundibugyo virus.

Kenya reported its first imported case on 6 October: a Kenyan citizen who had been living in the DRC and travelled to Kenya via Uganda.

On 20 October, Kenyan authorities confirmed a ninth case involving a close family member of the first patient.

Uganda, from which the Nigerian patient recently travelled, recorded 20 cases between May and June 2026. The country subsequently ended its outbreak after completing the required 42-day period without a new confirmed case.

World.title: Ebola in Abuja: 10 things Nigerians should know about the deadly virus
World.content:
The confirmation of an Ebola case in Abuja, Nigeria’s capital, has put the country’s health system on heightened alert, 12 years after it successfully contained an outbreak that claimed eight lives.

The latest case involves a woman who recently arrived in Nigeria from Uganda and is currently receiving treatment in isolation. Health authorities have identified 44 contacts and commenced intensive tracing and monitoring efforts to prevent further transmission.

Although officials have moved swiftly to contain the case, the development has revived concerns about Ebola, one of the world’s deadliest infectious diseases.

The outbreak has been linked in reports to the Bundibugyo virus, a type of Ebola virus for which no licensed vaccine is currently available. However, PREMIUM TIMES could not independently confirm which specific Ebola virus caused the imported case in Abuja.

Ebola is a severe infectious disease that can be fatal without prompt medical attention.

Understanding how the virus spreads, recognising its symptoms and knowing how to protect oneself are essential.

Here are 10 things Nigerians should know.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

1. Ebola belongs to the Filoviridae family

Ebola disease is caused by viruses belonging to the Orthoebolavirus genus within the Filoviridae family, commonly known as filoviruses. Scientists have identified several species that can cause illness in humans, including Ebola virus, Sudan virus, and Bundibugyo virus. This distinction matters because vaccines and treatments may not be equally effective against every species.

2. Ebola is one of the world’s most dangerous viral diseases

The disease can cause severe illness affecting multiple organs and has recorded fatality rates ranging from 25 to 90 per cent in previous outbreaks. However, survival chances improve significantly when patients receive early diagnosis, rehydration and supportive medical care.

3. Ebola does not spread through the air

Unlike COVID-19, influenza or other respiratory infections, Ebola is not airborne. People become infected through direct contact with the blood, vomit, saliva, urine, faeces, or other bodily fluids of someone who is ill with the disease. The virus can also spread through contact with contaminated clothing, bedding or medical equipment.

4. Symptoms can take up to 21 days to appear

According to the World Health Organisation (WHO), symptoms may develop anywhere between two and 21 days after exposure. Early signs include fever, severe weakness, headache, muscle pain and sore throat. As the illness progresses, vomiting, diarrhoea and, in some cases, bleeding may occur.

5. Ebola can look like malaria or typhoid

One of the challenges in detecting Ebola is that its early symptoms resemble those of common diseases such as malaria and typhoid fever. This is why healthcare workers rely on laboratory testing, travel history and contact history to confirm suspected infections.

6. Infected people become contagious only after symptoms begin

A person exposed to Ebola cannot transmit the virus before symptoms appear. Once illness develops, however, the risk of transmission increases significantly through contact with bodily fluids. This is one reason health authorities monitor exposed contacts for 21 days.

7. Good hand hygiene helps reduce risk

Regular handwashing with soap and water remains one of the simplest and most effective preventive measures. Alcohol-based hand sanitisers can also help where appropriate. Health officials have advised Nigerians to maintain good hygiene practices and remain vigilant.

READ ALSO: Africa CDC calls for urgent global support as Nigeria confirms Ebola case

8. Avoid contact with bodily fluids and contaminated materials

People should avoid direct contact with the blood, vomit, urine, faeces and other bodily fluids of anyone suspected of having Ebola. Soiled clothing, bedding and medical materials may also harbour the virus and should be handled only by trained personnel using proper protective equipment.

9. Dead bodies can still transmit Ebola

The virus can remain active in the bodies of people who die from the disease. Traditional burial practices that involve washing or touching corpses have contributed to past outbreaks. Health authorities therefore recommend that trained teams manage the burial of suspected or confirmed Ebola victims.

10. Report symptoms or exposure immediately

Anyone who develops symptoms after possible exposure should immediately contact public health authorities and seek medical advice. People identified as contacts should fully cooperate with monitoring teams, provide accurate information, and promptly report any symptoms. Early reporting can save lives and help prevent further spread.

For now, health authorities are urging calm rather than panic.

Nigeria’s successful containment of the 2014 outbreak demonstrated the effectiveness of rapid case detection, isolation, contact tracing and public cooperation. As officials respond to the Abuja case, those same measures remain the country’s best defence against further transmission.

World.title: Protests in France, Spain, other European countries persist
World.content:
The protests in France and some other parts of Europe have continued as protesters remain persistent in their call for action over the high cost of living, low wages, poor-quality education, and corruption.

From France to Portugal, Albania, and Italy, social unrest continues. The demonstrations have been marked by looting, injuries, and running battles between the police and rioters.

In Spain and Portugal, tent camps have sprung up to protest unaffordable housing amid strong uncertainty among European youth.

The unrest comes as far-right parties gain public acceptance and record electoral gains. Europe also faces a critical moment in its support for Ukraine, with President Donald Trump seeking to establish relations with President Vladimir Putin of Russia.

In France, it comes ahead of France’s election, which is scheduled to be held in April 2027.

Right-wing politicians are seizing the chaos as their moment. Experts have said the combination of severe street protests, soaring energy costs, and weak centrist leadership is creating a perfect political climate for anti-establishment campaigns.

Earlier in the week, Maria Le Pen of the far-right National Rally party attributed the looting and destruction that trailed the demonstrations to the “decades of immigration” to France.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

She presented her party as capable of restoring order and said President Emmanuel Macron’s leadership no longer has any “credibility or authority.”

The politician is already far ahead in recent polls and is considered likely to be the next leader.

Meanwhile, French authorities said they have arrested over 2,400 people across the country.

Portuguese police also arrested 55 people in Lisbon.

PREMIUM TIMES reported that the violent demonstration in France began as a small school protest at Saint-Exupéry high school in a Parisian suburb on 21 September.

It initially attracted little attention, then snowballed into wider social unrest across Europe.

President Emmanuel Macron declared earlier in the week that “nothing justifies” the violence.

He said that “listening to the anger” doesn’t mean those who vandalised and looted will go unpunished.

He also promised “full transparency” on the police’s response to the protests.

World.title: Osun plans statewide AI surveillance system, drones to tackle insecurity
World.content:
The Osun State Government has announced a plan for a statewide surveillance network using artificial intelligence-enabled cameras, drones and radar to monitor security threats across communities, schools, businesses and other public facilities.

Governor Ademola Adeleke, who disclosed this on Tuesday, said the initiative is being developed in partnership with Chinese technology company Hefei Shengwen Information Technology Company Limited.

According to a statement by the governor’s spokesperson, Olawale Rasheed, Mr Adeleke met executives of the company on Monday to discuss and finalise details of the proposed project. The delegation was led by Cai Jianfei, the company’s director of international operations, and Nemo Guo, its manager of overseas operations.

The planned system will link surveillance technologies to a central Command and Control Centre, where security developments across the state would be monitored in real time.

“The planned security projects include the installation of a comprehensive and state-of-the-art security and intelligence system and platform in Osun State in order to ensure security coverage of the entire State. The security status of the entire State will be monitored from the Command and Control Centre,” the statement read.

The tools listed by the government include artificial intelligence-enabled cameras, drones, radar, robotics and Internet of Things devices. The statement added that the project will also include a safe-school initiative and a mobile application that would allow residents to connect with the command centre.

The proposed coverage also extends to banks, industries, farms, mining sites, commercial centres, bus parks and motor garages across major towns and routes in the state.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

“Our plan is to create an inclusive security platform that will fully secure and protect our people. From schools, hospitals, businesses and border communities, this initiative is a strategic option,” Mr Adeleke said.

The governor said the initiative would build on his administration’s establishment of the Osun State Security Trust Fund, which he cited as part of efforts to strengthen the state’s security infrastructure.

Mr Jianfei described the proposed project as an inclusive approach to protecting residents and businesses and invited Mr Adeleke to China for a working visit, according to the state government’s statement.

Osun’s security threats

Osun State has faced growing security concerns in recent months, including killings linked to political violence, suspected cult clashes and communal disputes.

In June, the state government said several political killings remained unresolved, while civil society group Kimpact Development Initiative documented 73 election-related violent incidents resulting in 29 deaths between October 2025 and June 2026.

The concerns have continued beyond political violence. In October, Mr Adeleke summoned security chiefs following a spike in security breaches, particularly killings reportedly involving rival cult groups. The state has also recorded deadly communal disputes and other violent crimes, raising concerns about residents’ safety.

World.title: Sule Lamido’s son denies, money laundering, bribery charges against him, his father, others
World.content:
Mustapha Lamido, son of former Jigawa Governor Sule Lamido, on Tuesday, denied the bribery and gratification charges brought against him, his father and others by the Economic and Financial Crimes Commission (EFCC).

Mr Mustapha, the third defendant, denied the allegations before trial judge Ijeoma Ojukwu of the Federal High Court in Abuja.

He testified as the fifth defence witness.

The EFCC is prosecuting the ex-governor alongside his two sons – Aminu and Mustapha, on N1.35 billion money laundering charges.

Others defendants in the case are Aminu Abubakar, Bamaina Company Nigeria Ltd, Bamaina Aluminium Ltd, Speeds International Ltd and Batholomew Darlington Agoha as 4th to 8th defendants respectively.

The EFCC alleged in the 37 charges that Mr Lamido abused his position while serving as governor between 2007 and 2015.

The commission accused him of laundering sums of money received as kickbacks from companies that were awarded contracts by the Jigawa State Government under his leadership.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

The defendants, however, pleaded not guilty to all the counts.

In his testimony on Tuesday, Mustapha, led in evidence by defence lawyer Joe Agi, a Senior Advocate of Nigeria (SAN), told the court that the allegations in the entire 37 counts were untrue.

He said all the sub-contracts awarded by Dantata and Sawoe Construction Company to their companies were duly executed and paid for.

Mustapha deneid that the several millions of naira mentioned in each of the counts were indirectly paid as bribery and gratification to Mr Lamido, who was governor at the time.

He said though his father was a director in the companies, he managed them without the ex-govenor’s interference.

He said he bidded for the sub-contracts with Dantata and Sawoe to supply bitumen, diesel, among others, and that the contracts were executed without his father’s contribution.

When Mr Agi took the the witness through each of the counts, he den8ed all the allegations.

“Was it the first defendant (Sule Lamido) who asked you to supply products to Dantata and Sawoe,” the lawyer asked.

“No my Lord. I have been a businessman all my life,” Mustapha responded.

He told the court that he started car sales when he was in university in 2002.

According to him, he borrowed N1 million from his father to start the business.

“Speeds International Ltd that I run, I sell cars. I took night bus from Kano to Lagos without my father’s knowledge then to Birnin Republic to purchase cars,” he said.

He said his father introduced him to the late Aminu Dantata before he became the governor of Jigawa.

Asked if he was the only supplier to Dantata and Sawoe, he responded in the negative.

He insisted that all the sub-contracts done with Dantata were legitimate and genuine.

Earlier, Mustapha, who said he lives in Kano, said he supplies goods and services, including petroleum products.

When Mr Agi asked him if he knew the defendants, Mustapha said: “Yes, the fitst defendant is my beloved father.

“The seond defendant (Aminu) is my elder brother. The fourth defendant is a family friend,” he said.

He also said that the three companies- Bamaina Company Nigeria Ltd, Bamaina Aluminium Ltd and Speeds International Ltd are family companies while Agoha (8th defendant) is a manager of all the companies.

He said Bamaina Company Nigeria Ltd was incorporated around 1984, and that after the company was incorporated, they started dealing in petroleum products.

When the lawyer asked him if he had documents to back the petroleum business, he responded in affirmative.

“Yes, we have but during post-election violence in 2011 in Kano State, some hoodlums launched an attack on our head office; Bamaina Nigeria Ltd and Bamaina Aluminium Ltd.

“The office was burnt down, and most of the documents were lost,” he said.

Mustapha, however, said that there are police extract, court affidavit where the companies were listed, report of the post-election violence and items listed, including the report of compensation by the Kano State government, as proof.

Judge Ojukwu admitted the documents in evidence because there was no objection by the prosecution lawyer, Chile Okoroma, a SAN.

When Mr Agi asked Mustapha if efforts had been made to get new documents, he said: “I had to go to my father’s archive in my village to get the photocopies.”

He said approval was gotten by his father to construct a filling station on 20 December 1984 at Bamaina Village in Birnin Kudu Local Government Area.

Some documents sought to be tendered by Mr Agi were opposed by Mr Okoroma, who prayed the court to reject them. The documents opposed by the prosecution included a Directorate of Fire Service letter to the Department of Petroleum Resources (DPR), Conoil letter to DPR, Bamaina’s letter to DPR, Nigerian Midstream and Downstream Petroleum Regulatory Authority (NMDPRA) Permit and car sale agreement.

The judge, in a ruling, held that the defence had satisfied the provision of the law since the documents sought to be tendered were original copies.

She, therefore, admitted them in evidence and marked them as Exhibits 84, 85, 86, 87 and 88 respectively.

After Mustapha was cross-examined by the EFCC lawyer, the defence closed their case.

Judfe Ojukwu adjourned the matter until 12 January 2027 for adoption of final written addresses.

(NAN)

World.title: FIFA U-17 Women’s World Cup: Flamingos beat Puerto Rico to revive campaign
World.content:
Nigeria’s Flamingos revived their campaign at the 2026 FIFA U-17 Women’s World Cup with a 2-0 victory over Puerto Rico in their second Group B match in Morocco on Tuesday.

Oluwakemi Adegbuyi opened the scoring in the 25th minute before Precious Oscar struck in stoppage time to seal Nigeria’s first win of the tournament.

The result provided a timely response for coach Akeem Busari’s side, who began their campaign with a 2-1 defeat to Poland and needed a positive result to strengthen their hopes of reaching the knockout stage.

Nigeria started brightly, with Chidi Harmony coming close to breaking the deadlock in the 16th minute, only for her effort to crash against the crossbar.

The Flamingos eventually made their pressure count when Adegbuyi found the net in the 25th minute to give Nigeria a 1-0 lead.

Nigeria held their advantage until half-time, leaving Puerto Rico to find a response after conceding the opening goal.

The second half saw the Flamingos protect their lead before Oscar struck in the 90th minute plus three to confirm the victory and secure all three points.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

The win was particularly important for Nigeria after their opening defeat to Poland, in which Wiktoria Skrzypczak scored from the penalty spot in the 33rd minute before Natalia Skrok doubled the lead in the 65th minute. Oluebube Umejiaku pulled one back for Nigeria in the 79th minute, but the late response was not enough to avoid defeat.

Puerto Rico, meanwhile, suffered a second consecutive loss after opening their maiden FIFA World Cup appearance at any level with a 6-0 defeat to Korea DPR.

The victory gives Nigeria renewed momentum as they pursue qualification for the Round of 16.

North Korea defeated Poland 6-1 in the other Group B match. The big win over Poland gives the Flamingos an advantage ahead of Friday’s Group B clash with the Koreans.

Under the tournament format, the top two teams in each group advance automatically, alongside the four best third-placed teams across the six groups.

World.title: APC Campaign Council creates new directorates, names Betta Edu, youth, women’s affairs, ministers as directors.
World.content:
The PBAT/APC 2027 Presidential Campaign Council has announced the creation of a new Directorate of Stage Organisation and Management and leadership adjustments to the Directorates of Youth Mobilisation and Women Mobilisation.

The decision follows the inauguration of the Presidential Campaign Council and is aimed at strengthening the Council’s organisational structure, enhancing coordination and improving operational efficiency ahead of the 2027 presidential election.

Under the new arrangement, Farouk Aliyu has been appointed director of the Directorate of Stage Organisation and Management, with Adejare Bello serving as co-director.

For the Directorate of Youth Mobilisation, Ayo Olawande will serve as director, while Dayo Israel has been appointed deputy director.

Similarly, Mary Idele will serve as director of the Directorate of Women Mobilisation, with Betta Edu as deputy director and Imaan Suleman as secretary.

READ ALSO: APC denies assassination plot against Atiku as US lobbyist raises alarm

The adjustments reflect the council’s commitment to building a well-coordinated, inclusive and results-driven campaign structure capable of effectively mobilising Nigerians, particularly young people and women, in support of President Bola Tinubu’s re-election bid.

The campaign council expects the appointees to bring their experience, commitment, and organisational capabilities to their respective responsibilities as preparations for the 2027 presidential election intensify.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

All appointees are expected to work collaboratively with other directorates and relevant campaign structures to advance the council’s objectives and ensure effective implementation of its mobilisation and campaign strategies.

Signed:

H.E. Hope Uzodimma

Secretary,

PBAT/APC 2027 Presidential Campaign Council

World.title: The death of a public intellectual: Patrick Dele Cole, 1940–2026, By Reuben Abati
World.content:
Death is a fact of life, no living thing exists forever, not even nature itself, for it is written that even the best and the brightest, shall pass to the Great Beyond, to become one with Nature and the Grand Architect, to be remembered on this side of the Divide, thereafter by their deeds. And so here we are, in the past few days, in the communications and ideas community, mourning the passing of Patrick Dele Cole, known variously as P.D. Cole, or PDC, 1940 -2026, who died in London on October 17, 2026, at the ripe age of 86. He was a historian, administrator, newspaper columnist, an author, politician, a manager of resources, and one of the most outstanding figures in contemporary Nigerian journalism who lived a life of impact and influence and has now left behind a legacy and a leverage that shine luminously upon him beyond his own humble beginnings.

His death coincides perhaps by accident with two other moments of remembrance in our industry: the death recently of Professor Idowu Sobowale on October 8, a retired Professor of Mass Communications at the University of Lagos, who along with other distinguished scholars at the University of Lagos, including Professor Alfred Opubor, Professor Frank Ugboaja, Professor Onuora Nwuneli, Dr Dele Ogunade, Professor Olatunji Dare, and Professor Ralph Akinfeleye, over the years trained generations of journalism and public relations practitioners in Nigeria. PD Cole also passed away two days to the 40th anniversary of the mysterious death of Dele Giwa, whose writings were celebrated yesterday in Lagos with the publication of a collection of his writings titled “Dele Giwa’s Granite Journalism”, edited by Mr. Ray Ekpu, another icon of the profession, the last surviving member of the famous quartet that established the Newswatch magazine. Dr. Patrick Dele Cole stood at the intersection between scholarship, journalism practice, and public intellectualism, and accordingly, some of the most important developments in Nigerian journalism for over three decades had his fingerprints directly or in the shadows, either by direct participation or by proxy or association. He was associated with both the Daily Times (1975 – 1979) and The Guardian Newspapers (from 1983 – 2026), two major organizations that formed the tap roots for much of everything else in the Nigerian media system. Dr. Dele Cole will be remembered for the quality of his associations, his deep commitment to the institutions he served, and his contributions to deepening that essential interface between media, business, society and public service.

I met him at The Guardian newspapers where I practised journalism for over 21 years serving as member, editorial board and columnist, editorialist, essayist, deputy editorial page editor, deputy editorial board chairman, and eventually as editorial page editor/chairman, Editorial Board. Dr Cole was one of the father figures at The Guardian and a towering presence. He was a friend of the publisher, Mr. Alex Uruemu Ibru and a consultant to The Guardian Editorial Board in which capacity he was a regular presence and contributor to the newspaper’s editorial choices. When Mr. Ibru chose to set up a newspaper company in 1982, he had sought the advice of two of his friends – Chief Olusegun Osoba, a seasoned journalist, who had been editor of The Daily Times, and General Manager of The Herald Newspaper and Dr. Dele Cole, former Managing Director of The Daily Times who had also served in Nigeria’s Cabinet Office. Ibru had been advised by his elder brother, the wealthy and influential Chief Michael Ibru not to venture into a business that will throw him into conflict with authority and the firing range of Nigeria’s intolerant military government, but Ibru was motivated by the passion to publish a newspaper that would give voice to the downtrodden and the voiceless people of Nigeria. Osoba and P.D Cole encouraged him, and thus, The Guardian was born. Mr. Ibru had the resources to fulfil his dream. Osoba and Dele Cole recruited a team that had the capacity to build a newspaper that would be influential beyond Lagos, Mr. Ibru’s initial dream, rather, a newspaper that would be one of the best five in Africa written in the English language and definitely the best English language newspaper in Nigeria, and the West African sub-region. The newspaper surpassed the dreams of its founder. It became an institution. Its core team was made up of a tested editorial team from the Daily Times led by Mr, Lade Bonuola and Mr. Femi Kusa who manned the news production process and built a news war room that outmatched every other newspaper, and on the intellectual side, there was Dr. Stanley Macebuh, the liberal intellectual and prose stylist who built The Guardian into a better version of the Daily Times, an intellectual powerhouse that attracted the brightest writers and turned The Guardian Editorial Board into the equivalent of a first rate Faculty. Dr. Dele Cole had a hand in building that Faculty and it is a measure of his commitment, that long after Mr. Ibru’s death, and the newspaper industry in Nigeria had turned South, he remained faithful.

For a proper appreciation of the place of Dr. Dele Cole in contemporary Nigerian journalism, we have to return to his journey into the industry. Born on August 4, 1940, in Abonnema, Kalabari Kingdom, in present-day Rivers State, he studied at St. Bartholomew’s School, Enugu (1946 -1953), Baptist High School, Port Harcourt (1954 -1958), and Ibadan Grammar School (1959 – 1960). He left Nigeria in 1962, on a Federal Government Scholarship to study at the University of Otago in Dunedin, New Zealand, graduating with a First Class Honours in History in 1965. From 1966, he studied at the University of Cambridge, obtaining a Master’s in History and later a Ph..D in 1973. He was a Visiting Professor at the University of Pennsylvania, USA, in 1969, and a Fellow at King’s College, Cambridge. Upon his return to Nigeria, he served as an administrative officer in the Political Department of the Cabinet Office in Lagos. He distinguished himself so well at the Cabinet Office that when in 1975, the Murtala Muhammad administration decided to clip the wings of those it considered the irreverent journalists at the Daily Times, it chose to appoint Dr Cole as a non-executive director at the Daily Times, to oversee government’s interest, after the Federal Government had acquired 60% of the newspaper through NICON Insurance. By the way, the Nigerian government did not pay up its equity stake, it more or less seized the newspaper and its assets. Cole’s assignment was to check the boldness of the Daily Times and its editors. With Alhaji Babatunde Jose at its helm, the Daily Times had become a thorn in the flesh of the government. When Dele Cole arrived at the Daily Times, and was later appointed Managing Director in 1976, he did the very opposite of what he had been sent to do.

He preserved Jose’s legacy and defended the freedom of the press, editorial independence and the rights of journalists. He protected the right of the newspaper to write its own editorials, and the right of journalists to protect their sources as exemplified by the decision in Momoh v. Senate, which became a cause celebre. Cole’s most memorable contribution at The Daily Times, however, was that he revolutionized the newspaper’s editorial board by attracting to the team, a group of heavily educated writers and thinkers. He brought in the likes of Dr. Stanley Macebuh, Dr. Doyin Aboaba (later Abiola) and writers like Dele Giwa. He re-organized the newspaper’s editorial board after the American model, separating it into a think-tank, separate from the newsroom, with a loud, authoritative voice. This approach changed the editorial structure in the Nigerian media system permanently, and this was the model that was introduced at The Guardian from the very beginning, and was further deepened to turn The Guardian into an academic forum that also catered to the interests of business and the public sector. There was no other newspaper of that character before The Guardian, which inherited the best of the Daily Times and transformed it. When I arrived at The Guardian, I was a benefactor of what had already become an established tradition. Dr. Dele Cole was a major architect of that tradition. He was a regular presence at our Editorial Board meetings. It was a deliberately diverse, well-resourced board of accomplished and tested, experienced figures, men of calibre who had seen it all, in and out of government, in various fields of human endeavour. They enriched editorial decisions, but nobody had the final say, not even the Chairman and Founder of the company, Mr Alex Ibru. Editorial decisions were built through consensus, guided by the policy to express an informed opinion, written in elegant language, upholding the principles of fairness, balance and justice to all concerned.

Dr Cole was the quintessential public intellectual and polymath. He knew Nigeria intimately because he had studied it, worked for it and had served it in various capacities for so long, he knew almost all the important people of his time, in and out of the corridors of power. He was a natural go-to person. He served on the Presidential Panel on the History of Nigeria since Independence (1977), Nigeria-China Forum (1979), and was Nigeria’s Ambassador to Brazil and Argentina (1987 – 90). He was actively involved in party politics, diplomacy, public service and public discourse. In the early 90s, he was one of the leaders of the Social Democratic Party (SDP) on whose platform he sought the Presidency before the initial entire primary election process of 1992 was cancelled by the Babangida government. He was later Deputy National Chairman, South-South of the People’s Democratic Party (PDP), 1998 – 1999, and Special Adviser to President Olusegun Obasanjo on International Relations (1999 -2001). He was a supporter of Chief MKO Abiola who eventually emerged as the SDP presidential candidate and winner of the aborted 1993 Presidential election, as he defended the people’s democratic choices and the right of minorities to co-exist and prosper within a federal system. The various tributes that have been paid to him speak to the scope and breadth of his influence, and the high regard in which he was held by everyone who was privileged to know him. Notably, the Pan Niger Delta Forum (PANDEF) has declared seven days of mourning in his honour and in appreciation of his contributions to the socio-cultural and political development of the Niger Delta and his role in the formation and growth of PANDEF. President Olusegun Obasanjo whom he served in the Cabinet Office and later as Special Adviser on International Relations (1997 – 2007) describes him as “one of Nigeria’s finest intellectual pillars” and “a trusted ally whose counsel shaped pivotal moments in our nation’s history” and as “an indispensable linchpin of our foreign policy machinery…who worked tirelessly behind the scenes to repair Nigeria’s broken diplomatic ties…” . Governor of Rivers State, Simi Fubara says he is “a beloved elder statesman and a distinguished son of the soil”. Former Governor of Delta State, Chief James Ibori describes him as “a steadfast advocate of the Niger Delta cause whose actions reflected deep loyalty to his roots”. Dr Charles Omole, says he was “an exceptional gentleman, a brilliant mind, a former boss, and a cherished friend.” President Bola Ahmed Tinubu in a personally signed tribute writes that Ambassador Dele Cole “witnessed defining moments in Nigeria’s history and contributed to the nation’s development through his work in the media, diplomacy and public service. His life stands as a testament to the value of experience, principled engagement and commitment to the public good.”

Dr Cole wrote on various topics reflecting a catholic breadth, while reflecting on such issues as corruption, federalism, international affairs, youth unemployment, governance and the responsibilities, and he did this in a distinctive style, even till his last years as seen in such pieces in his column with the Vanguard Newspaper as “The radicalization of political conflict” (February 24, 2020), “Nigeria and the Rule of law” (April 6, 13, and 20, 2020), US military and Nigerian military (March 9, 17, 2020), Prof. Bolaji Akinyemi and “Visions” (August 4, 2020), “Where are the Nigerians?” (August 25, 2020), “Pay of the National Assembly Members” (September 8, 15, 2020), “Nigeria and abandoned projects (October 18, 2022), “Russia, Ukraine and war propaganda” (August 17, 2023) and in the Financial Times of London, “We have to track down the oil thieves” (July 23, 2022). He was also the author of Modern and Traditional Elites in the Politics of Lagos (1975) and Nigeria Since Independence: The First 25 Years: Politics and Constitutions (1989), in addition to introductions to books as well as articles in international journals. Beyond his writings, speeches, diplomacy and citizen engagements, Dr Cole was also a bridge builder who loved the good life. He, Dele Giwa, Stanley Macebuh and Yemi Ogunbiyi pioneered the gradual influx of intellectuals and academics into journalism and the trend of sartorial elegance in Nigerian journalism, to which he added a sassy touch with his ever-present big, Cuban cigars which more or less formed a part of his public persona. He was also an easy-going, approachable man who would call to discuss topical issues or provide useful guidance and he did so, literally, till his walking stick failed him. He has now transitioned to the Grand Lodge above after a lifetime of honour, hard work, impact, service and distinction in his earthly toils. He will be greatly missed. We celebrate him. Farewell, sir.
