World.title: Saudi finance minister promises to review delayed US$77 million solar energy loan for Belize
World.content:
Saudi finance minister promises to review delayed US$77 million solar energy loan for Belize

By Breaking Belize News Staff: Prime Minister John Briceño says he personally raised Belize’s long-delayed solar energy financing arrangement with Saudi Arabia’s finance minister during meetings in Bangkok, Thailand.

Briceño explained that he attended a small gathering involving several high-level participants, including the Saudi finance minister, where he took the opportunity to raise concerns over the delayed project.

According to the Prime Minister, the Saudi official was not fully familiar with the details but assured him that he would examine the matter.

Briceño expressed optimism that the discussion could help move the project forward.

Belize signed a US$77 million financing agreement with the Saudi Fund for Development in August 2023 to support the construction of a 60-megawatt solar energy project.

However, as Breaking Belize News reported in August, Minister of Public Utilities Michel Chebat confirmed that no funds had been disbursed three years after the agreement was signed.

Chebat previously attributed the delays to procurement requirements, engineering consultations and procedures imposed under the Saudi financing arrangement.

The government has also discussed restructuring the project to combine solar generation with battery storage.

While Briceño described his conversation with the Saudi finance minister as encouraging, he did not announce a specific date for disbursement or the start of construction.

World.title: PM blames two-year delay in battery storage project on disputed iguana sanctuary claim
World.content:
PM blames two-year delay in battery storage project on disputed iguana sanctuary claim

By Breaking Belize News Staff: Prime Minister John Briceño has again criticized bureaucratic delays at the World Bank, claiming that a dispute involving an alleged iguana sanctuary in San Pedro held up a major electricity storage project for approximately two years.

Speaking after returning from international financial meetings in Bangkok, Briceño said the government had been pursuing World Bank financing for battery storage facilities capable of supplying approximately 40 megawatts of electricity.

According to the Prime Minister, the project was delayed after concerns were raised that land earmarked for the development was being used as an iguana sanctuary.

Briceño disputed the claim, describing the person occupying the property as a squatter, and said World Bank officials were embarrassed when he explained the circumstances during their meeting.

He argued that the delay had serious consequences for Belize’s energy security.

The Prime Minister explained that battery storage would allow Belize to purchase cheaper electricity from Mexico during periods of low demand, particularly in the early morning hours, store the power and use it during peak consumption periods.

He suggested that the project could have helped Belize avoid some of the electricity supply problems it has experienced.

The World Bank announced the US$58.4 million Belize Energy Resilience and Sustainability Project in February 2025. The initiative includes battery energy storage systems at four strategic locations to improve electricity reliability and reduce dependence on imported power.

Briceño said the government is continuing discussions to resolve the outstanding issues while pursuing greater energy independence through solar and other renewable sources.

World.title: PM seeks extension of World Bank agriculture project as March 2027 deadline approaches
World.content:
PM seeks extension of World Bank agriculture project as March 2027 deadline approaches

By Breaking Belize News Staff: Prime Minister John Briceño says Belize is requesting an extension of a World Bank-funded agricultural development project, warning that complicated administrative requirements have delayed its implementation.

Speaking following his return from Bangkok, Briceño explained that the project is intended to assist small farmers in adapting to climate change through improved agricultural practices and technology.

However, he complained that the World Bank’s requirements and approval procedures have made it difficult for Belize to complete the necessary work within the prescribed timeframe.

The Prime Minister said he raised the matter directly with two World Bank vice presidents during his overseas meetings.

The project is scheduled to conclude in March 2027, but Briceño said the government has made the case for additional time to ensure that farmers benefit from the initiative.

According to the Prime Minister, a World Bank technical team is expected to visit Belize shortly to review implementation, assess the project’s successes and consider the government’s request for an extension.

The Climate Resilient and Sustainable Agriculture Project, approved in March 2022, aims to improve agricultural productivity and encourage the adoption of climate-smart farming practices. World Bank records identify March 31, 2027, as its scheduled closing date.

Briceño expressed optimism that the government’s discussions would help secure more time for the project, although no extension has yet been confirmed.

World.title: Belize seeks millions in financing to tackle sargassum crisis
World.content:
Belize seeks millions in financing to tackle sargassum crisis

By Breaking Belize News Staff: Prime Minister John Briceño says Belize is pursuing millions of dollars in international financing to address the worsening sargassum crisis affecting the country’s coastline.

Speaking upon his return from the IMF and World Bank Annual Meetings in Bangkok, Thailand, Briceño said discussions focused on securing low-interest financing with long repayment periods to support a more comprehensive response to the problem.

According to the Prime Minister, Belize is working to access an initial US$5 million, with hopes of securing an additional US$5 million. He also referred to a broader financing target of approximately $20 million, although he did not clarify the currency or how the additional funding would be secured.

Briceño argued that Belize and other Caribbean countries are being forced to bear the financial consequences of environmental challenges they did little to create.

The Prime Minister said the government is seeking regional and international cooperation to address the problem, which threatens tourism, coastal communities and livelihoods.

During his visit to Bangkok, Briceño had also outlined plans to seek World Bank financing for sargassum removal and to explore the possibility of converting the seaweed into energy.

The discussions have not yet resulted in a publicly confirmed financing agreement.

World.title: PM Briceño rejects claims that constituency development funds are used to buy political loyalty
World.content:
PM Briceño rejects claims that constituency development funds are used to buy political loyalty

By Breaking Belize News Staff: Prime Minister John Briceño has rejected suggestions that constituency development funds are being used to maintain political loyalty among voters, insisting that the programme allows elected representatives to respond more efficiently to community needs.

Speaking to reporters following his return from Bangkok, Briceño was questioned about concerns that ministerial allowances and constituency development spending could contribute to political clientelism.

The Prime Minister dismissed the suggestion, arguing that the Constituency Development Fund was established to give area representatives greater flexibility to address urgent problems within their divisions.

He explained that under previous arrangements, representatives often had to seek assistance from various government ministries to carry out relatively small projects, including fixing drains, repairing school facilities and undertaking community improvements.

According to Briceño, the fund allows area representatives to make decisions more quickly without navigating lengthy administrative processes.

He also maintained that allocations are determined based on the number of registered voters in each constituency and that the programme is available to representatives from both the People’s United Party and United Democratic Party.

The Prime Minister described the system as successful and rejected the suggestion that it was designed to encourage political loyalty.

His comments come amid continuing public debate over government spending, political patronage and the accountability of funds administered through elected representatives.

Briceño maintained that the objective of the programme is to deliver assistance to communities more effectively and efficiently.

World.title: International News: Hobby Lobby founder walks away from $22 Million in Halloween sales over Christian beliefs
World.content:
International News: Hobby Lobby founder walks away from $22 Million in Halloween sales over Christian beliefs

By Zoila Palma: David Green, founder of the American retail chain Hobby Lobby, says he gave up more than $22 million in Halloween merchandise sales after deciding that selling the products conflicted with his Christian faith.

According to a segment on Newsmax’s “National Report”, Green recalled that the company had generated millions of dollars from Halloween merchandise before he felt spiritually compelled to stop selling the items.

“I was carrying Halloween merchandise as an example and we sold over $22 million worth of it,” Green said.

He described Halloween as “a dark holiday and a celebration of death,” expressing concern about merchandise featuring blood and horror.

Instead, Hobby Lobby offers seasonal decorations associated with autumn and Thanksgiving, including pumpkins, scarecrows and leaves.

Green said his decision reflects a broader commitment to maintaining the company’s religious principles, even when doing so means sacrificing potential profits.

“We will never compromise our Christian faith or our integrity for more money,” he said, adding that he believes God has blessed the company in the long term.

World.title: Briceño responds to Dean Barrow’s criticism, says government remains focused on social justice
World.content:
Briceño responds to Dean Barrow’s criticism, says government remains focused on social justice

By Breaking Belize News Staff: Prime Minister John Briceño has responded to criticism from former Prime Minister Dean Barrow, arguing that his administration remains committed to improving the lives of Belizeans despite challenges within government.

Speaking with reporters following his return from Bangkok, Briceño said Barrow had acknowledged that the People’s United Party administration was doing some things right.

The Prime Minister conceded that his government was not perfect and that mistakes had been made, but insisted that his administration attempts to correct problems when they are identified.

He rejected the suggestion that recent controversies had distracted the government from its broader objectives, maintaining that social justice remains central to its policies.

Briceño also declined to become involved in the internal affairs of the United Democratic Party, saying his priority was maintaining focus within the PUP and delivering on the government’s commitments.

His response follows remarks made by Barrow during an October 8 interview with 7 News, in which the former Prime Minister criticized what he described as serious problems involving governance, dishonesty and divisions within the current administration.

Barrow also acknowledged challenges facing his own party, suggesting that the UDP had not yet developed into a sufficiently strong opposition.

Briceño maintained that his government’s focus remains on addressing the needs of Belizeans rather than becoming distracted by political criticism.

World.title: NWC seeks 51 per cent tariff increase
World.content:
Acting NWC President Kevin Kerr

KINGSTON, Jamaica — The National Water Commission (NWC) has applied to the Office of Utilities Regulation (OUR) for a 51 per cent tariff increase, a move that could affect its approximately 500,000 customers.

Acting NWC President Kevin Kerr told the Public Accounts Committee (PAC) on Tuesday that the application was submitted to the OUR last Friday, adding that the regulator is expected to make an announcement shortly.

Kerr said the proposed increase is tied to an investment plan designed to secure funding for the company’s priority projects.

He warned that if the OUR does not approve the full 51 per cent increase, the NWC would have to revise its investment plan.

Kerr also noted that members of the public would have an opportunity to provide feedback through a consultation process before the OUR makes a determination on the application.

The NWC has argued that the increase is necessary to bring its revenues in line with its expenses. The commission last received a tariff increase in 2019.

NWC Chief Financial Officer Fabian Christie told the committee that the company’s revenue position had deteriorated over time, particularly in relation to customer payments.

He said the proposed increase was needed to keep pace with rising operating costs, including energy expenses.

World.title: 11 things only a Queen’s girl would know
World.content:
In this file photo, Miss Jamaica World 2010 Chantal Raymond strikes a pose with a group of students from the Queen's School.

From the famous ‘Holy Ground’ to the lizards roaming the school grounds, The Queen’s School had its own quirks, traditions and unwritten rules, according to the St Andrew-based institution’s alumni community.

Based on Observer Online’s discussions with past students, here are 11 things that will have any Queen’s girl reminiscing about life at the institution.

1. Holy Ground

Holy Ground never looked or felt particularly holy, so why was it called that in the first place? That remains a question worth asking. One thing was certain: students know the spot well, as it was reserved for devotions and, on occasion, punishment. It was hardly the place anyone wanted to visit for the wrong reasons!

2. Big Tree

Big Tree was one of the most recognisable landmarks on the school grounds. Towering over the area, it served as an outdoor lunchroom, complete with concrete tables and chairs where students gathered to eat, chat and socialise. And when all the seats were taken, the tables became seats, too. Rules or no rules, a girl had to find somewhere to sit!

3. The Hall

The Hall was the designated space for music and drama classes, but it doubled as a favourite hangout for several cliques. Getting students to leave was sometimes a task in itself, particularly for Mr Heriage, who old girls remember having had his hands full trying to get everyone out. For some, it was a classroom; for others, it was the place to catch up with friends.

4. Etheline Aiken

Legendary former principal who served as headmistress from 1976 to 1992. It was under her stewardship that The Queen’s School won the 1978 Girls’ Athletic Championship. Former students remember her as being strict, holding students accountable and requiring them to behave as proper young ladies. But, at the same time, she was well-loved.

5. The ‘iguanas’

Queen’s had lizards in every shape, size and colour imaginable. They were so plentiful that it sometimes seemed there were more lizards than students on the grounds. Whether perched somewhere in plain sight or scurrying across the grounds, these reptiles were a familiar part of the school environment.

6. The ‘Chiney’ shop across the road

The wholesale across the road was a popular stop before and after school. From bag juice and cake soap to rags and socks, it supplied students with a range of essentials. Despite repeated warnings not to cross the road to visit the shop, students somehow found themselves making the trip day after day.

7. Smithy, aka Mr Smith

When it came to Mr Smith, there were two sets of students: those who were lucky enough to be in his class and those who wished they were. Affectionately known as Smithy, he brought a distinctive personality and energy to Mathematics and Accounts lessons, making the subjects enjoyable. His famous Mathematics marathons were another highlight, giving students plenty to remember long after the lessons ended.

8. Reverend Pointsette’s prayers

Reverend Pointsette’s devotions could feel especially long when students had to stand in the blazing sun. Some would deliberately arrive late in the hope of missing part of the session, while her voice coming over the speaker in the afternoon was often met with collective sighs across the school. Those prayers may not have been everyone’s favourite part of the day then, but their value is something many have come to appreciate with time.

9. The in-school vendors

Every form seemed to have its own go-to vendor, making it easy to find a snack or treat after lunch. But the offerings went well beyond food. From haberdashery items and CDs to clothing, these enterprising young women catered to a variety of student needs. Even better, some have since registered their businesses and are thriving in their entrepreneurial ventures, showing that the hustle extended well beyond the school gates.

10. Mrs Keane-Dawes

Another long-serving principal, Mrs Keane-Dawes made it her duty to monitor the school gates in the mornings, earning her reputation as the school’s very own gate police. Strict but understanding, she commanded respect while ensuring students remained disciplined and focused. Her firm approach, balanced with compassion, helped create an environment in which students were encouraged to excel.

11. The standpipe

The standpipe, originally used to water the school grounds, often became a busy wash-up station shortly before the morning bell. Girls would gather to wash their faces and freshen up, with cake soap and soap dishes in abundance. With just 15 minutes to go before classes, the area could become quite crowded as everyone tried to get ready in time for the school day.

– Carlysia Ramdeen

World.title: Where is the outrage?
World.content:
Minister of religion Lisean Gordon delivering the sermon during the Heritage Week Thanksgiving Service at the Greater Highway Church of Christ Apostolic in Caterwood, Trelawny, on Sunday. Looking on are Mayor of Falmouth C Junior Gager (left) and moderator Leisa Dawson. (Photo: Horace Hines)

CARTERWOOD, Trelawny — Minister of religion Lisean Gordon has criticised what she described as the public’s readiness to demand justice when police officers use force, but silence following the killing of two members of the Jamaica Constabulary Force (JCF) last Friday.



Preaching under the theme ‘Let the Children Know’ during a Heritage Week Thanksgiving Service at the Greater Highway Church of Christ Apostolic in Caterwood, Trelawny, on Sunday, Gordon said the lack of comparable demonstrations demanding justice for the slain cops reflects a troubling imbalance.

“They may be somebody’s father, somebody’s son. Nobody came out because we have placed in the heart of ungodly people that we are allowing them to take over this country, all in the name of politics,” said Gordon as she addressed the service hosted by the Jamaica Cultural Development Commission (JCDC) in Trelawny and the Trelawny Municipal Corporation.

Two members of the JCF’s Special Operations Branch, Corporal Trevoy Shaw and Constable Devoney Rose, sustained fatal gunshot wounds during a firefight with men who had barricaded themselves inside a house in the Five Miles area of St Catherine on Friday.

Three civilians, Errol Hussey, his son Malique Hussey, and nephew Javoun Cogle, also died in the incident while a 10-year-old girl was left nursing a gunshot wound.

Delivering the sermon, Gordon condemned the tendency to vilify members of the police force without knowing the circumstances surrounding an encounter, and charged that media coverage and circulating recordings often fuel premature judgements.

Gordon linked the hostility towards law enforcement personnel to a broader erosion of respect for authority, and contended that political allegiance is encouraging Jamaicans to excuse behaviour they might otherwise condemn.

“There is something called the hidden curriculum, which we sometimes forget about. The hidden curriculum: What they see us do is what they will do,” said Gordon, who is also an educator.

She also took issue with verbal attacks against political leaders, including Prime Minister Dr Andrew Holness and Opposition Leader Mark Golding, warning that adults risk normalising disrespect among children who observe and absorb their behaviour.

“This disrespect that we put up with…because we are affiliated to a party, and to politics, it must stop. Disrespect is disrespect, and everybody who leads us needs to be respected, whether they are on the Opposition side or they are on the ruling side,” declared Gordon.

She argued that while children are taught to assert their rights, adults are neglecting the importance of responsibility and accountability.

“But we teach them about their rights, but no longer teach them about their responsibility,” Gordon said as she insisted that parents and other adults must uphold discipline, principles, and respect rather than retreat from the challenges of raising the younger generation.

She warned that Jamaica faces a dangerous escalation of disorder if the erosion of these values continues, describing the threat as a storm more severe than Hurricane Melissa.

“I am afraid of what is coming to Jamaica. There is a storm coming that is worse than Melissa… It’s called a storm of lawlessness, it’s called the storm of disorder, and it’s coming towards us. It’s worse than a Category 5,” said Gordon.

The minister of religion urged Jamaicans to reflect on the values they are passing on to their children as she argued that a meaningful inheritance extends beyond material possessions.

Meanwhile, mayor of Falmouth C Junior Gager, in his remarks, called on Jamaicans to preserve the legacy of the national heroes through their everyday actions rather than limiting remembrance to speeches and ceremonies.

“Our national heroes stood firm in the face of adversity, injustices, challenges, and paved the way for the freedom and opportunities we enjoy today,” Gager said.

He urged citizens to serve their communities, stand up for what is right, invest in young people, and work together to build a better Jamaica.

Gager also underscored the Church’s role in strengthening families and communities through prayer, mentorship, compassion and outreach, helping young people embrace their heritage and recognise their potential.

World.title: Ochie ‘Lovers Rock’ gets Hollywood pop-in
World.content:
Jimmy Fallon, host of The Tonight Show Starring Jimmy Fallon on NBC, hangs out with Steve James, promoter of Lovers’ Rock: A Night of British Reggae on Friday in Ocho Rios, St Ann.

A Hollywood power player showed up at Lovers Rock: A Night of British Reggae last Friday.

Jimmy Fallon, host of The Tonight Show Starring Jimmy Fallon on NBC, surprised the packed house at Ocean’s 11 Bar and Restaurant in Ocho Rios, St Ann.

Fallon popped into the venue with Wayne Jobson, the Jamaican impresario who is an influential figure in the Southern California reggae scene.

Steve James, who started ‘Lovers Rock’ earlier this year, was surprised when the American comedian appeared.

“I was very shocked! We had received an indication that he might attend, but there is a big difference between hearing that someone may show up and actually seeing them there,” he told the Jamaica Observer. “When we saw him we were pleasantly surprised and delighted. His attendance was certainly an unexpected highlight of the evening.”

James said Fallon mingled with patrons, most of whom are fans of lovers’ rock, the genre that emerged in the United Kingdom during the late 1970s and early 1980s.

Since 2014 Fallon has hosted his late-night talk show, which is consistently one of the top-rated in the United States.

Beres Hammond also attended Lovers Rock: A Night of British Reggae, which saw a performance from singer/bassist Lloyd Parks.

The South Florida-based James, who hosts the Real Rock Radio show, led the line-up of selectors who played songs that defined the lovers’ rock movement. Others manning the turntables were Martin Mitchell; Twinn Spinn from Fetedayzradio.com; DJ Jacko from King Jammy Sound System; Buppy C from Vibes FM London; and Lady Gee, formerly of Choice FM London and Vibes.

“The atmosphere was fantastic! Many patrons expressed how much they had missed hearing this kind of music. For them, it was more than just a night of entertainment; it was a nostalgic journey that transported them back to their days in the UK,” said James, who is considered an authority on lovers’ rock.

The genre produced several stars, most of whom were born in the United Kingdom to Jamaican parents. They include Janet Kay, Peter Hunnigale, and Maxi Priest.

Lovers Rock: A Night of British Reggae was first held during Reggae Month last February at Pon Top Seafood Grill and Bar in Kingston. The second staging took place at the same venue in May.

The fourth is scheduled for Kingston in February.

World.title: Netball Jamaica boss talks up Sunshine Girls’ chances in Horizon Series
World.content:
Jamaica’s Sunshine Girls will face England’s Roses in the four-Test Horizon Series, with the first two games set to be played in England on November 21 and 22 at the Copper Box Arena. The Sunshine Girls will then welcome England to Jamaica on December 5 and 6. (Photo: Naphtali Junior)

NETBALL Jamaica (NJ) President Karen Baugh has promised entertainment galore as the Sunshine Girls look to tackle England’s Roses in the Horizon Series next month.

The four-Test series was announced at a press conference held at S Hotel in New Kingston on October 13, 2026. The first two games are to be played in England on November 21 and 22 at the Copper Box Arena.

The Sunshine Girls are set to welcome the Roses to Jamaica on December 5 and 6.

“When Jamaica and England meet on a netball court you can expect intense competition, a bit of drama, excitement, and if Jamaica has anything to do with it, a little extra flair,” Baugh said.

“…This is much more than just two netball matches… it is an international sporting event, a celebration of our Sunshine Girls, and an opportunity to showcase the best of Jamaica netball and Brand Jamaica. This is definitely a rivalry worth watching.”

The Horizon Series — contested in honour of netball icons Molly Rhone of Jamaica and Jean Hornsby of England — began in 2024 with a classic.

Baugh recalled her favourite match, one she ranks alongside the 2026 Commonwealth Games win over Australia.

“That first match here against England, [in] the last second, we were leading by one and Shanice [Beckford] literally ran down the clock to prevent them from scoring again — and we won in the last second to tie the series. We went on to win the last game and won the series 2-1,” she said.

That Jamaica team had trailed 1-0 after the England leg — drawing the first, losing the second — before coming home to win the series.

In 2025 Hurricane Melissa forced the cancellation of the Jamaica leg, and England won the two matches played in England.

“The trophy, our trophy, is currently in England so we have a question to settle in 2026: Will the Rhone Hornsby Trophy be coming home?” Baugh asked.

In a historic first, Jamaica’s men’s team, The Suns, have been invited by England Thorns to play the curtain-raiser in London.

“It is a great opportunity for the male players to showcase their talent, and we wish The Suns every success in what is promised to be an exciting contest,” Baugh said.

Baugh said that for the home leg of the series, fans will get two matches for the price of one. England’s Roses Pathway team will tour Jamaica for a three-match series against the Jamaica Development Squad.

The first match will be on December 3, with the other two serving as curtain-raisers on December 5 and 6.

“You want to come really early. You want the place to be electric,” Baugh said.

Baugh said that the series forms part of preparations for the 2027 World Cup in Australia and comes on the back of a stellar year.

At the 2026 Commonwealth Games in Glasgow, Scotland, the Sunshine Girls won silver, stunning world number one Australia 46-45 in the semi-final before going down to New Zealand in the final.

“That was a statement to the world that Jamaica is among the very best in world netball,” Baugh said.

World.title: READY TO COMPETE
World.content:
Jamaican winger Jamone Lyle (centre) is expected to feature prominently for Jamaica at the FIFA Under-17 World Cup in Qatar in November. Here he is seen dribbling away from Canada’s Eloi Breton (right) and Ulrich Zamble during the Concacaf Under-17 Qualifiers encounter between Jamaica and Canada in Costa Rica on February 11, 2026. (Photo: JFF Media)

WITH the FIFA Under-17 World Cup now less than 30 days away, national under-17 Head Coach Wendell Downswell says the group have had to make the most of a less-than-ideal preparation period as they look to ensure they’re ready to compete at the tournament.

The young Reggae Boyz are set to make their third appearance at the global eventwhen it kicks off in Qatar on November 19. Jamaica have been drawn in Group E with European giants Italy, Ivory Coast and Uzbekistan.

The team booked their spot back in February at the 2026 Concacaf U-17 Qualifiers. However, they haven’t been able to secure international matches since.

Downswell, though, says they have made the best of the options available to them.

“It’s not been the ideal preparation that we have had because we were not able to get an international game; we were exploring at least two international games,” he

told the Jamaica Observer.

“However, we have been having camps — probably about four to five with the core of the players — which is good. And what we do is we prepare them in such a way that we use the Premier League teams and the Tier 2 teams as part of the measuring stick to see where we are in terms of the necessary preparation, and the boys have been responding very positively.”

“The coaching staff have explored all the possibilities to stretch these players somewhat similar to opposition that we’ll be up against in the tournament itself. So, hopefully this level of preparation, this kind of limitation that we have, will be of utmost significance for us going forward.”

Downswell says the technical staff have been closely keeping track of all the players they intend to select for the squad. However, he says several factors, including the ongoing ISSA Schoolboy Football, season haven’t made life easy.

“We release them and then some of them come back, [and] some come back with injuries here and there, knocks here and there,” he said. “[But] we have been having conversations with them. We have another camp coming up on the 6th and we have been having dialogue with the schools, so they won’t be released from the 6th up to our departure on the 14th.”

Downswell, who previously guided Jamaica’s U-17 team to the 2011 World Cup, says the players have been put through extensive preparation on and off the field, ahead of the tournament.

“We’ve put in place tactical preparation and the mental aspect of the players to get them fully focused regarding this task ahead. We have placed a lot of emphasis on the mental aspect of preparation, and the players have been responding in a positive way,” he said.

“Also, the whole preparation going in[to] international [games] — how we play the first 10 minutes, 5 minutes, the various tactical manoeuvres that we have done for the players to assimilate and adapt from a tactical standpoint — these are some of the things that we have been working on.”

Jamaica struggled in their two previous World Cup appearances, exiting at the group stage in 1999 and 2011 without recording a win in six matches.

Donwswell, though, is confident these young Reggae Boyz can break that trend and create history for the country. “I’m very upbeat, very enthusiastic about going, and at the same time our intention is to compete,” he said.

“Our first game’s against Italy [so] what we will do, the fact that we haven’t gotten much international exposure, so to speak, since February, [the plan] is using each game as part of our preparation and hoping that it lends itself in such a way that we are able to come out of the zone and take it from there.”

The squad, which is expected to feature new senior Reggae Boyz Jahmarie Nolan and Jamone Lyle, is set to be finalised by the first week of November.

World.title: When Granny’s Jamaican House Becomes the Mood Board
World.content:
Crochet, embroidery and handmade textile details bring texture and unexpected craftsmanship to the table.

Remember Granny’s house? The mahogany furniture that was built to last several lifetimes. The crocheted doilies strategically placed on every available surface. The lace and eyelet curtains. The tufted sofas and chairs that were definitely not for everyday sitting. The cabinet filled with the “good” glasses and patterned china that nobody was allowed to touch. And, of course, those decorative lampshades.

For years, many of us would have looked at these things and thought: old fashioned. Today? Put them on a mood board and suddenly they’re vintage, layered and chic.

Welcome to the wonderful cycle of design, where what was once considered old can become the next big trend.

Take mahogany, for example. In an old Jamaican home, dark, heavy wooden furniture was everywhere — dining tables, sideboards, coffee tables and those formidable chairs that seemed almost indestructible. After years of lighter woods dominating event design, deeper wood tones are beginning to feel sophisticated again. Pair mahogany with contemporary florals, beautiful linens and modern lighting and it takes on an entirely different personality.

Then there’s eyelet and lace. We remember them as curtains blowing at the window or perhaps a tablecloth brought out when company was coming. Now those same textures can inspire gorgeous linens, napkins and decorative details for weddings. Styled correctly, they feel romantic and intentional rather than old-fashioned.

And let’s talk about lampshades. Those decorative fabric shades that were once a fixture in Jamaican living rooms are finding their way back into stylish interiors and event design. Table lamps are appearing on dinner tables, bars and lounge areas, creating a warm, intimate, residential feeling that overhead event lighting simply cannot replicate.

Then there are the tufted sofas and chairs. Once associated with formal living rooms and furniture that children were warned not to climb on, tufting is having another moment. Used selectively in a contemporary lounge setting, a beautiful velvet tufted sofa or statement chair can add richness, character and just enough old-world glamour.

Even patterned china is having its moment. Remember those beautiful plates displayed behind the glass doors of the cabinet? Mix-and-match floral china, coloured glassware and vintage silver pieces can now transform a tablescape and make it feel collected rather than rented straight from a catalogue.

And yes, even crochet deserves another look. Perhaps we don’t need a doily under every vase, but crochet, embroidery and handmade textile details can bring texture and craftsmanship into an event in a way that feels personal and unexpected.

That’s really what this return to nostalgia is about.

We spent years trying to make everything sleek, minimal and perfectly matched. Now there’s something refreshing about a room that feels as though it has a story. The Jamaican homes many of us grew up visiting were layered. Things were collected over generations. Furniture was kept, repaired and passed down. The “good” pieces had meaning.

The trick is not to recreate Granny’s entire living room at your wedding.

Choose the memory, then reinterpret it.

A mahogany table with contemporary flowers. Eyelet linen with modern tableware. Patterned china against an unexpected tablescape. A beautiful lampshade incorporated into a bar or dinner setting. A tufted velvet sofa paired with contemporary coffee tables.

Suddenly, it isn’t old-fashioned. It’s nostalgic Jamaican style with a modern point of view.

So perhaps the next time you walk into an old Jamaican home and see that lampshade, embroidered cloth, tufted chair or piece of mahogany furniture you once thought was terribly outdated, don’t be so quick to dismiss it.

You might just be looking at your next event mood board.

World.title: Maybe it’s personal: Europeans worry Trump just likes Putin more than Zelenskyy
World.content:
As they scratch their heads for explanations for Trump’s latest turn against Ukraine, some European officials and diplomats think it comes down to the president’s personal preferences, as much as his country’s political aims.

“I do think it’s a personal thing,” said former British Cabinet minister David Lidington, now distinguished fellow at the Royal United Services Institute, a leading security think tank in London. “Trump is self-centered — his personal predilections for dictators and autocrats, his desire to give opportunities to U.S. businesses … are very important parts of his motivation.”

In private, EU officials agree. “Trump doesn’t like [Ukrainian President Volodymyr] Zelenskyy. He just doesn’t like him,” said one government official who has observed both men closely. “That makes it harder to get the U.S. to help on peace. Everything is a rational business deal with Trump, until it’s not.”

A diplomat from an EU country — granted anonymity, like others in this report, to discuss sensitive matters — said the inconsistent Trump could change his mind again and reverse recent moves against Ukraine. The U.S. president has chopped and changed on many issues, “except one thing,” the diplomat said. “He seems to be supportive of the Russians.”

“He’s been critical of Ukraine, the EU, NATO, but hardly ever said anything critical about Putin. It is striking. We have to deal with an administration that seems to be more pro-Russian than anything else,” the diplomat said.

The White House didn’t immediately respond to a request for comment.

World.title: Poland’s government votes to ease abortion laws in challenge to conservative president
World.content:
Still, neither bill would allow abortion on request up to 12 weeks of pregnancy, as Tusk's Civic Coalition promised during the 2023 election campaign. The multi-party coalition includes many conservatives and lacks agreement on the liberalization going this far.

Both bills now move from the lower chamber, or the Sejm, to the Senate, where they seem poised to pass, but their eventual fate remains uncertain. President Karol Nawrocki, an ally of the nationalist Law and Justice (PiS) party, said before his election in 2025 that he would not sign legislation easing abortion rules.

“By refusing to sign [the abortion] legislation, the president is hurting people," Włodzimierz Czarzasty, speaker of the Sejm, said Tuesday before the votes. "If he wants to hurt women, he will hurt them. I think women will see that and hear that.”

Tusk's coalition government will likely keep turning up the heat on the president and PiS if Nawrocki blocks the liberalization, as he has said he would.

Overriding a presidential veto requires a three-fifths majority in the Sejm that the Tusk-led coalition doesn’t have. The proposals that passed Tuesday lingered in a parliamentary committee for two years before surfacing, spurred by the campaign heating up 12 months before the next general election, slated for late 2027.

Overturning restrictions

At the parliamentary level, ending criminal penalties for helping women with abortion passed with 217 votes in favor, 213 against and three abstentions. The other bill won a slightly clearer majority of 233 for, 203 against and a single abstention.

World.title: US to offer Putin face-to-face talks with Zelenskyy and Trump
World.content:
Vladimir Putin attends an event in Moscow on March 18, 2025. | Pool photo by Maxim Shemetov via AFP/Getty Images

Steve Witkoff will fly to Russia for discussions about peace proposals on Wednesday.

U.S. special envoy Steve Witkoff will offer Vladimir Putin direct talks with President Donald Trump and Ukraine’s Volodymyr Zelenskyy in an effort to secure a ceasefire.

The proposal for three-way leaders’ negotiations on a peace proposal, the first such summit since Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine began in 2022, was announced at a press conference Tuesday after talks in Norway between Zelenskyy and Witkoff.

Norwegian Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Støre, who hosted the talks, said Witkoff will travel to Russia Wednesday and set out proposals for peace terms, including the idea of a three-way summit between the leaders. The meeting in Oslo came after days of high tensions between Ukraine and the U.S. president.

World.title: China threatens retaliation if UK follows the EU on tariffs
World.content:
A worker inspects an electric car at a Zeekr factory on Meishan Island in Ningbo, China on April 18, 2025. | Hector Retamal/AFP via Getty Images

China urged Britain to follow World Trade Organization rules and warned it against copying Brussels’ approach, arguing that tariffs on Chinese EVs would be discriminatory.

LONDON — Beijing has threatened to retaliate if the U.K. raises tariffs on Chinese electric vehicles, aligning with the European Union.

Responding to POLITICO’s story that Britain was looking to act in “lockstep” with the bloc to counter China’s market dominance in electric cars, a spokesperson from the Chinese Ministry of Commerce said: “If the U.K. insists on imposing restrictions on Chinese electric vehicles, China will resolutely retaliate and safeguard the legitimate rights and interests of Chinese industries.”

The U.K. is currently working with its European partners to avoid a 10% electric vehicle tariff from the beginning of next year, when stricter rules of origin under the Brexit trade deal kick in.

World.title: French presidential race largely unaffected by unrest, first post-riot poll shows
World.content:
The poll was conducted online from 8 p.m. Saturday — after rioting and looting had begun — until Monday.

Le Pen remains well ahead of the pack with 34% to 38% of the vote in the various scenarios tested. Given France’s presidential election moves to a two-person runoff if no candidate obtains a majority of votes on the first round, the battle for second place is shaping to be the most crucial story of the election.

That fight looks like it will be a tight one.

Mélenchon’s position remains similar to what it was before Saturday, despite the attempt by the government and his opponents to tie him to the unrest. The Ifop Fiducial survey has him either in sole possession of second place or tied for it in the various scenarios tested, though his lead on his nearest competitors — center-right former Prime Minister Edouard Philippe and center-left MEP Raphaël Glucksmann — is in some cases within the margin of error.

“The first feedback we’ve had from the ground — including from areas where we’re not held in high regard — is that the tactic of blaming us for everything isn’t working,” said a high-level Mélenchon campaign operative, granted anonymity to discuss internal campaign analysis.

Paris prosecutor Laure Beccuau told broadcaster TF1 on Monday that she “absolutely [could] not confirm” the government’s analysis based on the profiles of those arrested and placed under investigation in the French capital so far.

World.title: 5 things the EU wants to change about its Arctic policy
World.content:
The EU plans to set up a pilot research project using satellite and maritime observation in 2027 and share ship-tracking data to help identify Russian shadow fleet vessels.

In the longer term, it wants EU countries to lead on a maritime security hub to pool intelligence on threats ranging from undersea cable sabotage to illegal fishing. It also calls for setting up an Arctic Cable Hub alongside NATO to monitor and protect subsea cables in the North Atlantic and the Arctic. The strategy lacks any information on funding for these projects, however.

Finnish MEP Mika Aaltola of the European People’s Party said the new focus on the Arctic is long overdue.

“Europe hasn’t been thinking about [the Arctic] enough,” Aaltola said. “Because of the ice melting and climate change, it’s becoming kind of the next great game. And if that happens, then what are the European positions when it comes to Russia, China and also the United States?”

2. Access to energy resources

The new policy sticks with EU promises not to drill for fossil fuels in the Arctic.

“The EU remains committed to ensuring that oil, coal and gas stay in the ground, including in Arctic regions,” it reads. Instead, Brussels promises to develop renewable energy projects in the region but drops an old commitment to convince the rest of the world to follow its lead.

World.title: Kallas buys time on EU response to US sanctions against the ICC
World.content:
Multiple lawmakers continued to push for a faster response in a plenary session in Strasbourg. But while Kallas acknowledged their calls, she said the EU executive would take time "to analyze the full legal implications, to open dialogue and look for solutions." The sanctions are expected to be implemented after a 180-day delay starting from Oct. 9.

U.S. President Donald Trump's administration had already targeted nine judges and the chief prosecutor of the Court, cutting them off from all U.S. service providers, including banking services.

Irish European Affairs Minister Thomas Byrne, who represents Dublin's presidency of the Council of the EU, told lawmakers that the sanctions delay provides "an opportunity for dialogue, which we should take advantage of while remaining ready to take all necessary measures," as laid out by EU leaders in a statement issued after their gathering last week.

Washington is openly campaigning to dismantle the ICC “brick by brick,” and urging countries to quit the court’s founding charter. Kallas said that "decisions by Niger, Mali, Burkina Faso, Chad and Venezuela to reject or even withdraw from the ICC risk eroding the foundations of global justice."

"The ICC is under attack at precisely the moment when we need it the most," Kallas said, citing the Court's investigations of Russian war crimes in Ukraine. The EU will continue to engage with partners to strengthen the court, she said, warning countries under pressure from the U.S. to leave the body: “This also has clear consequences for their relationship with the European Union.”

"The European Union has practical means to do more," Kallas said, adding that she would be in the Hague this week.

World.title: Government expected to approve Jackdaw gas field on Wednesday
World.content:
An oil rig is seen off the coast of Scotland on April 24, 2026. | Andy Buchanan/AFP via Getty Images

Developers have been waiting for a fresh decision on the controversial gas field since January 2025.

LONDON — The government is set to approve Jackdaw, a major proposed gas field off the coast of Scotland, on Wednesday.

One senior government official and two people briefed on the plans told POLITICO they believed an announcement was planned for Wednesday. The official and one of the two people said it was expected in the early morning.

Energy Secretary Miatta Fahnbulleh is scheduled to sign off the environmental statement, overseen by the Offshore Petroleum Regulator for Environment & Decommissioning. The North Sea Transition Authority is also expected to rubber stamp the project's field development plan.

World.title: 'Time to make a deal,' Trump tells Zelenskyy as he complains US has got 'nothing back' from Ukraine
World.content:
US President Donald Trump said on Tuesday that he wanted his Ukrainian counterpart Volodymyr Zelenskyy to "make a deal" with Russia as he complained that the United States had received "nothing back" for its support for Kyiv.

 

Speaking to the media in the White House, Trump said: "We want Zelenskyy to make a deal. He can make a deal."

"He could have made a deal two years ago when we had our little chat in the Oval Office," he continued, seemingly referencing the pair's heated exchange during a meeting in early 2025. "He's going to have to want to make a deal, because I don't think his people are going to stand for it any longer."

Zelenskyy and Trump have endured a volatile relationship since the US president began his second term in January last year, but it has soured further in recent weeks after Trump struck a diesel deal with Russian President Vladimir Putin and criticised the impact of Ukrainian strikes on Russia's energy sector on global fuel prices.

On Tuesday, Trump - who is gearing up for key midterm elections to determine the make-up of Congress for his final two years in office - seemed to pin the blame for the ongoing war on Zelenskyy, repeatedly saying he had had the opportunity to make a deal and that the US had got nothing in return for its help "except grief, death," and "tremendous monetary loss."

"We have given tremendous amounts to Ukraine; we've got nothing back. Other than high diesel," Trump added. "The American taxpayers are tired of it."

"It's time to make a deal," he said.

Zelenskyy's Oslo talks

Trump's comments came shortly after Zelenskyy met with a US delegation headed by special envoy Steve Witkoff, who is scheduled to travel to Russia for a meeting with Putin on Wednesday.

Following the talks in Oslo, which also involved Finnish President Alexander Stubb and Norwegian Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Støre, Zelenskyy had appeared relatively positive, telling journalists he had recently held a constructive call with US Secretary of State Marco Rubio and calling for a trilateral meeting with Trump and Putin.

Zelenskyy also addressed reported restrictions on US intelligence sharing during a press conference with the Nordic leaders, saying he was "thankful" that "intelligence works now."

"I'm speaking about early warning, what is very important for our people, for children, adults, civilians, because we can hear when ballistic is coming," he said.

In a post on social media later in the evening, Zelenskyy added: "It was constructive because all of us want peace – Ukraine, Europe, the United States. And we will see what happens tomorrow."

World.title: Spain: Guardia Civil rescues family and dogs from rising floodwaters in Oliva
World.content:
Spain’s Guardia Civil has rescued a family and their dogs from a flooded home in Oliva, as heavy flooding continues to affect parts of the Valencia region.

 

Footage released by the Spanish police force shows an officer carrying a woman on his back through the floodwater, followed by a man being led to safety. The family is then taken out of the flooded town in a Guardia Civil vehicle.

Aerial images filmed from a rescue helicopter reveal large areas submerged near the coast, with emergency crews continuing operations to reach residents trapped by the rising water.

World.title: UK Typhoon fighter jets to fly 'defensive' missions to help protect Saudi Arabia from Houthi attacks
World.content:
The United Kingdom has pledged to provide "additional defensive military support" to Saudi Arabia as it continues to come under attack from Yemen's Houthi rebels, the Ministry of Defence announced on Tuesday.

 

In a statement, the department said Typhoon fighter jets would fly "defensive counter air missions" in an effort to support the defence of Saudi cities and "critical national infrastructure" from aerial attacks.

"These aircraft will operate in a defensive role and will not conduct offensive strikes against the Houthis," it said. "The UK will provide an RAF A400M to support the movement of defence materiel within Saudi Arabia, alongside UK military advisers to support Saudi staff officers."

British Defence Secretary Wes Streeting branded Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia as "absolutely despicable and dangerous for the region."

"In particular, people will bring to mind the bombing of civilian airports that led to hundreds of casualties," he told British media as he outlined the move, calling the attacks an "intolerable escalation."

The Saudi-led coalition forces - which were formed in 2015 to back Yemen's internationally recognised government - have reported increasing Houthi missile attacks on Saudi Arabia in recent weeks.

The Houthis declared a naval blockade of Saudi Arabia in July and have since been launching increasing attacks on Saudi cities and shipping, further heightening tensions in the Middle East.

A Houthi strike on Riyadh's King Khalid International airport earlier this month left 13 people dead and more than 300 injured, according to Saudi Arabia's General Authority of Civil Aviation.

World.title: Investment summit: German government strikes AI deal with Nvidia
World.content:
Shortly before the investment summit in Berlin, Nvidia boss Jensen Huang delivered a sharp slap in the face to Germany. He said it pains him to see how far this economically advanced country has fallen behind. And the 63-year-old CEO of the world's most valuable company gave what he sees as left-behind Germany some blunt advice: "Just get to work!" ("Just get on with your work!")

 

Yet Jensen Huang evidently still believes in Germany, because at a fireside chat with Chancellor Friedrich Merz, a crucial AI deal was agreed, according to media reports. As first reported by Handelsblatt, the federal government intends to contribute a nine-figure sum in euros to the cooperation.

The combination of German engineering expertise and cutting-edge AI technology is expected to give Germany's economic base lasting strength, Merz and Huang stressed.

In total, the chancellor said, the investment summit in Berlin produced commitments worth 800 billion euros up to 2028. Some 200 company bosses gathered for the meeting.

Amazon to invest 16 billion euros in Germany

Another US corporation, internet giant Amazon, plans to invest around 16 billion euros in Germany in 2027, as was also announced at the investment summit in Berlin. A third of the money is to be channelled into expanding data centres for Amazon's cloud provider AWS.

According to Amazon, around 3,000 employees already work in Germany for its cloud services subsidiary AWS. The planned 4.8 billion euros for AWS in Germany will be invested primarily in the Frankfurt am Main area.

Businesses urged to make their data available to AI

Nvidia says it invested almost a billion dollars in Germany in 2025. The US corporation, headquartered in California, holds stakes in numerous German start-ups and companies. Huang repeatedly stresses that data must be seen as a national resource, which should not be exported but used to build a "national intelligence".

Around a dozen German companies are expected to take part in the project with Nvidia, which is being supported by the federal government, including Siemens, Audi and AI start-up Black Forest Labs from Freiburg im Breisgau. Nvidia is already working with Siemens in Erlangen on device production.

Chancellor Merz called on companies in Germany to open up their industrial data to artificial intelligence, in order to safeguard the competitiveness of sectors such as the car industry. Maintaining Germany's industrial base is, the CDU leader argued, a crucial advantage over other economies.

Did Friedrich Merz manage to convince leather-jacket fan Jensen Huang with his comments about traditional German virtues?

In Berlin the chancellor actually declared: "Germans are considered hard-working, go to bed early and get up before sunrise. (...) On holiday we are the first on the beach and lay out our towels even before breakfast. And when we agree on delivery dates, we stick to them."

On the beach in Travemünde - how well is the German economy doing? Michael Probst/Copyright 2026 The AP. All rights reserved

Most recently, the outlook for the German economy has brightened somewhat. The International Monetary Fund (IMF) now expects growth of 1.3 percent in Germany in 2026, after previously forecasting just 0.7 percent. Whether a further upswing will materialise thanks to investments by US tech giants remains to be seen.

World.title: EU Parliament approves standard form for claiming refunds on disrupted travel
World.content:
The European Parliament has approved, by an almost unanimous vote, new rules to protect passengers when their travel is disrupted.

 

Travellers across the EU will be able to claim a refund using a standard form, which will be made available on the European Commission’s website in all EU languages and will cover all modes of transport.

Passengers are entitled to a full refund within 14 days and intermediaries such as travel agents or online booking platforms are included in the reimbursement obligations, which was not clear in the previous legislation.

If an intermediary does not provide the reimbursement in the time due, the airline is obliged to step in and make the payment to the passenger concerned.

"We are prioritising the rights of our citizens over the profits of airlines,” said Italian Socialist Matteo Ricci, the MEP in charge of the regulation.

The rules also strengthen the rights of people with disabilities: where necessary, a companion will be able to travel with them on a flight free of charge, as is already the case on buses, trains and ships.

The regulation passed with 652 votes in favour, two against and eight abstentions. It builds on a major overhaul of air passenger rights adopted in July, which made refunds easier to obtain and requires airlines to include one free item of hand luggage in the fares displayed online.

World.title: France's Macron begins state visit to Qatar as part of wider Gulf tour
World.content:
Qatar’s Emir Sheikh Tamim bin Hamad Al Thani welcomed French President Emmanuel Macron with full state honours, including cannon salvos and a cavalry procession, as he began his two-day state visit to the Gulf nation on Tuesday.

 

After the official welcome ceremony, the two leaders met at Lusail Palace to discuss strengthening strategic ties between France and Qatar, including energy security, defence and regional stability, as well as investments and cooperation in multiple fields.

Macron was received at Hamad International Airport by Qatar’s Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of State for Defence Affairs, Sheikh Saoud bin Abdulrahman bin Hassan Al Thani, after fighter jets escorted his plane on arrival as part of the state visit honours, followed by a state motorcade procession through Doha towards Lusail.

Macron's state visit to Qatar concludes his regional Gulf tour to develop strategic partnerships also with the United Arab Emirates, Kuwait and Bahrain, where the French leader secured pledges of additional energy supplies from Gulf partners.

The tour has already produced commitments for additional diesel. The French presidency said France had secured pledges for an extra 200,000 tonnes a month from the UAE and Bahrain, around 100,000 tonnes from each.

Including supplies from Saudi Arabia, the commitments totalled 295,000 tonnes a month, equivalent to just over 10% of French consumption, the Élysée said.

In a speech to the French nation on Sunday after a weekend of violent protests that engulfed France, Macron said he would travel to the Gulf countries to secure France’s energy supplies and to address the grievances over fuel prices and the cost of living, while his government worked with fuel distributors to ensure those efforts translated into lower prices for consumers.

Energy security and regional ties

Macron is accompanied by French business leaders including the chief executives of France's largest energy companies, TotalEnergies and Engie. TotalEnergies already has substantial interests in Qatar, including a partnership with QatarEnergy in the North Field East LNG expansion project, one of the world's largest.

Qatar’s foreign ministry said Tuesday’s talks would be followed by a strategic dialogue on Wednesday to discuss "many regional matters of mutual concern,” covering energy, the economy, investment and defence.

Speaking at a briefing in Doha, the ministry’s director of media and communication, Ibrahim bin Sultan Al Hashmi, described France as a friend and ally and underlined its position during the ongoing regional crisis.

France was among Qatar's main defenders during the Iran war, securing the Gulf country's air defence with fighter jets and other capabilities and is now seeking to develop additional defence ties.

The visit also builds on wider investment ties. During the Emir’s 2024 state visit to France, Qatar pledged €10 billion in investment across sectors including energy transition, artificial intelligence, aerospace, and healthcare.

World.title: IRGC mines set tankers ablaze as Tehran threatens expanded attacks
World.content:
Iran's IRGC said two oil tankers struck mines the elite paramilitary had laid in the Strait of Hormuz, setting both vessels ablaze, as Tehran threatened further attacks on shipping and cutting undersea cables while promising to unveil new weapons in its arsenal.

 

The IRGC said in a statement that the tankers tried to use what Iran unilaterally designates an unauthorised route through the strait's southern section, near the Omani coast.

"With the explosion of mines laid by the IRGC Navy in the illegal passage south of the Strait of Hormuz, two offending tankers were set on fire and brought to a standstill," the IRGC statement said. Neither vessel was named nor was the precise location disclosed.

Tehran has no recognised authority under international maritime law to restrict or authorise passage through the Strait of Hormuz, which is subject to the right of transit passage under the UN Convention on the Law of the Sea.

The UK Maritime Trade Operations (UKMTO) reported on Tuesday that it had received an account of "an incident between an oil tanker and military forces" on Monday, some 121 nautical miles east of the Omani city of Duqm. UKMTO reported no damage or casualties and did not identify the vessel.

The IRGC also claimed that their air defence system had shot down a US MQ-9 drone over the strait on Monday night. A US official, speaking to US media outlets, dismissed the claim as untrue.

Some Iranian domestic outlets, including the state-affiliated Fars agency, reported that a US airstrike hit a naval base in Konarak in Sistan and Baluchistan province on Monday, wounding two military personnel and targeting an air defence installation. Washington has not commented on the report.

IRGC spokesperson Hossein Mojabi threatened on Monday to target undersea internet cables in the Gulf and the strait, saying "new weapons will be unveiled" with the aim of, in his words, removing US military presence from the region.

'We do not leave any blow unanswered'

Iran's foreign ministry spokesperson Esmail Baghaei said Tehran would retaliate against any US attack.

"In practice we have shown that we absolutely do not leave any blow unanswered," he said in response to reports that Washington had urged Iran to hold back in the event of a strike on Kuh Kalang.

"A US attack on Kuh Kalang and Iran not responding is fantasy and empty talk," Baghaei said.

The IRGC-affiliated Tasnim news agency quoted an unnamed Iranian security source as saying uncertainty over decision-making authority in Washington was complicating negotiations, naming Vice President JD Vance, Secretary of State Marco Rubio and Trump administration negotiators Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner as figures whose respective roles remained unclear to Iranian officials.

Arsenio Dominguez, secretary-general of the International Maritime Organisation, said about 6,000 seafarers have been stranded in the strait since the war began. He criticised shipowners for continuing to send crews into the area.

US media have previously reported that the Pentagon was deploying the USS Theodore Roosevelt carrier strike group and the 13th Marine Expeditionary Unit to the Middle East, adding approximately 10,000 sailors and Marines to the region by the end of November. Washington has not confirmed the deployment.

Roughly one-fifth of the world's oil passed through the Strait of Hormuz before the war that began with US-Israeli strikes on Iran in late February. Both Tehran and Washington have implemented blockades in the strait, while Iran has repeatedly targeted cargo vessels using the southern section of the waterway.

World.title: Zelenskyy visits Norway amid Trump White House tensions
World.content:
Ukrainian President Zelenskyy met with Norwegian and Finnish leaders in Oslo and held talks with Trump envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner. Trump is pressuring Zelenskyy to "make a deal" with Russia.

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy visited Norway on Tuesday as Ukraine faces renewed tension in its relationship with US President Donald Trump and his administration.

Finland's Stubb: 'Today was a good day for peace'

During the visit, Zelenskyy met with Finnish President Alexander Stubb and Norwegian Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Store in Oslo, along with Trump envoy Steve Witkoff. The US president's son-in-law, Jared Kushner, joined the meeting remotely.

Store described the meeting involving the European and the US sides as "good and constructive" at a press conference.

"US and European teams have done substantive work on key issues together with Ukraine," Store said.

Stubb said, "Today was a good day for peace." The Finnish president said Witkoff intends to fly to St. Petersburg on Wednesday to meet with Russian leaders and discuss ideas from the Oslo meeting.

Trump envoy Steve Witkoff was not present at the press conference after the meeting Image: Jonathan Nackstrand/AFP

The Oslo meeting comes as Zelenskyy has accused the US of withholding intelligence from Ukraine in advance of Russian strikes and delaying the delivery of interceptor missiles.

Zelenskyy: Early intel warnings from partners on Russian strikes resume

Zelenskyy said he held a phone call with US Secretary of State Marco Rubio earlier in the day and said Ukraine is now receiving early warnings from its partners ahead of Russian strikes.

"We are thankful that intelligence works now, and I'm speaking about early warning, which is very important for our people, for children, adults, civilians, because we can hear when ballistic is coming," Zelenskyy said of the Russian-launched missiles while standing next to Finnish and Norwegian leaders.

There are also media reports that Trump, Russian President Vladimir Putin and Chinese President Xi Jinping could hold a meeting to possibly discuss Ukraine and other issues.

"I don't know what the trilateral meeting will be about between America and China, and Russia, it's up to them," Zelenskyy said, but added that if Ukraine is discussed, it would be acceptable only if Ukrainians are at the negotiating table.

Trump ramps up attacks on Zelenskyy as US midterms loom

Earlier this month, Zelenskyy criticized a deal struck between the Trump administration and Russia to buy Russian diesel fuel. Oil and gas export revenues are vital for the Russian economy and war efforts in Ukraine.

How Trump is helping Putin To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Trump has criticized Zelenskyy and blamed Ukrainian strikes on Russian oil refineries for high diesel prices. Prices have increased dramatically since Iran closed the Strait of Hormuz in response to US attacks.

Zelenskyy on Tuesday said he is supportive of Trump's suggestion to stop attacks on energy sites, with Russia also doing the same in regard to Ukraine as part of an "energy ceasefire." However, Zelenskyy said Russia is unwilling to stop its attacks on Ukraine.

At a recent European Union summit in Brussels, Zelenskyy smiled at the suggestion that he is being made a scapegoat by Trump.

The US president is looking for someone else to blame for high domestic energy costs ahead of midterm congressional elections onb November 3. If the opposition Democrats take back control of the US House and Senate, it could constrain Trump's powers in his last two years in office.

In comments to reporters at the White House on Tuesday, Trump said he wants Zelenskyy to "make a deal" with Russia and suggested Moscow has the upper hand.

Ukraine has been fighting off a full-scale Russian invasion since February 2022. In the past, Trump has blamed Zelenskyy for the war and on Tuesday again said it was up to Kyiv to end the Russian invasion.

“We want Zelenskyy to make a deal,” Trump told reporters in the Oval Office. “We’ve given a lot to Ukraine. We’ve gotten absolutely nothing back except grief, death, tremendous monetary loss.”

Trump said he also spoke with Putin about Stephen Hubbard, a retired US teacher detained in Russia accused of acting as a mercenary for Ukrainian forces.

"I've been talking to President Putin about Mr. Hubbard. I've been talking to him at length. I've asked him to release him. Let's see what happens," Trump said.

World.title: Nigeria records its first Ebola case, in capital Abuja
World.content:
Nigeria has reported its first known case of Ebola during Africa's latest outbreak originating in the DRC. Health Minister Muhammad Ali Pate said the patient was a woman who had recently flown to Abuja from Uganda.

Nigeria's Health Ministry on Tuesday confirmed that the country had recorded its first known case of Ebola in the current outbreak. A woman who recently arrived from Uganda tested positive for the virus.

The outbreak is thought to have started in the east of the Democratic Republic of Congo, not far from the Ugandan border, with Uganda the second country to record infections. It also recently spread to Kenya in limited numbers, with nine known cases recorded this month.

The overwhelming majority of known cases, however, remain confined to the DRC, particularly its eastern provinces.

Congo's Ebola crisis: Fear, mistrust and a growing outbreak To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

What do we know about the Nigerian case of Ebola?

Health Minister Muhammad Ali Pate said that the patient was a woman who had "recently arrived on an international flight from Uganda."

She first began to exhibit symptoms on October 7, and was admitted to a private Abuja hospital on October 11, before being tested and diagnosed with Ebola. He said authorities had already begun tracing 44 people identified as contacts of the patient.

"We are doing everything possible to contain this case by tracing all contacts the individual may have had," he said.

Nigeria's Center for Disease Control said two weeks ago that it was stepping up surveillance after the first recorded cases in Kenya, saying it was improving the country's preparedness for a possible outbreak.

"These efforts have focused on early detection, isolation and referral, laboratory diagnosis, infection prevention and control, contact tracing, risk communication and protection of healthcare workers," the agency said.

Nigeria created an Ebola task force in June.

"We do not want a repeat of what happened during the last outbreak when a carrier entered the country, and everyone was scrambling to respond," Femi Gbajabiamila, chief of staff to President Bola Tinubu, said when the task force was announced. "We have covered a lot of ground and established structures to address any potential threat."



Kenya has also been put on alert this month after identifying a cluster of nine cases, which officials believe all revolve around one initial patient Image: Andrew Kasuku/AP Photo/dpa/picture alliance

Over 9,000 cases in current outbreak, the fastest-growing on record

While Ebola does not spread as readily as highly contagious viruses like the flu or COVID, it is considerably more dangerous to those who do contract it.

The current outbreak, involving a lesser-known strain, the Bundibugyo Ebolavirus, has led to more than 9,000 confirmed cases and more than 4,300 deaths, a fatality rate of almost 50%.

Almost all the cases and deaths are confined to the DRC, even as more countries become involved. The first patient in Kenya died, and authorities believe the other eight known cases are all part of a cluster beginning with him. They say there's no sign of a spread beyond his contacts.

Uganda, which borders the Ituri province outbreak epicenter in DRC, reported 20 cases and two deaths quite much earlier this year. It was then declared Ebola-free in late August by the World Health Organization after reaching 42 days since a confirmed case. Tuesday's case in Nigeria could potentially put this status back into question, given the Health Ministry's comments on the patient's travel history.

This year's outbreak is already the second-largest on record and by far the fastest-spreading — although modestly improved testing and diagnostic capacity may also contribute to the higher numbers.

The West African Ebola epidemic of 2014-16 led to around 11,300 deaths from around 28,500 cases — but that was over a span of around 30 months. This outbreak was first declared in May of this year, although researchers believe it likely began in small numbers of cases several months earlier.
