World.title: Changes to Dentistry Under Croatian Health Insurance Fund
World.content:
October the 20th, 2026 – There are changes to certain aspects of dentistry within the scope of the Croatian Health Insurance Fund, with white fillings being part of the shakeup.

Instead of the previous amalgam fillings, the installation of white fillings at the expense of the Croatian Health Insurance Fund (HZZO) has been announced, even when they aren’t going to be placed on the front teeth. Poslovni reports that amalgam fillings entered history on the 1st of July, unless a dentist assesses that such a filling is necessary due to the patient’s particular health needs. This measure was introduced in Croatia on the basis of an EU regulation.

dentists are still charging…

In practice, however, the matter is somewhat different: the use of a white filling still comes with a cost if the patient wants a white composite filling of the kind that, according to HZZO rules, they should receive free of charge on their front teeth. The dentist will most often not offer a choice, but will allegedly place a composite filling and then charge the patient for it. Anyone who wants a free white filling must request it, but must also inform themselves beforehand, because each of the materials used has its own characteristics. We received information that the free white filling visually completely differs from the tooth base and looks “like cement”.

These are glass-ionomer and hybrid glass-ionomer cements, which have good characteristics for replacing the former amalgam fillings, but cannot match composite white fillings. Research in European countries where these materials have been used for about 20 years shows that the disadvantages of glass-ionomers are more frequent chipping, limited resistance to abrasion and erosion, and strength below the values for composite. Persons who had such fillings installed had a higher rate of fractures and abrasions of the fillings than with composites, as well as colour deviations.

economic status and purchasing power in dental medicine

“The key problem is the fact that white fillings do not cover all the indications in which amalgam can be used,” emphasises Irma Šavorić, president of the Association of Contracted Doctors of Dental Medicine MODDUS HR. This means that the choice of material should not be only a matter of aesthetics but also of the concrete clinical situation.

“Indications are key, and problems usually arise when something is not in a specific indication,” Šavorić states. Patients, she says, as a rule do not come with a request for a particular type of filling, but make the decision in conversation with the dentist. In this, the patient’s economic status, i.e. purchasing power, can play a role, especially when there is a choice between a filling covered by insurance and one that requires additional payment. The fact that a certain material is more expensive does not automatically mean that it is more suitable for every situation, this doctor of dental medicine explains.

“Materials have different characteristics and limitations, so the choice should primarily depend on the indication,” she concludes. The price of 30 to 80 euros per tooth will be important for a considerable part of citizens when deciding between the two types of white filling.

the right to free composite fillings until you’re 18

The right to a free composite filling for all teeth, regardless of which tooth is involved, is now held in Croatia by children up to 18 years of age, pregnant women and breastfeeding mothers. For all other citizens who do not want to pay extra for such fillings, the health insurance fund will, according to the announcement of the Ministry of Health, secure from 10 to 12 million euros annually.

The MODDUS HR Association was founded in order to clearly define issues related to materials, indications, financing and the position of dentists who work in different models of dental healthcare. From the HZZO they are requesting a correction of the financing model, warning that the existing model could lead to longer waiting times for patients and reduced availability of certain services.

World.title: HŽ to Invest €7.4 Million – Here Are the Croatian Cities Covered
World.content:
October the 20th, 2026 – HŽ is set to invest a fortune in the country’s future railway plans, with multiple Croatian cities covered by the plans.

HŽ Passenger Transport has issued a tender estimated to stand at a whopping €7.4 million excluding VAT for the arrangement and modernisation of six workshops for the maintenance of trains across the country. Poslovni reports that more specifically speaking, these will be located in Vinkovci, Solin, Osijek, Pula and Varaždin. The tender was published on Monday in the Electronic Public Procurement Notice, and offers can be submitted until the 26th of November.

According to the tender documentation, the most money is planned for Solin, where two workshops will be arranged for €2.73 million. For Osijek the estimate is €1.59 million, Varaždin €1.48 million, Vinkovci €998,000, and for Pula €606,000. At all those locations construction, electrical and mechanical works are planned, as well as the procurement and installation of equipment for the maintenance of trains.

For example, for one of the Solin workshops the project states that it is in poor condition and that it needs to be adapted for the maintenance of existing and new trains. Therefore inspection channels for examining trains from below and a platform for inspecting equipment on the roof will be made in it, and the roof, floor and lighting will also be renewed.

The works will be carried out gradually, beginning in January 2027 and continuing until January 2028, and at each workshop they should last 119 days. First in line are Vinkovci, which will take place from the 12th of January to the 10th of May 2027, and the final one is Varaždin, where the works should finish on the 3rd of January 2028, should all go as planned.

The deadlines have (at least according to the documentation) been set so that too many workshops don’t end up being closed at the same time and so that trains can be regularly maintained even during the works. Completed parts of the halls can be returned to use after they pass expert supervision. The most advantageous offer will be selected according to price and quality, and one of the criteria is also the length of the warranty period, which must not be shorter than two years. Bidders can compete for one, several or all locations.

World.title: Croatia Lagging Further and Further Behind on Innovation Ranking
World.content:
October the 20th, 2026 – Despite being the home of many successful startups, Croatia keeps on lagging further and further behind on the innovation ranking.

Croatia has unfortunately fallen six places on the Global Innovation Index ranking for 2026 and is now in 46th place among 139 countries. Index reports that the Academic Trade Union warns that such a result is a consequence of the Government’s poor economic and innovation policy, and particularly highlights the weak cooperation between universities and the economy. It is calling for the establishment of a special ministry that would deal with higher education, science and innovation.

According to the latest report of the World Intellectual Property Organisation (WIPO), Croatia was in 40th place last year and this year has fallen to 46th. Of the 39 European economies covered by the research it is in 28th place. The Academic Trade Union considers this to be yet another warning that Croatia must change the way it develops the economy, science and higher education.

croatia is getting further behind european innovation leaders

The Global Innovation Index compares economies according to approximately 80 indicators, among which are investments in research and development, education, technology, the business environment and the application of innovations. Switzerland is in a highly impressive first place for the 16th year in a row, followed by Sweden and the United States of America.

In fourth place came South Korea, fifth Singapore, sixth the United Kingdom, seventh the Netherlands, eighth Finland, ninth Denmark, and tenth China. The Academic Trade Union warns that Croatia lags behind European economies in all the main areas assessed by the index.

croatia has nowhere near enough cooperation between universities and industry

According to the trade union, one of Croatia’s greatest weaknesses is the cooperation between universities and industry, for which they point out that Croatia is only in 84th place. Connecting research with production and entrepreneurship should, they believe, be one of the foundations of economic development. The trade union stresses that for years it has been warning the Croatian Government of the need for better linking of the academic community and the economy, but that its proposals are not being implemented. For these exceptionally poor results, they hold the responsible officials accountable, especially the leadership of the Ministry of Science, Education and Youth. They claim that the responsible persons insufficiently follow the results of international research and do not understand the importance of innovations for the development of the economy.

is a new ministry on the horizon?

The Academic Trade Union proposes the establishment of a Ministry of Higher Education, Science and Innovation. The new ministry, according to their proposal, should coordinate the work of the National Innovation Council and encourage cooperation between universities, scientific institutions and companies. The trade union demands that innovation become the third fundamental task of universities, alongside education and scientific work. It also proposes the adoption of a Law on Innovation that would regulate the financing and functioning of the Croatian innovation system.

could croatia’s investment in r&d ever equal 3% of gdp?

Among the trade union’s proposals is an increase in investment in research and development to 3 percent of Croatian GDP. They also demand a doubling of the number of researchers employed in the economy, especially holders of doctorates, so that Croatia can reduce the lag behind the European Union average. The new ministry should also facilitate the coordination of different state institutions when it comes to innovation, the application of new technologies and their transfer from scientific institutions into the economy. The Academic Trade Union considers that such changes would enable stronger development of industry, increase its contribution to the economy and in the long term contribute to the growth of the standard of living. They called on the government to accept their proposals and change the previous policy of developing science, higher education and innovation.

World.title: Why Your Ancestor’s “Austrian” or “Italian” Passport Doesn’t Mean You Aren’t Legally Croatian
World.content:
October the 19th, 2026 – Croatia hasn’t always been the Croatia we know. You may have ancestors that are listed as being Austrian, Italian or Hungarian, but you might still be legally Croatian.

If you’ve curiously started digging into your family’s emigration history, you have likely unearthed a treasure trove of century-old documents: ship passenger manifests, American or Canadian naturalisation petitions, and faded, yellowed draft cards. However, for a massive segment of the Croatian diaspora, specifically those whose families left Europe during the peak migration waves between the late 1800s and the 1920s, these documents often bring a frustrating surprise.

Under the column labelled “Country of Origin” or “Nationality,” your ancestor’s record might not say “Croatia” at all. Instead, it might explicitly state “Austria,” “Hungary,” “Yugoslavia,” or even “Italy”. For many diaspora members, this feels like an immediate dead end. The common assumption by the mere mortal is as follows: If my great-grandfather left Europe as a citizen of the Austro-Hungarian Empire or the Kingdom of Italy, I must not qualify for Croatian citizenship by descent. Despite this being a common assumption, it’s fortunately totally incorrect. In the eyes of modern citizenship law, an imperial passport from 1910 doesn’t erase your legal right to a modern Croatian passport today. However, proving your lineage across a century of shifting borders requires navigating a complex historical and bureaucratic maze.

roots don’t recognise changing borders, but the ministry of the interior does

To understand why your ancestor’s old paperwork says “Austria” or “Italy,” you have to look at the tumultuous geopolitical history of not only Croatia but the wider region. Before the modern Republic of Croatia declared independence on October the 8th, 1991, the territory was repeatedly carved up, absorbed, and governed by various empires and federations, with a lot of bloodshed in between.

First we need to go all the way back to pre-1918 when Croatia was part of the once mighty Austro-Hungarian Empire. Emigrants from Zagreb, Slavonia, Dalmatia and even the furthest-flung islands all travelled on Austrian or Hungarian documentation. Then came the interwar period & WWII. Following the Treaty of Rapallo in 1920, sections of Istria, Rijeka, Zadar, and several Dalmatian islands (including Cres and Lošinj) were annexed by what was then the Kingdom of Italy. People from these regions suddenly became legal Italian citizens, changed their names to Italian variants, and emigrated under the documentation bearing the Italian flag. Then, from 1945 to 1991, Croatia and the countries of the region became part of the various iterations of Yugoslavia.

You can see how Croatian citizenship applications can often become very confusing territory, but the authorities are fully aware of Croatia’s blurry past and as such even blurrier documentation. When the Croatian Ministry of the Interior evaluates an application for citizenship by descent, they don’t care what a clerk at Ellis Island wrote down way back in 1912. They care about geographic reality that corresponds to modern-day Croatia and historical municipal tracking.

Under the current Croatian Citizenship Act, the key question is whether the specific town or village your ancestor emigrated from sits within the modern, legally recognised borders of Croatia as it is today. If your great-grandfather was born somewhere near Split back in 1905, he was technically born under Austro-Hungarian rule, but because Split is indisputably Croatian territory today, the bloodline connection remains legally valid, long after Austria-Hungary’s demise.

here’s where diy croatian citizenship applications often come to grief…

While the law very much allows for these problematic and complex geographical and historical shifts, the burden of proof rests entirely on the applicant. This is where DIY applications frequently fall apart, stall, and end up shoved to gather dust on a shelf somewhere. If you submit an application to a Croatian consulate with an American death certificate stating your grandfather was born in “Austria,” alongside a modern birth record request, the reviewing officers require a meticulous paper trail that bridges the historical gap. You must prove two things simultaneously in such cases.

The first is what’s known as the registry match. Initially, you need to locate the original historical birth or baptismal record in the local municipal registry or church archive within Croatia, confirming they were registered on that specific territory once upon a time. After you’ve cleared that hurdle, you need to deal witu name and identity reconciliation. What this means is that you need to prove that the “Giovanni” or “Giuseppe” listed on an Italian emigration record from Istria is legally the exact same person as the “Ivan” or “Josip” recorded in the local village archives. You can imagine how difficult this is without administrative help.

If your family came from an area like Istria or Zadar that switched between Italian and Slavic administration, records may be split between different archives, written in different languages (Latin, Italian, or old Croatian scripts), or filed under completely altered surnames.

solving the runaway border problem

Navigating various international treaties, century-old municipal border adjustments, and dual-language archives is a daunting task for anyone working from North America, South America, or Australia. It requires a level of historical expertise and local administrative access that standard translation services or internet databases simply cannot provide. This is where the specialised, ground-level infrastructure put in place by services like Croatian By Descent becomes an invaluable asset for the busy American diaspora.

Instead of letting your application get derailed and shoved to the back of a massive pile by a confusing historical paper trail, their team functions as both legal researchers and archival detectives. They know exactly how to trace your mysterious, multi-national ancestors through the shifting territorial registries, cross-referencing old land records and municipal books to establish an airtight geographic proof for the Ministry of the Interior. They dismantle Croatia’s age-old runaway border problem by making sure your ancestral files are organised, properly reconciled, and professionally translated, transforming deeply confusing geopolitical hurdle into a successful, legally sound submission package.

Skip the administrative confusion and verify your historical eligibility with the expert team at Croatian By Descent, who can make sure changing borders and complicated political histories don’t come between you and your EU passport. This service uses knowledgeable lawyer partners who can readily assist clients with obtaining their family’s records from Croatia, as well as dealing with them after the fact throughout the process.

World.title: Croatia Has Been Unable to Connect Istrian Railway for 150 Years
World.content:
October the 19th, 2026 – The Austro-Hungarians constructed the Istrian railway in just 3 years, but Croatia has been totally unable to connect it for 150!

Istria is the only Croatian region from which trains don’t actually run into the rest of Croatia. Although trains have been running across the peninsula for 150 years, a direct connection of the Istrian railways with the Croatian railway system is only now being planned. Dubravko Grakalic reports for Index that the Istrian railways are connected, primarily because of geography, to the neighbouring Slovenian ones – a project from the 19th century and the era of Austro-Hungarian rule. Back in 1867, when the line was opened to traffic, Emperor and King Franz Joseph I arrived in Pula by train via Slovenia. To this day, Istrian railway destinations are still reached in the same way.

From Zagreb to Pula by train, via Ljubljana, one travels only at weekends. The train departs on Friday and after a seven-hour journey arrives at Pula station. From Pula back to Zagreb it returns only on Sunday. Passengers are also offered transport by train to Lupoglav, then by bus to the Rijeka–Zagreb line. The paradox of the Istrian railways, which today mainly serve freight traffic and local travel to Buzet, has an interesting historical and political context.

austria-hungary’s railway construction

“The railway in Istria was built back in 1876, with the line from the direction of Divača in Slovenia to Pula 122 kilometres long and a branch line 21 kilometres long from Kanfanar to Rovinj, which until that time had been the strongest economic centre of Istria. Although the Istrian population had wanted a railway earlier, because of other interests in the centre of the state in Vienna, whose primary goal was the construction of the line to the main maritime port of the monarchy in Trieste, completed in 1857, the construction of the railway in Istria was of secondary importance,” Dr. Sc. Josip Kajinić, curator of the Croatian Railway Museum of HŽ Infrastruktura and one of the authors of the recent exhibition on the railway in Istria, told Index.

“Circumstances changed as a result of foreign-policy circumstances that led to the construction of the monarchy’s main naval base in Pula in 1853, alongside which a shipyard was also launched. In those new circumstances the monarchy needed a safe and good transport link for the delivery of raw materials and military equipment, and given the poor and sparse road network and the danger from the sea for maritime traffic that threatened from the Kingdom of Italy after its unification, the decision was finally taken to build a railway line in Istria.

The line to Pula was built because of the naval base and the shipyard, and its branch to Rovinj for economic reasons. Because of the already mentioned danger that threatened from the sea, the Istrian railway was built through the interior,” Dr. Kajinić notes. The Istrianer Staatsbahn, as the railway through Istria was called in Austria-Hungary, was built at state expense. The law on it was passed on 22 April 1873, while the 122-kilometre line was built in less than three years by the company Frolich from Graz. Work began in Pazin in December 1873, and some twenty thousand workers worked on it. The cost was lower than planned – 12,760,469 florins. The line was solemnly opened in August 1876, and regular traffic started the same year in September.

By way of comparison, HŽ Infrastruktura began in 2025 the reconstruction of fifty kilometres of the line from the state border to Sv. Petar u Šumi. The plan is for the reconstruction to be completed by the end of 2028. Austria-Hungary built thirteen railway stations, five bridges and the Hum tunnel on the Istrian line.

the development of the line

In 1878 a track was built on the Pula waterfront, from the station to the shipyard. A more interesting line was built in 1887, a twenty-kilometre stretch from the Slovenian Hrpelje via Kozina to Trieste, which shortened the journey between Pula and Trieste. It operated until 1959 and is now an arranged cycling route. A similar fate befell the route of the narrow-gauge railway Poreč–Trieste, known as the Parenzana, Porečanka or Istranka.

“The former 123-kilometre-long narrow-gauge Parenzana line connected Trieste and Poreč, and for a length of 78 kilometres it passed through Croatian areas of Istria. It was built in 1902 and was in use until 1935. Its route is very well preserved and is today used for tourist purposes,” Josip Kajinić adds. The cycling and walking path is called the “Path of Health and Friendship” because it connects three countries.

from the former yugoslavia to the modern day

After the collapse of the once mighty Austria-Hungary, the first extension of the Istrian railways was launched by the then Yugoslavia with the construction of the Lupoglav–Štalije line in 1951. With it the railway was brought to the port in Raša Bay. The Kanfanar–Rovinj line was suspended in 1966 because of the developed road traffic.

“Throughout history the railway in Istria was managed by several administrations – from the Austrian, the Italian, briefly the German during the occupation in the Second World War, and after it the Yugoslav Railways, and since 1991 it has been under the management of the Croatian Railways, today HŽ Infrastruktura d.o.o.,” curator Josip Kajinić says and adds: “Today on the railway line between the Croatian-Slovenian border and the terminal station in Pula there are eight stations and 16 stops. This line is special in that it is probably the most authentic on the entire railway network in the territory of Croatia, with the largest number of originally preserved station buildings and other track facilities.”

michael portillo spotlights a vodnjan station

The cult British travel writer Michael Portillo presented in 2025 in the BBC series “Great Continental Railway Journeys” the station in Vodnjan with its old-fashioned technology that is still in use today.

The story of the railways in Istria is also shown by the recent exhibition “Gremo na makinu!” at the Historical and Maritime Museum of Istria in Pula, as well as the steam locomotive of the FS 835 series located next to the station building in Pula, which is a protected cultural asset and part of the holdings of the Croatian Railway Museum. “With the exhibition we wanted to show how important the railway was for the development of Istria, not only in a transport and economic sense, but also in the everyday life of people. We sought, along with a historical overview of the construction and development of the lines, to present objects that tell us about the functioning of the railway and the people who worked on it. It is particularly interesting that part of the exhibited material is available to the public for the first time, and the former lines that, although they no longer exist today, played an important role in connecting Istria are also covered,” they say for Index at the Historical and Maritime Museum of Istria in Pula.

The government and Croatian Railways have also revived the plan to connect with the Istrian lines by a tunnel through Učka. Although the foundation stone for the construction of the tunnel under Ćićarija was laid as early as 1993 by the then Croatian president Dr. Franjo Tuđman, the state company HŽ Infrastruktura only in May 2026 signed a contract for the documentation and conceptual design of that tunnel. The project should be completed in two years and will cost around two million euros. When the Istrian railways will be directly connected with the rest of Croatia is still not remotely known.

World.title: New Interactive Earthquake Map Reveals Where Danger in Croatia is Greatest
World.content:
October the 19th, 2026 – A new interactive earthquake map reveals here the danger in Croatia is the greatest, with southern Croatia in particular in quite the precarious spot.

Croatian scientists have produced a new seismic hazard assessment for Croatia that incorporates the experiences of the Petrinja earthquake and data on the soil beneath our cities. Index/Nenad Jaric Dauenhauer reports that the danger is greatest along the Adriatic coast, especially down south in the wider Dubrovnik area. The results also reveal something a little less obvious: for low and rigid buildings, including family houses, the new assessment along the coast and far inland in the area of Petrinja gives higher seismic loads than those prescribed, while for high buildings, it mostly gives lower ones.

This new map could serve as a scientific basis for a new Croatian national annex to Eurocode 8, the European standard for earthquake-resistant construction. It describes how strongly the ground could shake, with a certain probability, but it does not announce the date of the next earthquake nor does it itself reveal which building will survive.

why does croatia need a new earthquake map?

The Zagreb earthquake of magnitude 5.5 that struck back in March 2020 and the Petrinja earthquake of magnitude 6.2 later that same year in December showed just how devastating the combination of strong shaking and vulnerable buildings can be. Dubrovnik was almost destroyed in 1667 by an earthquake of estimated magnitude around 7, and Zagreb was struck in 1880 by an earthquake of magnitude around 5.9.

“Destructive earthquakes here are not a footnote in history. That is precisely why probabilistic seismic hazard assessment is the right framework for design and spatial planning across Croatia,” explained Professor Snježana Markušić from the Geophysical Department of the Faculty of Science (PMF) in Zagreb, the first author of the paper. The current Croatian seismic hazard map, an integral part of the national annex to Eurocode 8 from back in 2011, is based on earlier research. In the meantime, scientists have collected new earthquake records and data on local soil conditions, and in 2024 the second generation of Eurocode 8 was also published.

The new assessment was prepared by Snježana Markušić, Iva Žilić, Tomislav Fiket and Anja Majurec from the Geophysical Department of PMF in Zagreb, Davor Stanko from the Faculty of Geotechnical Engineering in Varaždin, and Tvrtko Korbar from the Croatian Geological Survey. The paper was published on the 17th of September 2026 in the journal Bulletin of Earthquake Engineering (BEE).

earthquakes don’t care about borders

Seismic hazards in Croatian cities are also influenced by earthquakes outside of Croatia. For Dubrovnik, for example, the seismic areas located on the territories of both Montenegro and Albania are very important. That is why the processed area is considerably wider than Croatia. Foreshocks and aftershocks were removed from the earthquake catalogue, because the model describes the long-term frequency of mainshocks. “90,003 mainshocks remained, only 14.9 percent of all recorded events. Almost three quarters were aftershocks,” says Tomislav Fiket from PMF.

The authors divided the wider area of Croatia and neighbouring countries into 32 zones according to geological structure, seismic activity and faults, and performed the calculations in the open-source program OpenQuake. “Three large tectonic units – the Adriatic Foreland, the Dinarides and the Pannonian Basin – create very different conditions in the Earth’s crust, so faults across the country move in different ways. We incorporated that diversity into the model, for each zone separately,” explains Tvrtko Korbar from the Croatian Geological Survey.

Two similar houses, one on solid rock and the other on thick deposits of softer soil, will not shake equally during the same earthquake, because softer deposits can amplify the shaking. An important novelty of the paper is therefore the inclusion of soil data, instead of calculating only for solid rock. “A model that includes the actual surface of the terrain directly encompasses the amplification of shaking due to local soil, instead of it being subsequently estimated with a simplified factor,” says Davor Stanko from the Faculty of Geotechnical Engineering. How important local differences are is also shown by a study of Zagreb published in 2025, in which Markušić and Stanko participated. It turned out that in the central and south-eastern parts of the city thick, unconsolidated deposits can amplify seismic waves.

dubrovnik and central dalmatia are areas of concern

The overall seismic hazard is by far the greatest along the coastline, especially down in the Dubrovnik-Neretva area and a little further north in central Dalmatia. Scientists express this danger by the maximum ground acceleration during shaking, in units of g. One g is equal to the acceleration of gravity (9.81 m/s²), so a value of 0.40 g means that the maximum horizontal ground acceleration during shaking reaches 40 percent of that amount. The greater the acceleration, the greater the loads buildings are generally exposed to, but their response also depends on the properties of the structure.

With actual soil conditions taken into consideration, the new assessment gives around 0.40 g across Dubrovnik, 0.32 g in Split, 0.27 g in Rijeka, 0.24 g in Zagreb, 0.22 g in Petrinja and 0.08 g in Osijek. This means that in each of those cities there is about a 10 percent probability that the peak ground acceleration in the next 50 years will exceed the stated value. This is not the strongest possible shaking, nor is it the magnitude of the earthquake: magnitude describes the energy released at the earthquake focus, while ground acceleration describes how strongly the ground shakes at a particular place. “The areas of Sisak, Moslavina and Petrinja, despite the strong earthquake sequence of 2020, according to our results belongs to the group of moderate hazard,” says Markušić. Nevertheless, even weaker shaking can cause great damage if buildings are poorly constructed.

earthquakes have no schedule

The information that a certain level of shaking has a return period of 475 years is easily misleading. It does not mean that such shaking comes once every 475 years and that after it follows centuries of calm. It’s a statistical description: the annual probability of exceedance is about 0.2 percent, which over 50 years, the usual lifespan of a building, accumulates to about 10 percent. The model assumes that earthquakes have no “memory”, as with rolling a die: the previous result does not determine the next one. For critical infrastructure a rarer, stronger shaking is also important, with a return period of 2,475 years and about a 2 percent probability of exceedance in 50 years.

what a single house does and what a building does during an earthquake are very different…

Every building has a natural period of oscillation, the time of one full swing, and it amounts to about a tenth of a second per storey: a family house oscillates with a period of about 0.1 to 0.2 seconds, and a building of about ten storeys with a period of about one second. A building sways most strongly when oscillations of a period similar to its own predominate in the ground motion, similar to a swing that we push at the right moment. According to the new assessment, that shaking is strongest in all the observed cities for a period of 0.2 seconds, i.e. precisely for low buildings.

That’s why low and rigid buildings on the coast and in Petrinja could be exposed to higher seismic loads than those provided for by the current design spectrum. For high and flexible buildings, which sway more slowly, the new assessment almost everywhere gives lower loads than those prescribed. The comparison is nevertheless not entirely equal because the current spectrum refers to solid rock, while the new assessment also includes local soil.

“The results indicate that a map prepared for a uniform reference rock, when local soil is taken into account, can in some places underestimate and in others overestimate the hazard. There is no single correction factor applicable throughout the country,” Markušić explains.

“For the faults responsible for the strongest earthquakes in Croatia, such as the Petrinja and Pokupsko faults, there are still not enough complete data for them to be reliably modelled separately. Their inclusion is a priority for the next generation of models,” explained Korbar. “Croatia’s database of strong earthquake records is still relatively small. Its expansion, together with the preparation of a more detailed national soil database, is one of the key next steps,” adds Žilić.

will the new map force construction rule changes?

The new research represents a scientific study of probabilistic seismic hazard assessment, not a national annex to the standard, and does not prescribe legally binding design values. “We offer a scientific basis on which the competent authorities can rely when they start preparing the new annex that Croatia must adopt for the second generation of Eurocode 8,” Markušić emphasises. The new Croatian earthquake danger map will therefore not change the regulations overnight. It gives the competent authorities a new basis for decisions, and citizens a clearer picture of the hazard. The safety of an individual building still needs to be assessed according to its structure, condition and the soil on which it stands. The greatest value of the new map will be that better knowledge about earthquakes is turned into safer construction.

World.title: 40% of Croatian Retirees are in Poverty, Soup Kitchen Use Increases
World.content:
October the 19th, 2026 – An appalling 40% of Croatian retirees are now living in poverty according to the latest data, with soup kitchen use increasing in a country that keeps pushing the inflationary limits.

According to the latest data from the Croatian Bureau of Statistics, almost every fifth citizen of Croatia lives on the absolute brink of poverty. Index reports that for Croatian retirees, the figures are even more disgraceful, as almost 40% of them actually do live in poverty. What a staggering paradox it is when a country so full of highly expensive resorts and throngs of tourists is also dealing with growing queues in front of soup kitchens.

After decades of work, many people still do not have enough to live a dignified life. “In general, I think that the majority of pensioners don’t live with dignity. I consider a dignified life to be when a person who has worked for 40 years can in retirement live normally, afford to go to the theatre or cinema, and afford the majority of ordinary things,” stated Višnja Stanišić, president of the Croatian Pensioners’ Trade Union.

When a large part of the pension goes on utility bills, many have no choice but to seek help. In the soup kitchens they are greeted every day by volunteers. “Some come who don’t even have boxes to pack the food into, they come literally with ordinary plastic bags and pack the food into them. Quite a lot of poor people come,” volunteer Lovro Maričić revealed.

The situation is also worsened by Croatia’s constantly rising prices. Inflation in September amounted to a deeply concerning 4.7%, which is the second consecutive month of growth. The biggest cause is energy prices, which have risen by approximately 20%. Such growth hits those with the lowest incomes the hardest.

“Every single pensioner has their own personal inflation to try to deal with because they spend on five to six products whose prices have risen considerably more than the official rate, for some by as much as 10%,” Stanišić explained.

“We’ve proposed an amendment with which we’ll cover more than 30,000 pensioners living within the City of Zagreb. We intend to raise the threshold for financial assistance from a pension of 350 to 500 euros,” said Matej Mišić, president of the SDP of the City of Zagreb. While politicians announce more measures, in the soup kitchens the situation is getting harder and harder. “It could be said that the number of users is even higher than last year. Today was quite busy and a lot of people came,” volunteer Lovro Maričić concluded.

World.title: Former Mayor Claims Split Has Been “Disgraced” Worldwide
World.content:
October the 19th, 2026 – Former Split mayor Ivica Puljak has claimed that Split has been “disgraced” worldwide after the violent clash between Torcida and Ajax.

Former Split mayor Ivica Puljak commented on Torcida’s procession ahead of the Hajduk–Ajax match, when antisemitic, Nazi and Ustaše slogans were chanted through the city streets. Index reports that he said that the footage has spread around Europe and the world and that Split has been disgraced. “We owe an apology to the Jews and to all decent people because that is not us, that is not our city,” Puljak stated, Dalmacija Danas reports.

Puljak stressed that condemnations of the incident are not enough if one wants to prevent the repetition of such events. He believes it is necessary to speak openly about the causes and sees responsibility in politics and in the authorities’ attitude towards the return of extremist symbols into public space. “This didn’t start last Thursday and it didn’t start on the street. For years, we’ve been watching a politics for which the most important thing is to stay in power and which for that reason has allied itself with anyone, regardless of where they come from. That same politics has for years silently watched as the dark past returns to public space,” Puljak said.

an (expected) swipe at hdz…

He added that tolerating such phenomena can be understood as permission and opened the question of possible deals between members of the ruling party and fan groups. He also expressed suspicion that this is a staging by HDZ.

“Have certain people from the ruling party made a deal with fan groups that they will have their support at elections, and then these will tolerate everything they do? And who knows what else is hidden behind those deals,” Puljak asked. As a second important problem Puljak singled out clientelism and employment in the public sector. According to his estimate, in Croatia there are at least 10,000 managerial jobs that were not created because of the needs of society, but because of HDZ’s needs for employment.

“croatian society needs to be reset”

He called for the abolition of such positions and said that a change of government must not mean the replacement of party cadres. “The rule must be simple and without exception: always and only the best,” he said. Puljak stated that Croatian society needs to be “reset” and placed on the foundations of science, reason and humanism.

“Those who shouted through Split last Thursday were not defending Croatia, nor Christianity, nor humanism, but were disgracing all three,” he declared. He explained that the symbol of his political option is a broom, with which he wants to convey that long-standing problems need to be removed. “We need to sweep away what has been accumulating in the corners for years, and that is clientelism, corruption and tolerance of hatred,” he said. He concluded his message with a call to citizens for joint action. “Croatia deserves it. Split deserves it. Let’s do it together,” he urged.

World.title: Women serve across Estonian Defense Forces as country's demographics shift
World.content:
Women can hold their own across the Estonian Defense Forces, officials say, as demographic shifts make their role in the country's wartime reserve increasingly important.

While conscription and national defense obligations in Estonia currently still apply only to men, Anu Rannaveski, director general of the Defense Resources Agency (KRA), said women in the EDF are by no means limited to support roles.

"Women currently serve as conscripts in units across the board, including those with greater mental and physical demands, such as Special Operations Forces (ESTSOF) and the Engineer Battalion, as well as throughout military intelligence," Rannaveski said.

Around 50 women volunteer for conscription each year, a figure that has remained steady over the 13 years women have been allowed to serve. In some years, half of the women who complete conscription have gone on to pursue military careers.

"They can handle any unit," she emphasized, noting that around 250 women serve across the EDF on active duty.

But demographic changes in Estonia could make their participation increasingly important. Around 8,000 young men currently reach conscription age each year, but in recent years, annual births have fallen to just 4,000 to 5,000 boys.

The country needs about 4,100 conscripts a year to maintain its wartime reserve.

"From 2035 onward, filling conscript ranks without women will become quite difficult," Rannaveski acknowledged.

Women can request specific unit

The KRA chief said women are held to the same standards as men in service. "Sometimes on marches, women will even carry the gear of weaker men," she added.

They do, however, receive one accommodation: the agency generally tries to place women volunteering for service in the unit they choose.

"We try to accommodate their preferences when it comes to choosing a unit for conscription," Rannaveski said. "With the exception of units with their own selection process, such as ESTSOF and Cyber Command, where placement is based on candidates' overall ranking."

Rannaveski said young men in Estonia are liable for conscription between the ages of 18 and 27, while national defense obligations continue to apply to all men through age 61.

The EDF's next conscription intake is scheduled for February.

World.title: Cafe service coming to Elron's new Tallinn-Tartu trains
World.content:
New Škoda electric trains on Elron's Tallinn-Tartu route will offer onboard cafe service, letting passengers buy food and drinks during their journey.

The catering contract was awarded to Maitseelamused OÜ, a prepared-foods company owned by Estonian chef Joel Ostrat.

The onboard cafes will offer hot and cold drinks, sandwiches, desserts, salads and snacks, with plans to expand the menu.

"I want to bring restaurant-quality food and solutions to fast, modern trains," Ostrat said, including offerings passengers might not expect to find onboard.

While Elron has not previously offered food or drinks on board its trains, Edelaraudtee, which operated passenger trains in Estonia until 2013, offered its first-class passengers complimentary hot drinks and a menu including sandwiches.

Katri Kruuse, Elron's long-distance service manager, said the new Škoda trains will take the current operator's long-distance service to a new level.

"Our goal is to make the journey more enjoyable by keeping the products and services passengers need within easy reach throughout the trip," Kruuse said.

Preparations for the cafe service, she added, are in their final stages.

Estonian state-owned passenger rail operator Elron served 7.66 million passengers in 2025.

World.title: International tender launched for Tallinn film studio complex
World.content:
Tallinnfilm Studios has announced an international public procurement tender for the design and construction of a film studio complex planned for Paljassaare.

Tallinnfilm Studios director Joonas Tartu said the goal is to create an environment for filmmakers where Estonian and international film professionals can collaborate under the best possible conditions.

The approximately 6,000-square-meter complex will include three state-of-the-art film studios and the necessary support and auxiliary facilities. The film studios are scheduled for completion in 2028.

"Nearly 100 experts in their respective fields have participated in developing the concept for the complex to ensure that the future studio environment fully meets the requirements of modern film production. Modern studios and well-designed support infrastructure will help create an internationally competitive filmmaking environment, attract more film productions to Estonia and lay the groundwork for the growth and development of the local film industry," Tartu explained.

Tallinnfilm Studios construction manager Neeme Nõmme said the aim of the comprehensive procurement process is to find a partner capable of combining high construction quality, functionality and cost-effectiveness while understanding the project's broader cultural significance.

"Construction companies have until December 15 to familiarize themselves with the Tallinnfilm Studios project and submit their bids," he added.

"We expect professionalism, responsibility and high ethical standards from the construction companies participating in the tender. We want to create a complex that both its builders and all of Estonia can be proud of. Our goal is to build a film studio complex that meets international quality standards and will serve Estonia's film industry for decades," Nõmme said.

World.title: Study: Wetlands flora needs support to bounce back after restoration
World.content:
Restoring natural water levels alone may not be enough to rehabilitate severely degraded wetlands, according to a new study . Restoration efforts must also actively encourage vegetation recovery, writes Ilona Tamm, a junior research fellow at the University of Tartu.

Many wetlands around the world have been restored, but far less is known about whether these areas actually begin functioning as wetlands again. Monitoring often lasts only a short time and many projects lack sufficiently clear objectives against which to assess the success of restoration efforts.

When a peatland is drained, oxygen enters the peat, causing the organic matter stored there to decompose more rapidly and release carbon dioxide into the atmosphere. Raising the water level slows this process and helps prevent further peat loss, but a wet area is not necessarily a restored wetland. For that to happen, conditions must develop that allow vegetation characteristic of wetlands to grow again.

In our recently published study, my colleagues from the University of Tartu and the University of California, Berkeley, and I therefore examined two wetlands with long histories of drainage, tracking changes in water levels, vegetation and carbon dioxide and methane fluxes over four years following restoration. One of the wetlands, Ess-soo, is located on a former peat extraction site in southern Estonia, while the other, Hill Slough, lies in California's Sacramento–San Joaquin River Delta.

Both sites were restored in 2021 after decades of drainage and land use. Four years later, the results were surprisingly similar: restoring water levels had not led to significant vegetation growth.

Two very different wetlands, one similar concern

Vegetation generally struggles to recover at former peat extraction sites. Peat extraction removes much of the original vegetation and the seeds and other material needed for plants to spread. The remaining bare peat surface is acidic, nutrient-poor and dry. As a result, even a former peat extraction site that has been abandoned for decades can remain largely devoid of vegetation.

Ess-soo was originally a natural raised bog, but peat extraction in the second half of the 20th century fundamentally transformed the area. Restoration work began in 2021 at the 58-hectare former peat extraction site, which had been abandoned for nearly 30 years. The site was divided into several sections, with different restoration methods applied to each.

Our study focused on an 8.3-hectare section where drainage ditches were blocked and shallow pools were created to raise the water level and encourage the natural recovery of peatland vegetation. The aim was to keep the water level close to the ground surface and create conditions suitable for the return of vegetation characteristic of transitional mires.

Following restoration, a problem emerged at Ess-soo: conditions in different parts of the same site were either too dry or too wet. Lower-lying sections of the peatland remained permanently submerged, causing vegetation to decline, while water levels in higher areas fell too far below the surface.

During the dry summer of 2024, the water level remained too far below the surface across much of the study area for more than a month. Four years after restoration, vegetation still covered only about 30 percent of the drier ground. Sphagnum mosses, which are particularly important for the formation of new peat, were not found in the study area either before or after restoration.

At Hill Slough, the problem was different, but the outcome was similar. Located in a Mediterranean climate, the wetland underwent extensive diking and drainage beginning in the mid-19th century to make way for farming and livestock grazing. In 2021, the natural water regime was restored across the 100-hectare study area by opening the levees. The aim was to reintroduce tidal flows and improve habitats for wildlife characteristic of wetlands.

However, at Hill Slough, which had been cut off from its natural water regime for more than a century, the original wetland vegetation had undergone substantial changes. When the area was once again exposed to daily tidal fluctuations, leaving much of it frequently submerged, the vegetation that had been present before restoration rapidly declined.

Water levels fluctuated by more than a meter over the course of a day, while shifting soft sediments and unstable ground likely made it even harder for plants to establish themselves. As a result, Hill Slough became almost entirely a mudflat, with only a few plants managing to establish themselves along the higher edges of the site.

Lack of vegetation impacts climate benefits

Very slow vegetation growth means that wetland ecosystems recover only gradually, directly affecting the carbon cycle. Plants absorb carbon dioxide from the atmosphere through photosynthesis. When vegetation is sparse, carbon uptake also remains low.

At the same time, restoring water to a wetland has an important effect of its own. Under wet conditions, less oxygen can penetrate the peat, slowing its decomposition and potentially reducing carbon dioxide emissions. However, oxygen-poor conditions can also increase methane production. Therefore, assessing the climate impact of a restored wetland requires considering both carbon dioxide and methane.

Both study sites remained net sources of carbon throughout the monitoring period, meaning they released more greenhouse gases into the atmosphere than they absorbed. At Ess-soo, net carbon dioxide emissions during the drought year of 2024 were approximately 158 grams of carbon per square meter per year, compared with around 42 grams in the wetter year of 2025. Meanwhile, methane emissions increased from approximately six grams to nine grams. The lower carbon dioxide emissions were consistent with cooler, wetter conditions that may have slowed peat decomposition.

Emissions at Hill Slough were generally higher. Over the four-year period, net carbon dioxide emissions declined from approximately 334 grams to 270 grams of carbon per square meter per year. Methane emissions, meanwhile, increased after the first year and subsequently remained high, reaching approximately 22 grams.

The differences between the two sites are likely related to climate, vegetation and water regimes. For example, Estonia's cooler climate limits microbial activity and the decomposition of organic matter during winter. In other words, restoring water levels may have reduced some organic matter decomposition, but sparse vegetation meant that neither site had yet reached a point where carbon uptake by plants could offset emissions.

Slow recovery not inevitable

Such carbon fluxes are not unusual in restored wetlands with sparse vegetation. Carbon dioxide emissions at Hill Slough were similar to those measured at other restored wetlands in California's delta where vegetation had not returned. By contrast, strong carbon dioxide uptake has been recorded at restored wetlands with similar conditions but well-established vegetation.

Ess-soo's carbon balance was similar to that of partially vegetated former peat extraction sites undergoing restoration, while net carbon dioxide uptake has also been achieved at peatlands with more extensive vegetation. However, even well-established vegetation does not automatically mean that a wetland will become a net carbon sink every year.

The slow recovery of Ess-soo and Hill Slough does not mean that such outcomes should be accepted as inevitable. Vegetation in tidal wetlands typically becomes established within three to five years and, in the best cases, within just one year. There are also examples of former peat extraction sites, where recovery is generally slower, achieving full vegetation cover in approximately five years.

Rapid recovery often requires more than simply restoring water levels. Depending on the site, restoration efforts can include improving water management, preparing the soil, adjusting ground elevation and actively encouraging vegetation recovery, for example through planting or transplanting sphagnum mosses. No such active vegetation restoration measures were used in the sections of Ess-soo and Hill Slough examined in this study.

If monitoring shows that vegetation is not recovering or water levels are not behaving as planned, restoration measures should be adjusted rather than simply waiting. This requires setting clear, measurable objectives from the outset and monitoring results over an extended period. Sharing both successes and challenges is equally important, as comparisons between different sites can help improve the planning of future restoration projects.

This is precisely what the comparison between Ess-soo and Hill Slough demonstrates: similar obstacles can arise in very different wetlands. These findings do not diminish the need for wetland restoration. Rather, they show that successful restoration involves more than simply bringing back water — ecosystem recovery must be monitored and, when necessary, actively guided.

The study was published in the journal Restoration Ecology.

World.title: Ad agency Tank breaks apolitical streak to handle Reform Party's 2027 campaign
World.content:
According to agency founder and creative director Joel Volkov, the deciding factor was the Reform Party's values, which can stand up to far-right populist politics.

Kontuur Leo Burnett has previously handled most of the Reform Party's election campaigns, but the party decided to seek a new partner earlier this year.

Reform Party Secretary-General Kristo Enn Vaga told ERR that Tank was chosen for its fresh ideas and enthusiasm. Although the agency has no previous experience in political communications, Vaga believes it can bring new energy both to the party's campaign and to Estonia's broader political communications and public relations landscape.

Tank creative director Joel Volkov said the agency had ruled out working with other political parties but made an exception for the Reform Party.

"Tank has never produced political advertising in its 31 years of operation. When the Reform Party approached us in early spring 2026, we took some time to think before turning them down outright. This time, we decided to help," Volkov told ERR.

Volkov acknowledged that the Reform Party has struggled politically, with politicians making mistakes in difficult situations, going back on their word and communicating poorly. He said the party's declining approval ratings reflected those problems.

Nevertheless, Volkov believes the Reform Party retains considerable political value because of its liberal, pro-business worldview, which he considers essential to Estonia's future prosperity.

"We believe that these are precisely the kinds of values that can stand up to the rise of far-right populist politics without inciting hatred. Such politics are also spreading rapidly in Estonia, encouraged by foreign agents," Volkov said.

Joel Volkov. Source: Iris Tähema/ERR

According to Volkov, the Reform Party's main challenge is not name recognition, which remains high, but rebuilding public trust.

He argued that restoring trust requires politicians to acknowledge their weaknesses and mistakes rather than praise their own achievements. The process, he said, will take time, honesty and a willingness to demonstrate that the party understands voters' concerns.

Volkov described the Reform Party's new "pep talk" campaign as a creative response to that challenge, saying it could be one of Estonia's first election campaigns in which politicians focus on listening rather than dominating the conversation.

A clear enough campaign slogan?

Vaga said the party's campaign slogan, "A Clear Course for the Future," ("Kindel suund on tulevik") was developed in cooperation with Tank and carries a deeper political message.

He explained that certainty has traditionally been central to the Reform Party's messaging, particularly when it has held government responsibility. Given Estonia's challenging security environment, he said reassuring the public that the country is protected remains especially important.

The slogan's emphasis on the future is also intended to distinguish the Reform Party from political opponents that Vaga believes are focused on dismantling existing institutions and returning to the past.

Vaga said the Reform Party wants Estonia to continue developing as a country with expanding freedoms and a growing economy, arguing that building a more prosperous future for subsequent generations has been a central party objective for decades.

Prime Minister and Reform Party leader Kristen Michal made a similar argument on Vikerraadio Tuesday. He accused EKRE, the Center Party and Isamaa of wanting to move backward rather than forward in both their values and approach to technology.

Asked whether voters would understand the slogan's multiple meanings, Vaga acknowledged that not everyone would consider its deeper political message. However, he said the slogan would make sense to voters when presented alongside the Reform Party's name.

Kristo Enn Vaga. Source: Ken Mürk/ERR

Both Vaga and Michal also dismissed suggestions that the absence of Hanno Pevkur and Jürgen Ligi from campaign videos released over the weekend was deliberate.

Michal said the two politicians were likely traveling or otherwise unavailable when the videos were filmed. Vaga added that Pevkur had not yet confirmed whether he would run in the Riigikogu elections.

Election promises to be gradually unveiled starting in November

Looking ahead, Vaga said the Reform Party's campaign will include video and television ads, as well as outdoor advertising. The party will also begin announcing its election promises and revealing which electoral districts its candidates will contest.

While Vaga did not disclose any specific campaign promises, he said national defense and economic growth would remain key priorities. The party is also developing proposals on family policy, parental benefits, long-term energy planning and improving pensioners' living standards, including continued pension indexation.

According to Vaga, the Reform Party's election platform will be nearly 100 pages long, containing both specific proposals and broader commitments. The party plans to begin publishing it chapter by chapter in November.

Vaga also confirmed that the party will make changes to its lead candidates in several electoral districts, as some politicians who ran in the previous election will not be standing again.

He noted that Kaja Kallas, who headed the party's list in Harju and Rapla counties in the last election as Reform Party chair, now holds a senior position in Europe and is no longer active in domestic politics.

The late Siim Kallas will also be absent from the ballot.

Vaga said further details about the party's candidates and their electoral districts would be announced in November.

The Riigikogu elections are scheduled for March 2027.

World.title: Tallinn Old Town doubles as England for highly anticipated Indian film
World.content:
Tallinn Old Town recently transformed into early 20th-century England for the historical Indian film "The India House," bringing major Indian stars to the Estonian capital.

Directed by Ram Vamsi Krishna, the film follows Indian students in London who fought British colonial rule in the pre-independence era in the early 1900s.

The film takes its name from the North London student residence that became a key hub for Indian nationalist political activism between 1905 and 1910.

During filming around Tallinn's Old Town this fall, the picturesque Müürivahe tänav, for example, became Oxford Street, complete with British flags, while a major protest scene involving 150 actors was filmed by Cinema Sõprus.

Nafta Films founder and producer Esko Rips said that it was unusual for such a large crew to travel abroad for a shoot, with 47 Indian crew members in Estonia alongside Nafta Films' local team of around 70.

He said working across cultural and professional differences meant both teams had to adapt their communication and working styles. "We try to find common ground," Rips added.

'Tallinn feels like home'

Tollywood star Nikhil Siddhartha has more than 25 films to his name, including the 2022 Telugu blockbuster "Karthikeya 2," one of India's highest-grossing films.

Shooting for "The India House" marked Siddhartha's first-ever visit to Estonia, but he admitted it didn't feel that way.

"It just feels so welcoming," he said. "I don't feel like I've come to a different country; it feels like home."

Siddhartha also praised Tallinn's well-preserved Old Town and Estonia's collective efforts in supporting culture.

"Estonia is rich in culture," he said, "and I'm very happy to come visit it and shoot here."

Filming for Indian film "The India House" in front of Tallinn's Cinema Sõprus. October 2026. Source: press photo

Estonian slackliner Jaan Roose also joined the production as a stunt performer, handling falls, jumps and other action sequences. He said protective padding hidden beneath his costume helped cushion the impacts.

"I have to run on cobblestones, jump, fall and take a hit from a barrel," he said. "I'm doing anything that requires knowing how to fall."

The Indian production team considered filming in several European countries before choosing Estonia, Siddhartha said, thanking Rips personally for helping make the arrangements.

"The way they welcomed us, the way they described filming locations — we were blown away," the film star emphasized, adding that the film will also be shown in several Estonian movie theaters once released.

Film Estonia incentive's future uncertain

Rips said Estonia's 40 percent film production incentive helped secure the foreign film project. The "India House" team had visited other countries, including the U.K. itself, but filming there would have been more expensive.

After driving about 7,500 kilometers, scouting locations across Estonia a year ago, the filmmakers fell for Tallinn, choosing it over alternatives including Bulgaria and Lithuania.

The Estonian producer warned, however, that the Film Estonia incentive is poised to lose funding under the next government, set to be elected next March. Securing one production is only part of the challenge.

"I don't understand why our industry is being jerked around like this," Rips said. "Attracting a project here and working on it is one thing; attracting new projects is another, and we need them to keep the industry going."

World.title: Keidi Jaakson: How we talk about immigration matters
World.content:
In mid-October, Rainis Sinikas, head of the border and migration supervision department at the Police and Border Guard Board's (PPA) North Prefecture, told ERR that the situation with irregular migrants in Estonia is "difficult and could turn into a crisis situation," that administrative courts and local governments are overloaded and that the entire cooperation network is under great strain. A few days earlier, PPA chief Egert Belitšev warned that migration pressure could rise sharply as people try to leave Belarus ahead of winter, describing organized routes that cost each person up to €10,000. Interior Minister Igor Taro has called the situation "part of Russia's overall aggression tactics" and declared that Estonia must send a clear message that it cannot be used as a transit corridor. So far this year, the PPA has detained 542 people from 48 countries, both within Estonia and at its borders, and returned 120 of them to Latvia.

There are real operational and security challenges behind these numbers. According to Egert Belitšev, Russia and Belarus facilitate routes organized by criminal networks, with people paying thousands of euros to reach the EU. Processing people who arrive without documents, establishing their identities and routes and pursuing those responsible for facilitating irregular crossings is demanding work. ERR has reported that tighter border controls in Poland and Lithuania have redirected part of these flows towards Estonia. The pressure on local services is also documented: Rae Municipality, where the main detention center is located, is considering legal action against the state and the Social Insurance Board has acknowledged that it was unprepared for the increase. But public concern about immigration is not simply a reflection of how many people arrive across the border. It is also shaped by how much attention, and what kind of attention, the issue itself receives.

James Dennison and Andrew Geddes of the European University Institute's Migration Policy Center recently published "What Europeans Think About Immigration and Why It Matters," drawing on 25 years of survey data across Europe. Their research suggests that public attitudes towards immigration are more stable and more nuanced than commonly assumed and that, where they change, they tend to actually become more favorable over time. What changes more readily is what the researchers call salience: how much attention immigration receives as a political issue. This can be shaped by institutional communication, political rhetoric and media coverage. Speaking at the book's launch at the Center for European Policy Studies in Brussels, Dennison argued that people who consider immigration an important political issue are disproportionately likely to hold restrictive views. Raising the issue's profile can therefore benefit one part of the political spectrum. He also warned that political parties often confuse the growing prominence of immigration with a shift in what people actually believe about it, responding to heightened attention as though it necessarily reflected more restrictive public attitudes.

The language used to describe the current situation to the Estonian public should be proportionate to its scale. Repeated references to crisis and hybrid attacks can make the situation appear more acute and exceptional than the numbers alone suggest. Estonia has detained 542 people so far this year, while Latvia, which directly borders Belarus, recorded over 8,400 irregular crossing attempts by July 21. Across the EU, Frontex recorded approximately 74,000 irregular border-crossing detections in the first eight months of the year, down 35 percent compared with 2025. These figures measure different things and cannot be compared directly, but they provide context for assessing the language used. In an ERR report published on October 19, Taro himself said that Estonia had not yet exhausted its capacity to handle migrants and that the situation could only be described as a crisis once existing resources were no longer sufficient, with several hundred detention places across the country still vacant. By the interior minister's own measure, then, the situation has not reached the point of crisis, which makes the persistent language of potential crisis harder to account for.

Dennison and Geddes's research raises questions about how the current framing of immigration in Estonia may shape public perceptions. Detentions are routinely reported as separate events, often with considerable operational detail. PPA statements repeatedly warn that institutions are overloaded and that the situation could turn into a crisis. The interior minister has urged people to report suspicious individuals. Such communication may increase the prominence of immigration in public debate and encourage people to view it primarily through the lens of security, even if it does not change their underlying attitudes.

In the Spring 2024 Eurobarometer, 29 percent of Estonian respondents agreed that immigrants contribute positively to the country, tied with Cyprus for one of the lowest figure in the EU. The 2018 European Social Survey found that just over half of Estonians thought the state should allow few or no people of a different race or ethnic group to move to Estonia, though the same data shows that attitudes have been slowly becoming more favorable over time. Against this backdrop, repeatedly framing immigration as a potential crisis risks reinforcing the perception that it is primarily a threat.

The deliberate instrumentalization of migration by Russia and Belarus is a genuine security concern, yet recognizing that threat does not require treating everyone travelling along these routes as a threat in themselves. The largest groups among those detained this year come from Somalia, Sudan, Ethiopia, Eritrea and Bangladesh, several of which are affected by armed conflict or severe human rights abuses. EU law provides no visa for the purpose of seeking asylum, so in most cases protection can only be claimed once a person is already on European territory. Arrivals along these routes are unlikely to stop and Estonia needs the capacity to process them effectively.

And Estonia has demonstrated that it can mobilize considerable institutional capacity when the political and public context supports it. In 2022, more than 43,000 Ukrainian refugees arrived, amounting to over 3 percent of the population. The legal framework was different, the circumstances were different and the public solidarity was grounded in a shared sense of threat from Russia. But the experience shows what Estonia can organize when political priorities and public solidarity align. The question is whether the capacity can be rebuilt for people whose reasons for seeking protection may be less immediately legible to the Estonian public.

The debate also raises questions about who attracts suspicion and on what grounds. An operation in Nõmme on October 11 began when residents reported two dark-skinned men who appeared unfamiliar with the area. In August, ERR reported that police had already received unfounded reports about people based solely on their skin colour and PPA representative Indrek Aru acknowledged that in one case the person who had been reported "had all the necessary documents, was completely law-abiding and even spoke Estonian." In its account of the October incident, however, the PPA said that reports were generally prompted by behavior rather than race, while acknowledging that people from a different ethnic background stand out more in a suburb like Nõmme where residents tend to recognize one another. Sinikas also pointed to muddy clothing as one reason groups of migrants might attract attention in autumn.

The gender equality and equal treatment commissioner's 2024 report on racial discrimination documented experiences of racism among people of color in Estonia, including verbal abuse and physical threats, much of it unreported. The difficulty lies in how authorities distinguish legitimate reports based on specific behavior from suspicion based primarily on someone's appearance, particularly when the police themselves acknowledge that skin color can influence who attracts attention. That distinction deserves more public discussion than it currently receives.

World.title: Estonia could learn from Israel's crisis preparedness
World.content:
Estonia can learn from Israel's decades of experience with war, particularly when it comes to building shelters, warning the public about attacks and preparing people for crises, Israeli civil defense expert Yoram Laredo says.

Israelis have been hardened by various wars.

"Unfortunately, since the establishment of the state in 1948, there has been a war every 10 years. So, sadly, we have experienced different types of warfare," said Israeli civil defense expert Yoram Laredo on ERR's "Välisilm" foreign affairs program.

When it comes to shelters, for example, Israel is often held up as a model. However, the system in which everyone knows where to go has taken decades to develop. The turning point came with the 1991 Gulf War.

"That was a lesson we learned from the Gulf War. At the time, Iraq fired ballistic missiles at Israel for the first time. Following that tragic event, we introduced a rule requiring every newly constructed building and apartment to have a shelter. Today, 70 percent of Israeli citizens have a shelter in their homes. It takes time," Laredo said.

But what could be done more quickly, including in Estonia?

"My recommendation is to bring in engineers and inspect every underground parking garage. If they can be shown to withstand ballistic missile strikes, they can be designated as shelters for large numbers of people. These are things that can be done using existing resources," Laredo said.

The most important thing is to be prepared for a crisis.

"You need to prepare your citizens for what is coming and keep them informed. The information available must be shared because that is the first step toward resilience. People break down psychologically when something happens that they did not expect. If the government communicates with people and warns them that there will be power outages, communications disruptions and supply chain problems, and explains how these will be handled, citizens will be able to cope," Laredo said.

Estonia can also learn from Israel's approach to warning people about attacks.

"Israel has a highly sophisticated system that detects all objects flying toward the country, whether from nearby or far away, regardless of their shape or type. The most important element is the siren system. There are thousands of sirens on rooftops. In addition, mobile apps, the internet, radio and television all work in sync. Someone might be watching television, using their phone or standing outside — the system warns them that a missile is on its way. The best thing to do then is take shelter. After the first casualties, everyone knows what to do and people become very disciplined. Unfortunately, that is how it works," Laredo said.

However, when several generations have grown up without experiencing war, it is difficult to make people understand what they need to be prepared for.

"It is comparable to how we anticipate an earthquake in Israel. Our region experiences a devastating earthquake every 100 years. There has been no such earthquake in the history of modern Israel. The last one occurred 100 years ago, before the State of Israel was established. How do you convince the population that an earthquake could strike at any moment?" the expert said.

Israel learned a harsh lesson three years ago when one of the world's best intelligence services allowed the October 7 tragedy to happen because of overconfidence.

"You have to constantly reassess your strategic assumptions and paradigms. If you fail to do that and rely solely on technological superiority without questioning your interpretation of intelligence, things like this happen. That is Israel's most important lesson: Strategic assumptions and interpretations of intelligence must be constantly reassessed rather than rigidly adhered to," Laredo said.

Following October 7, the small state of Israel also had to evacuate large numbers of people.

"The State of Israel evacuated 125,000 people, including 60,000 from the north. Communities along the northern border were evacuated because, at the time, we did not know whether Hezbollah would open a second front there. Communities around Gaza were also evacuated. Those 125,000 people lived in hotels for almost two years. And that really costs a lot of money," Laredo said.

It is also essential to maintain a constant state of crisis preparedness.

"Preparing for a crisis is like a muscle that needs to be exercised constantly. If you do not exercise that muscle, you become exhausted and when a crisis strikes, you eventually break down psychologically. That is what we have learned. Unfortunately, we constantly face real incidents and wars, so we are practicing all the time," Laredo said.
