World.title: Opinion: ‘Irakli Bzhinava’s arrest in Russia is blow to freedom in Abkhaz society’
World.content:
Abkhaz Foreign Minister Oleg Bartsits discussed the fate of Abkhaz lawyer Irakli Bzhinava, who has been in a Russian prison since February 2026, with his Russian counterpart, Sergei Lavrov.

Irakli Bzhinava

Irakli Bzhinava holds dual Abkhazian and Russian citizenship and lives in Russia. The initial grounds for his arrest stemmed from a social media post he published on 23 December 2022, in which he criticised an agreement to transfer a famous state-owned holiday residence in Abkhazia to Russia. Russian authorities accuse Bzhinava over the post of “criminal intent to make public calls for activities directed against the security of the Russian Federation”.

In mid-September 2026, Russia’s Investigative Committee opened a second criminal case against Bzhinava, accusing him of “publicly justifying terrorist Shamil Basayev on the internet”.

According to Oleg Bartsits, Abkhazia’s Foreign Ministry remains in regular contact with the Russian side and also liaises with Bzhinava’s relatives and lawyers. The Abkhaz consul in Russia recently visited Irakli Bzhinava, and the authorities also arranged a meeting between him and his mother.

Bartsits adds that some issues remain unresolved, but they fall under the jurisdiction of Russian law enforcement agencies, and the Abkhaz side respects this. Since Bzhinava is a Russian citizen, Abkhazia’s authorities have limited scope for action, although members of the public are urging them to do everything possible to help their compatriot.

Prominent Abkhaz public figure Akhra Bzhania explains in his blog why Irakli Bzhinava’s case matters so much to Abkhaz society. In his view, by punishing Bzhinava for his dissenting views, Russia is trying to intimidate all Abkhaz people who share his position. And there are many of them.

Most Abkhaz people oppose agreements under which Russia seeks to take something from Abkhazia or derive some benefit from it. The issue of Shamil Basayev is also controversial: he received the title of “Hero of Abkhazia” for his participation in the 1992–93 Georgian-Abkhaz war. In short, many other Abkhaz people could have made — and have made — the statements that led to Bzhinava’s arrest.

Akhra Bzhania: “An effective state is possible only when society is free and responsible. Society acts as a reservoir, supplying the state with everything it needs: personnel, money and a worldview. It also holds the state to account through the press and political institutions.

This model works wherever society is free and confident in its natural rights. To a large extent, it works in Abkhazia too. Our society delegates power to the authorities not as a sacred function, but to represent its real interests. When the authorities begin to disregard those interests, a correction follows: the government resigns, and the overall political course returns to a path guided by our own sovereign interests.

A free and politically active society is what makes us strong, allowing us to advance our own agenda under the most difficult circumstances. Our freedom is our immunity against everything that threatens us — a fence that marks where other people’s interests end and ours begin.

Irakli Bzhinava’s arrest is an attack on this very immunity.

I do not believe there are any naive people in Abkhazia who think the charges against our compatriot are purely personal. Almost our entire society could face the same accusations on entirely legitimate grounds, because the overwhelming majority of us think exactly as he does.”

Therefore, Bzhinava’s arrest and the extremely harsh conditions of his detention aim not to counter his personal views, but to control the ideological climate in Abkhazia.

From now on, anyone who dares to criticise agreements between Russia and Abkhazia must consider the possibility of arrest on charges of “making public calls for activities directed against the security of the Russian Federation”.

We must respond appropriately to this, if only out of an instinct for self-preservation, not to mention civic solidarity. This applies to everyone: political parties, public movements, creative unions and parliament. In this case, the strength of our response will determine the extent of our freedom. We must defend Irakli Bzhinava not for his sake, but for our own.”

The terminology, place names and views expressed in this article are those of the author and do not necessarily reflect the editorial position of this website.

The case of Irakli Bzhinava

World.title: Uzbektelecom shares surge more than tenfold in 2026
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, October 21. Shares of Uzbekistan’s national telecommunications operator Uztelecom climbed to a record 20,499 soums (about $1,70) during trading, gaining 7.9% in a single session, as the stock continued its strong rally on the domestic market.

This was reflected in the statement by KAP DEPO.

By the end of the trading session, the shares had retreated and stabilized at around 20,000 soums (around $0,0017), according to the reported market data.

According to Trend’s calculations, the peak price of 20,499 soums (about $1,70) represented an increase of approximately 1,501 soums (approx. $0,12) from the previous session’s implied price of around 18,998 soums (around $1,58).

Since the beginning of 2026, Uztelecom shares have increased approximately 10.5-fold, while their value has risen 11.4% over the past 30 days. Over the past 12 months, the shares have gained approximately 10.3-fold.

Based on the reported multiples, the implied share price at the beginning of 2026 was approximately 1,952 soums (approx. $0,16), while the price 12 months earlier was around 1,990 soums (about $0,17). The 30-day increase suggests a price of approximately 18,399 soums (around $1,53) at the beginning of that period.

Uztelecom is Uzbekistan’s national telecommunications operator, providing fixed-line and mobile communications, broadband internet, digital television and cloud services. The company serves more than 10 million individual and corporate customers and plays a key role in the country’s digital infrastructure.

The company reported revenue of 10.51 trillion soums (around $872.6 million) in 2025, up from 8.96 trillion soums (approx. $743.9 million) in 2024. Its net profit reached 590.91 billion soums, compared with 41.63 billion soums (about $3.4 million) a year earlier, according to published financial data.

The stock’s price performance reflects changes in its market valuation, although share-price gains alone do not establish the underlying reasons for investor demand.

World.title: Georgia’s September trade deficit widens to $1.07B, year’s largest
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, October 21. Georgia’s trade deficit reached $1.07 billion in September 2026, according to the National Statistics Office of Georgia (Geostat).

According to Trend’s calculations based on Geostat’s monthly data, September’s gap was the largest of any month so far in 2026. It exceeded August’s $841.2 million deficit by 27.7% and ran 20.1% above the average monthly deficit of $894.3 million recorded over the first eight months of the year.

Imports rose to $1.8 billion in September, the highest monthly import figure of 2026 to date, while exports of $731.2 million came in below the July and August levels. Trend’s calculations show that the trade turnover of $2.53 billion in September was the second-highest monthly figure in the 2023-2026 period, after July 2026’s $2.56 billion.

The September result stands in contrast to the broader nine-month trend. Over January-September as a whole, Georgia’s trade deficit narrowed by 3.3% year-on-year to $8.23 billion, even as total trade turnover expanded 9.2%. Exports grew 19.6% over the nine months, significantly outpacing the 5.3% rise in imports. As a result, the deficit’s share of overall turnover fell to 40.1% - the lowest ratio recorded in the four years covered by Geostat’s data.

Monthly figures throughout 2026 show that export growth consistently outpaced import growth in most months. July remains the strongest month for exports, when shipments reached $793.9 million - the highest monthly total in the 2023-2026 series. September’s export figure, while solid, did not match that peak, and the sharp rise in imports produced the year’s largest single-month deficit.

More detailed statistics available for the first eight months of the year indicate that the overall export expansion has been accompanied by a structural shift. Domestic exports (excluding re-exports) rose 63.5% and already accounted for more than 60% of total exports. Motor cars remained the largest single export category but declined in volume, while petroleum products and precious metal ores and concentrates expanded sharply.

On the geographic side, Kyrgyzstan, China and Russia were the leading export destinations in January-August. Türkiye continued to rank as the top source of imports, followed by Russia and the United States. Türkiye, China and Russia remained Georgia’s three largest trading partners by total turnover.

World.title: Chronicles of Victory: October 21, 2020
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, October 21. The Azerbaijani Army launched a counter-offensive operation, later called the "Iron Fist", on September 27, 2020, in response to the large-scale provocation of the Armenian armed forces along the frontline.

The erupted 44-day Second Karabakh War ended with the liberation of Azerbaijan’s territories from nearly 30-year Armenian occupation and the restoration of territorial integrity.

Trend presents the chronicle of the 24-th day of the second Karabakh war:

- The publication is made on the official Twitter page of the President of Azerbaijan Ilham Aliyev due to the liberation from occupation of a number of villages in Fizuli and Jabrayil regions.

- The publication is made on the official Twitter page of President Ilham Aliyev on the liberation from occupation of the Minjivan settlement and 13 villages of the Zangilan region.

- President Ilham Aliyev interviewed by Japan’s Nikkei newspaper.

- The Ministry of Defense of Azerbaijan presents the latest data from the front, and also reports on the liquidation of the chief of artillery, battalion commander and battalion commander of the Armenian Armed Forces, the destruction of the battalion of the 556th regiment of the Armenian army

- The Defense Ministry presents a video of night and day artillery firing of the Azerbaijani Armed Forces.

- Azerbaijani MoD shows footage of newly-liberated Chereken village.

- Another Armenian UAV is destroyed, and a video of military equipment abandoned by Armenian units on the battlefield is made public.

- Air defense units of Azerbaijan discover and destroyed 3 more tactical UAVs of the Armenian Armed Forces.

- Armenia continues to escalate the situation in the front-line zone.

World.title: Azerbaijani families of missing persons stage protest outside European Parliament (PHOTO)
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, October 20. A group of Azerbaijani families of missing persons held a protest outside the European Parliament in Brussels, Belgium, on October 20. Organized by the “Garabagh Missing Families” Public Union, the demonstration took place at Place du Luxembourg, Azerbaijan’s Agency for State Support to NGOs reported.

A protest statement read out during the demonstration highlighted the plight of families who have been waiting for more than 30 years for news of their missing relatives. It said that 4,010 Azerbaijanis, including 71 children, 288 women and 319 elderly people, went missing during Armenia’s occupation of Azerbaijani territories.

The statement noted that 32 mass graves had been discovered in liberated Azerbaijani territories, with 328 missing persons identified through forensic genetic examinations and the remains of 273 handed over to their families. It called on Armenia to disclose relevant information and archives to help establish the fate of those still missing.

The families also appealed to the European Parliament, urging greater attention to the issue and stressing that the right to know the truth is a universal human right. Recalling the case of Elmira Dadashova, who died without learning the fate of her missing son after travelling to Geneva to raise the issue, they asked EU institutions: “How many more mothers must pass away without knowing the fate of their children?”

A special installation featuring photographs and clothing of missing Azerbaijanis, along with letters bearing messages from their perspective, was displayed during the protest. Visitors expressed solidarity by writing messages of support, tying commemorative ribbons and laying flowers.

Konul Behbudova, chair of the “Garabagh Missing Families” Public Union, called on Armenia to disclose information about mass grave locations and help clarify the fate of missing Azerbaijanis, stressing that no family should have to wait forever for answers.

On August 30 last year, the “Garabagh Missing Families” Public Union held a protest in Geneva in front of the “Palace of Nations,” where the UN’s European office is located, at the symbolic “Broken Chair” monument, which represents the cries of people suffering from all forms of armed violence. During the protest, personal belongings and documents of missing Azerbaijanis were displayed, and an original composition of slogans was presented, narrating their life stories and addressing humanity in their voice.

The union won the NGO Support Agency’s 2026 grant competition with its “Echoes of Absence” project.

Meanwhile, Gilavar Photo Club of Azerbaijan organized exhibitions in seven European cities — Geneva, Brno, Ljubljana, Sarajevo, Zagreb, Salzburg and Rome — as part of the “A Mine-Free World” campaign, highlighting mine threats in liberated Azerbaijani territories, including residential areas, cemeteries and sites near mass graves.

World.title: Family fears there will be deaths as NDIS changes hit close to home
World.content:
Shane Danes is a "social butterfly", a die-hard Parramatta Eels fan and loves classic Aussie rock.

The 64-year-old also lives with an acquired brain injury and spinal cord injury from a car crash 44 years ago and a fall in 2022.

"Shane is a bit of a local celebrity," said his support provider Michelle Doughty.

He also needs round-the-clock care at his home in the rural Queensland town of Goondiwindi, which is why Ms Doughty was so worried when the National Disability Insurance Scheme (NDIS) began to reduce his budget.

Mr Danes's funding through the scheme declined in October 2025 and again in April 2026 when his family attempted to get funding back to previous levels.

It meant his elderly parents, Toni and Merven Danes, both 90, had to support him for two hours each evening.

Shane Danes's support provider, Michelle Doughty, says they have had to reduce the social outings he enjoys. (Supplied: Michelle Doughty )

But they said he was left alone for an hour between 6am and 7am each day, when the family felt it was safest, because of the shortfall in funding.

Ms Doughty said she was so worried that on the third day of the new arrangement she came into work early on April 21 and found Mr Danes vomiting, which she feared could have been fatal had she not been with him.

"Shane would have aspirated, and the outcome wouldn't have been what it was," she said.

"Now, if we'd done that to an animal, we would be in trouble, but yet people expect us to do that to a human," she said.

Ms Doughty said because of this incident, her company decided to charge the NDIS less so they could spend more hours with him and barely broke even providing his care.

"I'm doing what I know is right for my beliefs," she said.

While the change to Mr Danes's care was made before reforms to the NDIS were legislated in August, his family, who all devote time to looking after him, said they are worried about his future.

Family stretched

Shane Dane's sister, Tracy Sullivan, 62, has cared for him for decades, along with their mother, and is desperate to keep him out of aged care.

She said the work includes hoisting, transfers, bowel and bladder management, personal care, meals, managing medication, and bed sore prevention.

Ms Sullivan said she supports her brother while managing paid work and caring for her grandchildren because of a lack of child care in the rural town.

"I love and enjoy being with him," she said.

"[But] it's been a bit of a hard slog."

Advocates stretched

Independent disability advocate Alyce Nelligan said Mr Danes's story was not unusual.

More than $2.8 billion was cut from NDIS participant plans between July 2024 and March 2026.

Alyce Nelligan says other families have experienced similar problems. (ABC Southern Qld: David Chen)

Ms Nelligan said some providers were picking up the slack after having to choose between their wages and keeping their clients alive.

"Nobody should be put in that position," Ms Nelligan said.

A National Disability Insurance Agency (NDIA) spokesperson said the safety and care of participants was its priority, and it carefully considers all information when deciding what funding and supports a participant should receive.

Family support

When the NDIS was rolled out a decade ago, Mr Danes's family were relieved he could finally have the life he deserved.

His local doctor, Goondiwindi GP Sarah Gleeson, said he thrived under his previous care arrangement.

"If someone could be the poster boy for NDIS, it would be Shane," Dr Gleeson said.

Shane Dane's family have been doing their best to fill the gaps in his care, but say they cannot keep this up. (ABC Southern Qld: Elly Bradfield )

She said since the changes there had been situations where he has been unable to have his catheter or stoma changed, which also impacted his quality of life.

"It impacts his dignity, and it impacts the small moments of independence that he can have," she said.

World.title: AFL sets date and time of AFL Origin between WA and SA
World.content:
The AFL has set the date for next year's State of Origin clash between Western Australia and South Australia.

The two states will clash at Perth Stadium on Saturday, February 27, marking South Australia's first Origin appearance in 28 years.

The match will begin at 4:40pm local time in Perth (7:10pm ACDT, 7:40pm AEDT).

"We are thrilled to officially confirm a date for AFL Origin in 2027, with Western Australia and South Australia set to reignite one of football’s greatest rivalries next February," AFL CEO Andrew Dillon said.

"[Perth] Stadium provided an incredible stage for AFL Origin's return earlier this year and we look forward to continuing to build on that momentum as we prepare for a meeting of two proud football states in Perth.

"We know football fans around the country will embrace the opportunity to celebrate the history, rivalry and unique spectacle that is AFL Origin."

WA and SA have not faced each other in a State of Origin since 1998, and the fixture coincides with the 150th anniversary of the SANFL competition.

State of Origin returned in 2026, with Victoria defeating WA by 36 points in Perth.

SA replaces Victoria for the 2027 edition, but the two old rivals will meet in 2028.

World.title: Weekend of West Bank violence embodies Israel's defensiveness over scrutiny
World.content:
Violence against foreigners in the occupied West Bank, particularly journalists, almost always garners greater attention than the reported daily attacks by Israeli settlers on Palestinians.

Often it's because the media is physically there at that exact moment, bearing witness to the crimes.

But it's also because of how the attacks prompt a very different response from authorities.

Unlike the assaults of Palestinians, which are often dismissed, ignored or sadly viewed as just part of daily life, those against foreign nationals are actually acknowledged.

Friday's beating of the Washington Post's Heidi Levine, and Saturday's attack against a group of European diplomats, are yet more sorry examples of this phenomenon.

The attacks by settlers took place amidst the olive harvest in the West Bank. (Reuters: Ammar Awad)

But this weekend's commentary from Israeli officials and the country's backers also marked a shift in rhetoric.

Some bristled in their defence of settlers and their conduct, which many around the world view as reprehensible, while others accused the media of another antisemitic beat-up and even complicity in some sort of a Palestinian entrapment of innocent settlers.

It's further evidence of what many humanitarian organisations often accuse Israel of — that is, treating settler violence as a public relations problem for the country, rather than a deeper issue with individuals using violence to enforce what they see as their biblical right to land.

And even though some suspects have since been arrested by Israeli police, the criticism of the political response remains, as it shows how the situation on the ground is unlikely to change for the Palestinians who continue to bear the brunt of the violence.

Denial surrounding journalist attack

Levine, an accomplished Jewish American photojournalist who has lived in Jerusalem for decades and covered conflicts around the world, was beaten by masked Israeli settlers in the village of Abu Falah, north of Ramallah.

Her camera, phone and passport were stolen. Her injuries were so severe that colleagues later reported she underwent surgery on her hand.

Levine herself said she feared she wouldn't have survived the attack had she not been wearing a helmet and flak jacket. It's important to also note, that protective vest had the word "press" clearly plastered across its front and back.

Heidi Levine was injured during an attack by Israeli militant settlers on Palestinians harvesting olives. (Reuters: Ali Sawafta)

Video from the scene showed Levine surrounded by settlers who threw her to the ground during the ordeal.

Compare that reality to the view Benjamin Netanyahu's office put forward hours later.

In a statement posted on X, and written in English rather than Hebrew given the international attention the case was getting, the Israeli prime minister's office said, "the facts surrounding the confrontation … remain unclear".

The statement went on to question whether it was the Israeli settlers or the Palestinians trying to harvest olives in Abu Falah who had "initiated the violence", and even suggested there was video showing Levine had been "immediately helped to her feet by the same unidentified individual" who had knocked her over during the "alleged assault".

'Israeli terrorists' target villagers' homes in days-long siege Palestinians in a small West Bank village have spent almost a week under siege from Israeli settlers, with members of the community accusing the Israeli military of complicity in the saga.

Despite insisting "Israel unequivocally condemns violence against anyone", the prime minister's office was questioning the account of a victim of a brutal attack that had been caught on camera.

The rationale for making such a claim appeared less about letting an investigation run its course, and more about sending a message to constituents in the middle of an election campaign.

"We will not allow disputed incidents to be exploited to demonise the hundreds of thousands of law-abiding Jewish residents of Judea and Samaria," the prime minister's office said, using the biblical names for the area of the West Bank.

Violence prompts conspiracies

From the moment the attack hit the headlines, social media erupted with the usual chorus of support for the settler cause.

But this time the defence also included more disturbing insinuations about the role of the media in the mess.

David Friedman, the US ambassador to Israel during the first Trump administration, claimed the attacks were "petty violence" which was "all performative and being reported by journalists" in an attempt to push new smears against Israel.

Vehicles at the site where Belgium's foreign minister says a delegation of European diplomats and officials were attacked by masked settlers. (Reuters: Emad Diab)

Another former American diplomat, Ellie Cohanim, seized upon commentary asking how journalists knew to be in Abu Falah ahead of the violence between settlers and Palestinians.

"I wish Israeli authorities would find a permanent solution to the agitators who are coming into Israel & these communities explicitly to start another blood libel," she posted on X.

Writer Adam Louis-Klein went even further, demanding a police and IDF investigation into the Washington Post and suggesting the journalists and their contacts could have played a role in "inciting or instigating or engaging in violence against Israeli civilians".

They were positions that not only sought to shift blame and responsibility, but also totally overlooked a basic journalistic principle — to anticipate news events.

For years, the olive harvest in the West Bank has been a flashpoint for violence between Palestinians trying to safeguard their income and settlers trying to destroy their crop.

It was therefore unsurprising that it was an issue on the radar of the media.

Add to that, as Israeli media has itself reported, some settler groups issuing call-outs to attend and disrupt the harvest in towns and villages across the West Bank, and the conspiracy theories fray even further.

Arrests a rare development

On Saturday, the crisis took another turn when a delegation of European diplomats and officials, as well as representatives from the Catholic Church, were attacked in Taybeh, a predominantly Christian community north-east of Ramallah.

Again, condemnations of violence were wrapped in significant caveats.

Loading...

Israel's Foreign Minister Gideon Sa'ar argued the group hadn't coordinated their movements with the IDF beforehand, and that could have helped with their security — something which again didn't deal with the root problem.

Then the prime minister weighed in.

"These reports come amid concerns about a coordinated campaign to smear Israel and the Jewish residents of Judea and Samaria during the annual olive harvest, relying on sensational headlines before the full facts emerge," his office said on social media.

"We may see further allegations in the coming days. By the time the evidence is fully examined, the reputational damage from premature conclusions may already be done."

Such comments are not entirely surprising given Israel is just a week away from an election, and they put Mr Netanyahu at odds with his political rivals who took a much firmer stance against the attacks.

Loading

But data about the crisis in the West Bank shows just how big the problem has become, and how the risk of ignoring it or diminishing it can end up fuelling the fire even further.

The United Nations said there had been 244 instances of settler attacks resulting in casualties or property damage from September 29 to October 12 alone.

An announcement on Monday that Israeli police had arrested 11 people in relation to the two weekend attacks on foreigners showed authorities were investigating the issue.

But it's a rare development, given the regularly reported lack of arrests and prosecutions of settlers when their victims are Palestinian.

And the chorus of allegations that Palestinians are actually to blame for it all only grows louder, after news a far-right political candidate's convoy was attacked by Palestinians on Monday afternoon while on a tour with pro-settler advocates.

World.title: Counselling available for Wangaratta residents reeling from Haines attack
World.content:
Trained Australian Red Cross volunteers will be in Wangaratta today to provide psychological first aid to residents still reeling from the attack on their local MP Helen Haines.

Ms Haines was unloading the boot of her car after attending an event in Mansfield when she was struck by a car and pinned between the two vehicles.

Her leg was amputated on Tuesday and she remains in Melbourne's Alfred Hospital in a critical condition as surgeons work to save her other leg.

Helen Haines live updates: Get the latest about the attack on the Victorian MP in our blog.

The driver, Brendan Nugent, 43, of Tarrawingee, is due to face Wangaratta Magistrates' Court today charged with dangerous driving causing serious injury and intentionally causing serious injury.

He was also charged with the federal offence of causing harm to a Commonwealth public official, which carries a maximum penalty of 10 years' imprisonment.

As bunches of flowers and handwritten letters pile up on the doorstep of her electoral office, vigils are being organised across the country in an outpouring of support.

Members of the Wangaratta community are in shock after Helen Haines was allegedly targeted in a violent attack. (ABC News: Annie Brown)

Several hundred community members gathered for a vigil at Wangaratta's Holy Trinity Anglican church on Tuesday afternoon.

People were seen hugging and crying on the church steps as they tried to process what had happened in their regional town.

Today, Australian Red Cross volunteers will be offering their support at the Ovens Riverside Square between 9am and 12 noon.

Victorian manger Fyowna Norton said unimaginable acts of violence could have a profound impact on a tight-knit community.

"Australian Red Cross volunteers are trained in psychological first aid, so we'll be in Wangaratta providing face-to-face support to community members and where floral tributes are being laid outside [Ms Haines's] offices.

"It is really important that people don't bottle up what they're feeling and that they seek support where they need to."

People embrace outside a church in Wangaratta after a vigil for Helen Haines on Tuesday. (ABC News: Annie Brown)

A virtual vigil

When Tracey Asquith heard the news about Helen Haines, she wanted the focus to be on the injured woman, her husband, children, friends and the community.

"I know they'll be hurting and she is going to face the biggest challenge," she said.

Within hours, Ms Asquith created a virtual vigil calling for people across Australia to pause on Friday, October 23 at 8pm (AEDT) to reflect on Ms Haines.

"What I hope is at 8pm Victorian time for 15 minutes, you light a candle, or turn on a battery-operated one, shine a torch or turn on your phone [torch] in your home, driveway, at a park or wherever you gather with friends and family and reflect on Helen and what she is going through," she said.

"The overriding sentiment is Helen has done nothing to deserve this."

More than 10,000 people have engaged with the virtual vigil idea on social media.

Governor-general support

Governor-General Sam Mostyn said she was "deeply shocked" by the attack on Ms Haines and contacted her office to speak with staff on Tuesday.

Sam Mostyn and Helen Haines with CFA members in Indi. (Supplied: CFA)

"They were able to reflect that while the actions of one person can cause immense harm, it is the rallying of the thousands they have experienced that tells us what is good and decent about the essential character of Australians, whether that is in Wangaratta or across the country," she said.

She said Ms Haines was a "highly respected" member of parliament who "proudly" represented the people of her electorate, always with dignity and respect.

"Helen and I were together recently in Euroa thanking first responders in her community for their selfless work," Ms Mostyn said.

"I want to extend my thanks to all those who responded so quickly to assist Helen and her team.

"I am sure all Australians would join me in sending her best wishes for a full recovery."

World.title: Ellis scores monster 47 points, most in WNBL game for over two decades
World.content:
Townsville's Abbey Ellis has produced one of the all-time great WNBL individual performances with a mammoth 47-point effort in the Fire's 86-68 away win over Adelaide.

The defending champions trailed 35-21 in the second quarter but outscored Adelaide 27-10 in the last term.

They improved to 1-1 while Adelaide dropped to 0-2.

Ellis kept her team afloat in the first half, scoring 25 of their first 33 points and their first 16 of the second quarter.

Her club record individual score, eclipsing the 45 points by Chandi Jones in 2005, was the equal fifth-highest in WNBL history and the largest in 21 years.

She joined league legends Lauren Jackson, Penny Taylor and Belinda Snell among the only players to record 47 points and six steals in a game.

"It's a pretty cool feeling," Ellis said.

She hit 16 of 24 from the field, nailing seven of 13 from three-point range.

"Credit to our team, we used the ball really well and found the hot hand," Ellis said.

Townsville coach Shannon Seebohm said Ellis was one of the bravest players he had coached.

"Abbey had probably one of the best games that I know I've ever seen In the WNBL, making huge shots, making big plays," Seebohm said.

"I said to her probably the thing I was most proud of her wasn't all the scoring, [it was] that she was fighting as hard as she could and defending her butt off."

Adelaide led by seven at quarter-time and Townsville scored the last seven points of the second quarter to get within three at the half.

As the game progressed, Townsville's defence improved and Ellis got more scoring support from Courtney Woods (14) and German centre Marie Gulich (13).

Alicia Froling grabbed 11 rebounds and Alexandra Fowler 10 to help Townsville collect 11 more boards.

Adelaide were shooting at 62 per cent from the field at half-time, but that dropped to 45 per cent by the end, as they scored just 25 points after half-time.

"We had a tough second half," Lightning coach Aja Parham-Ammar said.

Tayla Brazel led Adelaide's offence with a personal WNBL career-high of 19, at 72 per cent from the field.

Shay Ciezki tallied 13 points, Zitina Aokuso 12 and Opals star Steph Talbot had 11 and nine assists in her first game back from WNBA duties.

World.title: Nightlife venues embrace 'experience economy' as alcohol consumption falls
World.content:
On a muggy weeknight in central Queensland, a sea of young people dressed in bright activewear pack out a pub.

But they're not here for the booze.

The group is refuelling after taking part in a weekly run club, where runners can cash in on a meal discount at a rotating list of venues.

Harrison Boag says his drinking habits have changed since early adulthood. (ABC Capricornia: Jacob Gamble)

Tucking into a steak and salad, 26-year-old Harrison Boag says his alcohol consumption is close to zero drinks a week.

"I just enjoy being healthy and drinking wasn't helping with that, so I realised at a certain point it doesn't fit into my life," he says.

Mr Boag is not alone.

A Flinders University study found generation Z is 20 times less likely than baby boomers to choose to drink alcohol.

It's one of many challenges facing the nightlife industry, according to Queensland's first nightlife economy commissioner, John "JC" Collins.

John Collins says consumers' habits have changed and business costs have risen. (ABC News: Liz Pickering)

"Young people have been healthy, which is great, but … they're not spending as much over the bar," he says.

The Powderfinger bassist says the cost of doing business has "gone through the roof", with rising insurance, supply prices and wages.

" That balance of what's gone up and the revenues coming down is really squeezing most of the venues across the state. "

Pub owner Stephen Roberts hosts the run club group at his venue monthly and says nightlife culture has shifted away from just serving alcohol.

Stephen Roberts says the run club brings up to 100 young people to his venue. (ABC Capricornia: Jacob Gamble)

"We're sort of reaching out to a crowd that maybe we wouldn't have reached out to before [because] we're quite an old-school country-style pub," he says.

"It's less about drinking now and more about socialising."

The standing darts board is one of the main attractions at Stephen Robert's pub. (ABC Capricornia: Jacob Gamble)

Experience economy

Coined in a 1998 Harvard Business Review article, the "experience economy" is a concept that businesses can create more value by offering memorable experiences rather than simply selling products or services.

Felix Septianto says businesses can generate better word of mouth by offering memorable experiences. (Supplied: Felix Septianto)

University of Queensland Associate Professor Felix Septianto specialises in consumer behaviour and says nightlife patrons remember an event or experience over the beverage they ordered.

"We can buy a beer or a glass of wine almost anywhere … what makes people choose to go to a venue?" he says.

" People don't just buy products or services, they buy the feelings. "

Regional nightlife is centred around pubs and taverns. (ABC Capricornia: Jacob Gamble)

Dr Septianto says selling memorable experiences could help regional businesses perform well in a market with a smaller population base.

"When in the regional areas … we cannot always rely on getting new people," he says.

"Offering different activities and experiences would give our customers reasons to keep coming back."

Post-COVID nightlife

The nightlife economy commissioner's Moonside report flags changing patron behaviours after COVID lockdowns as another factor inhibiting the industry.

Jordan Baker-Moller used to manage a Rockhampton nightclub and recalls the city's nightlife before the pandemic as "vibrant" with ample entertainment options.

"You had heaps of venues open just in the CBD and genuinely thousands of people out across both Friday and Saturday night," he says.

Flamingos Rockhampton is the town's main nightclub. (ABC Capricornia: Jacob Gamble)

Mr Baker-Moller says he's witnessed a decline in young people coming out after lockdowns.

"COVID was a massive reset … in the way people view a night out and how the culture works.

"A lot of places didn't really recover."

Queensland's Safer Night Precincts give police expanded powers in designated entertainment zones. (ABC Capricornia: Jacob Gamble)

Among them was Mr Baker-Moller's former venue, which closed earlier this year.

"I do see the future … [being] around pop-up micro events that are centred more on the music and a particular culture and a particular vibe," he says.

On the main strip of coastal town Yeppoon, Leah Crowley's venue has had success honing in on one popular subculture: hosting drag queen nights.

"For our business, it's been amazing … it has been consistently a sellout," she says.

Leah Crowley says she's incredibly "proud" to host drag nights at her venue. (ABC Capricornia: Jacob Gamble)

Ms Crowley's restaurant has been hosting the bimonthly event for six years, and she says the appetite for unique events in the community is strong.

"The support here, the confidence in numbers was incredible," she says.

Elon Musk said SpaceX and Tesla have formed special committees to explore a potential merger, a preliminary step toward what would rank as the largest corporate tie-up of all time.

“I do think there’s a lot of merit to combining the companies,” Musk, the chief executive officer of both companies, said Tuesday on SpaceX’s earnings webcast. “There’s a lot to be gained from cooperating on developing superintelligence software.”

Elon Musk says that a merger isn’t certain and would require shareholder support. AP Photo/Matt Rourke

Musk said he isn’t participating in the committee discussions because he is a conflicted party, and that the committees have yet to agree on terms.

A blockbuster deal would unite Tesla’s electric vehicle, energy and robotics businesses with SpaceX’s rocket launch and satellite internet operations. Underpinning it all are the companies’ shared ambitions in artificial intelligence — or what some in the industry are now calling superintelligence — fuelling investments in areas such as data centres and driverless cars.

The US stock market mostly rose following strong profit reports from Equifax, Hasbro and other companies, while oil prices eased back after nearing their highest levels since the war with Iran began. The S&P 500 added 0.3 per cent. The Dow Jones Industrial Average rose 1 per cent, while drops for several big technology stocks including Apple and Meta Platforms weighed on the Nasdaq composite, which ended down less than 0.1 per cent. Wall Street climbed on the back of strong earnings reports as well as a slide in oil prices. AP The Australian sharemarket is set to advance, with futures at 6.45am AEDT pointing to a rise of 32 points, or 0.4 per cent, at the open., The ASX lost 0.3 per cent on Tuesday. The Australian dollar was trading higher at US70.03¢. Elon Musk said SpaceX and Tesla have formed special committees to explore a potential merger, a preliminary step toward what would rank as the largest corporate tie-up of all time.



“I do think there’s a lot of merit to combining the companies,” Musk, the chief executive officer of both companies, said on SpaceX’s earnings webcast. “There’s a lot to be gained from cooperating on developing superintelligence software.” Related Article Opinion

Trade wars China’s export boom is becoming its Achilles heel Stephen Bartholomeusz Senior business columnist SpaceX reported after the closing bell, posting a 161 per cent rise in revenue for the third quarter, beating estimates, buoyed by a surge in its AI business and steady growth at its Starlink satellite-internet unit. Revenue in the third quarter stood at $US14.58 billion ($20.8 billion), compared with analysts’ estimate of $US12.72 billion, according to data compiled by LSEG. Meanwhile, AI startup Anthropic recorded a net loss of more than $US80 billion in the first half of this year, including $US72 billion in accounting charges, the Wall Street Journal reported on Tuesday, citing a draft initial public offering prospectus. Stock prices tend to follow the path of corporate profits over the long term, and several companies delivered results for the latest quarter that were better than analysts expected. Big expectations for growth generally are what have allowed the US stock market to hit records recently despite worries about high inflation, higher interest rates and other challenges weighing on Wall Street.



Equifax rallied 11.3 per cent for one of the market’s biggest gains after reporting a bigger profit for the summer than analysts expected, despite high mortgage rates slowing some parts of its business. Hasbro climbed 11.2 per cent after the toy company said its Magic: The Gathering game made more than $US600 million ($857 million) during a quarter for the first time. 3M rose 5.8 per cent after the company behind Ace bandages and Scotch-Brite sponges likewise reported a stronger-than-expected profit, even as shoppers broadly feel discouraged by high inflation. Stocks also got a lift after the price for a barrel of Brent crude erased an early gain to fall 0.8 per cent to $US108.70. Earlier in the morning, it got near $US112 and approached its highest price since the war with Iran began in late February. The drop in oil prices will relieve some of the pressure on inflation, if it lasts. Brent’s price has been yo-yoing between $US97 and $US112 per barrel this month on uncertainty about when the energy industry will return to normal. For now, airlines and other companies with big fuel bills enjoyed the benefit of Tuesday’s drop. American Airlines rallied 3.7 per cent, and United Airlines flew 2.3 per cent higher.



Another winner was Braze, a customer engagement platform. Its stock soared 51.7 per cent to $US45.57 after Salesforce said it would buy the company for $US47.50 in cash for each share. Salesforce closed flat. Keeping the market in check was General Motors, which sank 6.8 per cent despite reporting a bigger profit than analysts expected. It also announced a program to send up to $US20 billion to investors by buying back its stock. The pressure is on companies to deliver bigger profits not only now, but also in the future. GM gave a forecasted range for profit over the full year of 2026 whose midpoint fell short of analysts’ expectations. AI stocks, meanwhile, continued to swirl. They’ve been at the centre of the market’s recent uneasiness, as euphoria around the technology’s boom gives way to worries that high interest rates in the bond market will slow the borrowing that’s allowed companies to buy so many AI chips. Last week was the US stock market’s worst since June because of weakness for AI-related companies. CoreWeave has been particularly shaky. It initially fell more than 6 per cent at the start of Tuesday’s trading, only to swing to a gain of 5 per cent before pulling back to a rise of 1.7 per cent.



Such reversals are nothing new for the company, which has borrowed money to buy AI chips that it rents out to customers over the cloud. A day earlier, it careened between a gain of 7 per cent in the morning and a loss of 3.5 per cent in the afternoon following last week’s tumble of roughly 25 per cent. Tuesday’s struggles for AI stocks began in Asia, where a South Korean AI company, Elice, confronted a rough welcome to the stock market. Its stock dropped 32 per cent in its first day of trading in Seoul. South Korea’s Kospi index fell 3.7 per cent overall. Related Article Australian Council of Trade Unions New ACTU president warns AI is automating entire jobs In other stock markets abroad, indexes in Europe pared bigger losses from earlier in the day. The CAC 40 in Paris slipped 0.4 per cent, and the FTSE 100 in London fell 0.3 per cent. A day earlier, indexes fell sharply across Europe following violent protests that could ultimately force governments on the continent to increase their spending to ease voters’ anger. That in turn could put more pressure on their bond markets, which are already strained because of worries about heavy debt loads and strained budgets.

Gqeberha: Mitchell Starc says Josh Hazlewood’s stomach bug left the Australians pining for another bowler at times as South Africa took control of the second Test, while insisting Nathan Lyon has put a brave face on his latest omission from the team. While Hazlewood returned to the team on day three, Starc said he was still feeling the effects of the illness that confined him to the team hotel the previous day, and that his absence had a cumulative effect on the rest of the attack. Mitchell Starc claims the wicket of Temba Bavuma. Getty Images Beau Webster took up much of the slack with his seamers, but like skipper Pat Cummins finished wicketless, as did Durban surprise packet Matt Renshaw. “Coming into the game, you don’t know you’re going to be a man down there,” Starc said. “So Beau bowled a lot more than he probably expected to, and I thought he bowled quite nicely. Beat the bat a lot, so he probably played that role, that holding role a bit more, and came from both ends.



“We saw him there at the end, bowling with the part-timers a little bit as well. If you know you could be a man down from the start, you’re probably playing a different make-up, aren’t you? But yeah, unfortunately, Josh has had a dodgy prawn or something, and he’ll be fresh legs for the second innings.” Starc and Lyon have long been close, and the fast bowlers referenced his teammate’s emotional boundary side interview during the Gabba Ashes Test, when he said he was “filthy” to be left out. Loading “Not sure he was doing his sideline reporting today,” Starc said. “Yeah, everyone wants to play every game. You’re naturally going to be disappointed when you don’t get put in the 11. “He’s been around long enough to put his shoes back on and be the team man that he is, he’s been on the boundary most of the day today, whether it’s down at fine leg running drinks or just a little tap on the back.



“I think I’ve been left out plenty of times, and naturally disappointed that you don’t get to play. He’ll get another opportunity. We know his experience around the group.” Asked about bowling plans, Starc suggested that the changing nature of the surface had presented a few questions for Cummins. Josh Hazlewood returned from a stomach illness. Getty Images “Josh did pretty well to get through the overs he did with the way he was feeling,” Starc said. “There’s not as much lateral movement as it was on that first stint on day one. Once the ball got a bit older and softer, it was quite a true surface. “We changed a few different plans there. At times we went full and short, and other times we hung it out there and they played pretty well. So, yeah, credit where it’s due. It’s a nice wicket, but they played pretty well.”



Editor's pick Australian cricket Maddinson out for a duck after Proteas declare for mammoth 9-425 Proteas captain Temba Bavuma noted that Cummins had favoured the short ball attack for much of the day, on a slower surface than Durban, and that he was expecting more of the same. “He has been quite aggressive, Pat, in terms of his plans,” Bavuma said. “So I think I wasn’t I wasn’t surprised from that point of view. I mean, we were expecting it. Marco was expecting it, but I guess it’s one thing expecting it. You still have to be able to play it, right? “But yeah, I think the way he, I guess, complements his bowling attack, all the other guys, and all of them have different challenges, if I could call it that way. Yeah, but definitely not surprised that he used that. He used that tactic in Kingsmead. He did the same thing here. Probably Cape Town, if he’s still feeling good, he’ll probably do the same.” Some eyebrows were raised when Kagiso Rabada bowled the first over of Australia’s innings in conditions where the floodlights had completely taken over. Nic Maddinson was dismissed fourth ball before the umpires decided it was too dark for anything but spin to be used.



Bavuma admitted he had delayed his declaration because he was concerned the light would be too dim for the start of Australia’s innings. “I was a bit hesitant to be honest, but that was because of the light,” he said. “ … the sun went into the deep clouds, we weren’t able to bowl the seam, so I was happy to come tomorrow, give the guys as much break as they can, the bowlers at least. But in saying that, we made the decision, and we made some ground tonight.” News, results and expert analysis from the weekend of sport are sent every Monday.

World.title: Christina Applegate reveals she was misdiagnosed with MS
World.content:
CultureCelebrityCelebrity life Christina Applegate reveals she was misdiagnosed with MS Mark Kennedy and and Chris Hook October 21, 2026 — 7:58am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

Christina Applegate, who has candidly shared raw details about her journey with multiple sclerosis for years, revealed on Monday her doctor says she doesn’t have the autoimmune disease and was misdiagnosed. “I’m back at square one where I don’t know what’s going on with me,” the actor said on the latest edition of her podcast, MeSsy, which she co-hosts with Jamie-Lynn Sigler, who has been public about her own battle with MS. Christina Applegate revealed during her podcast that she doesn’t have multiple sclerosis. AP “She came into my room, and she said, ‘Congratulations, you don’t have MS’. I was not happy at all, everybody else was so happy, crying,” Applegate said. Sigler then cut in and agreed: “When you first told me my first words were, ‘You can dance again’ because that’s just where my head goes.”



Applegate said the misdiagnosis presented further challenges. “You don’t get misdiagnosed and suddenly, I’m better. I haven’t gotten better, Jamie, if anything I have gotten worse, so I’m back at square one,” she said. Applegate, a veteran performer who came to fame on the sitcom Married With Children and was most recently seen in the Netflix series Dead To Me, publicly announced in 2021 that she was diagnosed with the disorder that causes the immune system to attack the cells in the central nervous system. In August, Applegate was discharged from the hospital after an almost four-month stay, according to Page Six. Her journey with the autoimmune disease was also detailed in her memoir You With the Sad Eyes, which was published earlier this year.



On Monday’s podcast, Applegate revealed that despite the misdiagnosis, she still has “every symptom of someone with MS”, and added: “I still have to use wheelchairs when I go to the doctor’s office. I can’t walk from the car to the room.” Applegate in 2020. AP There is no single test for MS, and a diagnosis usually involves ruling out other causes. It can take years and seeing multiple doctors before one puts the clues together. Applegate said the news had put her in an odd place since she and Sigler had become prominent advocates for people with MS. “It’s weird because I feel like I let everybody down,” she said. “It’s very unnerving, and it’s really confusing for me.”



Applegate on stage at the 2024 Emmys. AP Most autoimmune diseases, especially in adults, aren’t caused by a specific gene defect. Instead, various genes that affect immune functions can make people susceptible. Scientists say it then takes an “environmental” trigger, such as an infection, smoking or pollutants, to set the disease in motion. In her memoir, Applegate is candid about unpredictable symptoms that have forced her to use diapers and scoot downstairs on her backside. “My life has in some ways shrunk to the size of my California king,” she writes in her book. The Emmy-award winning actor also revealed in her memoir that had been diagnosed with early-stage breast cancer at age 36 during routine checks, and underwent a double mastectomy before being declared cancer-free.



The experience left her soul-searching, and she poured her energy into breast cancer charity Right Action for Women, founded in 2008. “It was my way of coping with how brokenhearted I was to lose my breasts,” Applegate wrote in her memoir, according to the New York Post. “To this day, I feel emotionally and physically mangled by what I went through, but the organisation mitigates the terrible loss I felt and feel.” With AP Get a note directly from our foreign correspondents on what’s making headlines around the world.

World.content:
Shadow treasurer Tim Wilson says his need for a personal security detail has increased significantly since he returned to parliament at the last election, saying accessibility to the public is of particular importance to MPs.

“When I was last in office, I only had AFP protection occasionally. Now it is not an insignificant part of my duties, and I know I’m not alone in that. But we also need to look on the positive side, which is that when you have a public profile, when you stand up and you take responsibility, people are going to recognise you,” Wilson told News24 this morning.

Shadow treasurer Tim Wilson. Dominic Lorrimer

“Of course, we’ve had a horrific incident where somebody’s taken advantage of that. I was only a petrol station about 20 minutes ago, and I had three people come up to me and chat to me about policy, about issues. The guys at the servo wanted a selfie, so it’s one of these situations that it’s the big risk that we all face when we’re in public life,” he said.

Wilson was first a federal parliamentarian from 2016 to 2022, before losing his Melbourne seat of Goldstein. He won the seat back from independent MP Zoe Daniel at the 2025 election. The MP did not hold a portfolio during his first stint in federal parliament.

“I don’t want to live in a country where politicians need full-time security. I don’t want full-time security. But the reality is, there’s proportionate risk that members of parliament need sometimes when there’s particular types of events, and that is clearly becoming more common. And I don’t think anybody wants to see an environment where politicians need full-time security,” Wilson said.

Such reversals are nothing new for the company, which has borrowed money to buy AI chips that it rents out to customers over the cloud. A day earlier, it careened between a gain of 7 per cent in the morning and a loss of 3.5 per cent in the afternoon following last week’s tumble of roughly 25 per cent. Tuesday’s struggles for AI stocks began in Asia, where a South Korean AI company, Elice, confronted a rough welcome to the stock market. Its stock dropped 32 per cent in its first day of trading in Seoul. South Korea’s Kospi index fell 3.7 per cent overall. Related Article Australian Council of Trade Unions New ACTU president warns AI is automating entire jobs In other stock markets abroad, indexes in Europe pared bigger losses from earlier in the day. The CAC 40 in Paris slipped 0.4 per cent, and the FTSE 100 in London fell 0.3 per cent. A day earlier, indexes fell sharply across Europe following violent protests that could ultimately force governments on the continent to increase their spending to ease voters’ anger. That in turn could put more pressure on their bond markets, which are already strained because of worries about heavy debt loads and strained budgets.

Gqeberha: Mitchell Starc says Josh Hazlewood’s stomach bug left the Australians pining for another bowler at times as South Africa took control of the second Test, while insisting Nathan Lyon has put a brave face on his latest omission from the team. While Hazlewood returned to the team on day three, Starc said he was still feeling the effects of the illness that confined him to the team hotel the previous day, and that his absence had a cumulative effect on the rest of the attack. Mitchell Starc claims the wicket of Temba Bavuma. Getty Images Beau Webster took up much of the slack with his seamers, but like skipper Pat Cummins finished wicketless, as did Durban surprise packet Matt Renshaw. “Coming into the game, you don’t know you’re going to be a man down there,” Starc said. “So Beau bowled a lot more than he probably expected to, and I thought he bowled quite nicely. Beat the bat a lot, so he probably played that role, that holding role a bit more, and came from both ends.



“We saw him there at the end, bowling with the part-timers a little bit as well. If you know you could be a man down from the start, you’re probably playing a different make-up, aren’t you? But yeah, unfortunately, Josh has had a dodgy prawn or something, and he’ll be fresh legs for the second innings.” Starc and Lyon have long been close, and the fast bowlers referenced his teammate’s emotional boundary side interview during the Gabba Ashes Test, when he said he was “filthy” to be left out. Loading “Not sure he was doing his sideline reporting today,” Starc said. “Yeah, everyone wants to play every game. You’re naturally going to be disappointed when you don’t get put in the 11. “He’s been around long enough to put his shoes back on and be the team man that he is, he’s been on the boundary most of the day today, whether it’s down at fine leg running drinks or just a little tap on the back.



“I think I’ve been left out plenty of times, and naturally disappointed that you don’t get to play. He’ll get another opportunity. We know his experience around the group.” Asked about bowling plans, Starc suggested that the changing nature of the surface had presented a few questions for Cummins. Josh Hazlewood returned from a stomach illness. Getty Images “Josh did pretty well to get through the overs he did with the way he was feeling,” Starc said. “There’s not as much lateral movement as it was on that first stint on day one. Once the ball got a bit older and softer, it was quite a true surface. “We changed a few different plans there. At times we went full and short, and other times we hung it out there and they played pretty well. So, yeah, credit where it’s due. It’s a nice wicket, but they played pretty well.”



Editor's pick Australian cricket Maddinson out for a duck after Proteas declare for mammoth 9-425 Proteas captain Temba Bavuma noted that Cummins had favoured the short ball attack for much of the day, on a slower surface than Durban, and that he was expecting more of the same. “He has been quite aggressive, Pat, in terms of his plans,” Bavuma said. “So I think I wasn’t I wasn’t surprised from that point of view. I mean, we were expecting it. Marco was expecting it, but I guess it’s one thing expecting it. You still have to be able to play it, right? “But yeah, I think the way he, I guess, complements his bowling attack, all the other guys, and all of them have different challenges, if I could call it that way. Yeah, but definitely not surprised that he used that. He used that tactic in Kingsmead. He did the same thing here. Probably Cape Town, if he’s still feeling good, he’ll probably do the same.” Some eyebrows were raised when Kagiso Rabada bowled the first over of Australia’s innings in conditions where the floodlights had completely taken over. Nic Maddinson was dismissed fourth ball before the umpires decided it was too dark for anything but spin to be used.



Bavuma admitted he had delayed his declaration because he was concerned the light would be too dim for the start of Australia’s innings. “I was a bit hesitant to be honest, but that was because of the light,” he said. “ … the sun went into the deep clouds, we weren’t able to bowl the seam, so I was happy to come tomorrow, give the guys as much break as they can, the bowlers at least. But in saying that, we made the decision, and we made some ground tonight.” News, results and expert analysis from the weekend of sport are sent every Monday.

World.title: Christina Applegate reveals she was misdiagnosed with MS
World.content:
CultureCelebrityCelebrity life Christina Applegate reveals she was misdiagnosed with MS Mark Kennedy and and Chris Hook October 21, 2026 — 7:58am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

Christina Applegate, who has candidly shared raw details about her journey with multiple sclerosis for years, revealed on Monday her doctor says she doesn’t have the autoimmune disease and was misdiagnosed. “I’m back at square one where I don’t know what’s going on with me,” the actor said on the latest edition of her podcast, MeSsy, which she co-hosts with Jamie-Lynn Sigler, who has been public about her own battle with MS. Christina Applegate revealed during her podcast that she doesn’t have multiple sclerosis. AP “She came into my room, and she said, ‘Congratulations, you don’t have MS’. I was not happy at all, everybody else was so happy, crying,” Applegate said. Sigler then cut in and agreed: “When you first told me my first words were, ‘You can dance again’ because that’s just where my head goes.”



Applegate said the misdiagnosis presented further challenges. “You don’t get misdiagnosed and suddenly, I’m better. I haven’t gotten better, Jamie, if anything I have gotten worse, so I’m back at square one,” she said. Applegate, a veteran performer who came to fame on the sitcom Married With Children and was most recently seen in the Netflix series Dead To Me, publicly announced in 2021 that she was diagnosed with the disorder that causes the immune system to attack the cells in the central nervous system. In August, Applegate was discharged from the hospital after an almost four-month stay, according to Page Six. Her journey with the autoimmune disease was also detailed in her memoir You With the Sad Eyes, which was published earlier this year.



On Monday’s podcast, Applegate revealed that despite the misdiagnosis, she still has “every symptom of someone with MS”, and added: “I still have to use wheelchairs when I go to the doctor’s office. I can’t walk from the car to the room.” Applegate in 2020. AP There is no single test for MS, and a diagnosis usually involves ruling out other causes. It can take years and seeing multiple doctors before one puts the clues together. Applegate said the news had put her in an odd place since she and Sigler had become prominent advocates for people with MS. “It’s weird because I feel like I let everybody down,” she said. “It’s very unnerving, and it’s really confusing for me.”



Applegate on stage at the 2024 Emmys. AP Most autoimmune diseases, especially in adults, aren’t caused by a specific gene defect. Instead, various genes that affect immune functions can make people susceptible. Scientists say it then takes an “environmental” trigger, such as an infection, smoking or pollutants, to set the disease in motion. In her memoir, Applegate is candid about unpredictable symptoms that have forced her to use diapers and scoot downstairs on her backside. “My life has in some ways shrunk to the size of my California king,” she writes in her book. The Emmy-award winning actor also revealed in her memoir that had been diagnosed with early-stage breast cancer at age 36 during routine checks, and underwent a double mastectomy before being declared cancer-free.



The experience left her soul-searching, and she poured her energy into breast cancer charity Right Action for Women, founded in 2008. “It was my way of coping with how brokenhearted I was to lose my breasts,” Applegate wrote in her memoir, according to the New York Post. “To this day, I feel emotionally and physically mangled by what I went through, but the organisation mitigates the terrible loss I felt and feel.” With AP Get a note directly from our foreign correspondents on what’s making headlines around the world.

World.title: Costs keep rising: Cafe faces impossible choice
World.content:
Audio player for " Should you buy a house from your mother-in-law? " removed for printing Visit page to play audio: https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiJ9._f0.YIZs2-J2FpwgcBcJJb29s1vXmFAWHLh_p1oUyv-l-RA/business/2045782%2Fcosts-keep-rising-cafe-faces-impossible-choice

Angela Clements says the decision to close Pure Café in Whangārei is the result of increasing pressure from multiple directions - and economists are warning the situation could get worse.

Pure has been open for six years but will close on 27 November.

She said a lot of things had become a lot more expensive over that time. "We've been in the industry for about 15 years and things like dairy, milk cheese, those things have gone up probably 60 percent.

"I think the hardest thing is that the things we used to buy that were good quality are now out of our price range and the things that we can afford are just rubbish.

"Take cocoa powder, for example. We used to buy good quality cocoa powder for a reasonable price. Now the rubbish cocoa powder is the same price as the good stuff and the good stuff is out of our range.

"We either use a poor quality product or we put our prices up exponentially and then people just can't, they just don't buy, you know. Or the third option is the one that we've been taking lately is that we use a good quality product, but we don't put our prices up and then we just swallow the cost ourselves."

The cost of things like gas and power had also increased a lot, she said.

Stats NZ data showed restaurants and cafés may be trying to pass on some of the increases. The "restaurant and ready to eat" food group was up 3.1 percent over a year in its most recent data, compared to overall food price inflation of 2.4 percent.

Restaurant Association general manager Nicola Waldren said that group included everything from restaurants and cafés to takeaway food and it could involve a lot of different cost structures.

Restaurant Association general manager Nicola Waldren. Supplied

"Looking at the September index where prices in the group rose 3.1 percent, and 0.2 percent for the month, the annual rise is similar to grocery food at 3 percent and meat, poultry and fish at 3.2 percent, although the overall food figure is lower mainly because fruit and vegetable prices have fallen.

"Beyond food costs, hospitality businesses have also been dealing with some large increases in other costs they can't easily avoid. The same release shows household electricity prices up 9.5 percent over the year and gas up 11.4 percent. Commercial rates vary, but energy is a significant cost for businesses running kitchens, refrigeration and hot water throughout the day. Petrol prices also rose sharply in September, and some businesses are seeing higher fuel costs passed on through delivery surcharges.

"Having said that, we know any menu price increase is carefully considered, and our businesses are very aware that many households are under pressure. It's a careful balance between offering value for customers and keeping the business sustainable."

Clements said she was stuck in a position where the business could not afford to support even one full-time person.

"We consider ourselves fairly resilient but that's kind of running out. I don't think there's a great future for the industry for people that actually want a quality product. I'm uncomfortable serving up something that is not good for you and not made with quality ingredients. Look at bacon. We used to buy only New Zealand bacon but now New Zealand bacon is twice the price of imported bacon. So do you buy New Zealand bacon and price yourself out of the market or do you put imported bacon on a plate and feel bad about it?"

Westpac senior economist Satish Ranchhod. Supplied

Westpac senior economist Satish Ranchhod said its internal card spending data indicated there had been a lift in spending on takeaways and at restaurants since the start of this year.

But he said it was clear ingredient prices had increased, especially meat.

"Just as that's adding to households' grocery bills, it's also adding to the cost of producing takeaways and restaurant meals. I haven't heard anything from restaurant operators about fuel prices affecting their production costs. However, I have heard anecdotes from those in the agricultural sector about fuel prices pushing up their operating and transport costs. Over time, that could flow through to higher food prices."

BNZ chief economist Mike Jones said consumer demand in some of the discretionary spending categories was under significant pressure again as higher energy costs were felt.

Clements said she did not think there would be an improvement in the sector until households were feeling less pressure.

"It's not just the cost of stuff for us. It's the cost of people's grocery bills and power bills … we still have a lot of the same customers we used to have they just come less often and spend less money."

Hospitality was responsible for 15 percent of liquidations in the year to August, at a rate of 1.4 percent.

World.title: Former Kāinga Ora official among four charged over $4m in alleged bribes
World.content:
The Serious Fraud office has charged a former Kāinga Ora official and three others in relation to $4.2 million in alleged bribes.

The former Tāmaki Regeneration Company (TRC) official and two construction company owners are charged with corruption and bribery, in relation to government-funded contracts worth more than $26.3 million.

Two housing projects and a minor works project, awarded and delivered between March 2020 and March 2024, were used to allegedly funnel the bribes.

The SFO said some of the group's communications allegedly showed project invoices were adjusted to inflate the amount due to be paid. The adjusted invoices were then allegedly submitted to Kāinga Ora and TRC for processing.

The construction company owners allegedly bribed the former Kāinga Ora official with more than $2.6 million through 46 payments into five different bank accounts, and more than $507,000 in credits for the construction of a family home.

An additional $1 million in bribes was allegedly allocated to the former TRC official; however, the former Kāinga Ora official allegedly retained more than $900,000 in payments, with the TRC official allegedly receiving $171,250 in payments and gifts.

"This case involves contracts worth millions of dollars to provide new homes in Auckland neighbourhoods, for the benefit of our communities. The people overseeing these projects are expected to act with integrity," SFO Director Karen Chang said.

TRC was established by the government and Auckland Council to facilitate the regeneration of Tāmaki in Auckland. Kāinga Ora supported the government-owned entity with procurement for builders and developers, and ongoing project management and delivery support.

World.title: Morning Report Health Debate: Labour would keep coalition targets, National claims things 'heading in right direction'
World.content:
Audio player for " Morning Report Health Debate: Simeon Brown and Ayesha Verrall " removed for printing Visit page to play audio: https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiJ9._f0.YIZs2-J2FpwgcBcJJb29s1vXmFAWHLh_p1oUyv-l-RA/politics_election-2026/2049778%2Fmorning-report-health-debate-labour-would-keep-coalition-targets-national-claims-things-heading-in-right-direction

Morning Report Health Debate: Simeon Brown and Ayesha Verrall Morning Report Download MP3 21m

Labour has confirmed it will keep the coalition government's health targets if elected, while admitting some of its "three free GP visits" could be with a nurse practitioner rather than a GP.

Meanwhile, National has claimed the country's health system is "heading in the right direction", while pointing to the new Waikato Medical School - which would train another 120 doctors per year from 2028 - as its solution to pressures on GPs.

The comments came as Labour's Ayesha Verrall and National's Simeon Brown took part in Morning Report's health debate.

Verrall confirmed Labour's approach to the targets while discussing its plan for emergency departments, released on Tuesday.

Video player removed for printing https://players.brightcove.net/6093072280001/default_default/index.html?videoId=6407152289112

"We're going to keep the targets, but what we won't do is set the targets and then not resource the health system by not hiring any more nurses in order to deliver them," she said.

"That's negligent."

National's health spokesperson Simeon Brown derided Labour's healthcare proposals as little more than "a glossy document and a report and a review", while touting his own record.

"There is a lot more work to do. But you know, a 41 percent reduction in number of people waiting for an elective surgery for more than four months - that's a huge reduction.

"By no means is the health system fixed, but we are heading in the right direction."

Parties on what they'll actually do

During the debate, Verrall was put under pressure over how the already stretched GP workforce would cope with Labour's "three free GP visit" policy.

She said Labour would introduce "efficiency improvements" such as a triaging system to reduce acute demand.

Verrall also admitted the visit could be with a nurse practitioner rather than a GP.

Brown said Labour's policy was going to "clog up" the health system.

"I don't know why I need to have a free GP visit," he said.

He called on Labour to produce its modelling which supposedly showed how it would free up four-and-a-half million appointments. He said if that did not happen the health system would be overrun.

"What a scare tactic," Verrall shot back.

"Show us the modelling!" Brown said.

Asked for his solution to GP pressures, Brown pointed to the new Waikato Medical School which would train another 120 doctors per year from 2028.

RNZ / Cole Eastham-Farrelly

Parties discuss nurse numbers and cancer treatment

Asked about cancer treatment delays at Starship Children's Hospital, Brown said the situation was "incredibly distressing".

He accused Labour of politicising the issue, noting that 70 percent of the shifts were understaffed when Verrall was health minister.

"That's why Health New Zealand has recruited every single one of those vacancies," Brown said.

Verrall said those figures were not brought to her attention while she was health minister.

"We had a programme of hiring nurses under the pandemic. We took the gap in nursing incredibly seriously."

She accused the coalition of running a "deliberate policy of freezing nursing hiring".

Verrall said Labour did not have a target for growing the nurse workforce but would end the "hiring freeze".

Brown said the country "absolutely" needed more nurses, which was why the government was recruiting 2400 nursing vacancy roles "right now" across the healthcare system.

Morning Report presenter Ingrid Hipkiss put to Brown that full-time nurse numbers had increased by just 54 between March 2024 and March 2026.

"If you want to pick and choose timeframes - when Ayesha Verrall was the Minister of Health, the number of doctors in our health system dropped by 130. That's her record," Brown said.

Verrall responded: "Our government didn't have a deliberate policy of freezing the hiring of nurses - which it appears you do."

"We don't - do you have a policy of reducing the number of doctors? Was that your policy? No," Brown said.

Brown accuses Labour of having 'fiscal cliff'

As the debate shifted to funding for health promises, Brown accused Labour of having a "fiscal cliff".

"You haven't provided any additional funding in year four. You have a fiscal cliff for health funding in year four," Brown claimed.

Verrall rejected that, saying it was "a lie".

"Year on year, Labour will invest more in healthcare than National," Verrall said.

"Show me the money," Brown replied.

Parties weigh in on drug funding

Neither Brown nor Verrall were willing to commit to funding new weight loss drugs, like Ozempic, saying that was a question for Pharmac.

Brown said National had committed to an extra $604m over four years for Pharmac, to be redirected from foreign aid.

Verrall said that was "incredibly manipulative" because NZ First leader Winston Peters had already ruled out redirecting that funding.

"You know that will not survive coalition negotiations with Winston," Verrall said.

Debate ends on a positive note

Morning Report's health debate wrapped up with an uplifting moment, as Labour and National's health spokespeople hailed unsung heroes in the country's healthcare system.

Verrall named two care workers - Rebecca McCorkindale and Laura Patterson - who looked after her father before he passed away the summer before last.

"They provided expert, skilled, and compassionate care that was just such a relief to me and my mum. They deserve a pay rise, and they'll get one under Labour."

Brown gave a "shout out" to the head of Counties Manukau for Health New Zealand, Dr Vanessa Thornton.

He said Thornton was leading one of the busiest districts in the country, while also stepping in as an ED doctor.

A base jumper who got stuck on the side of an Auckland hotel by his parachute has been arrested and is set to appear in court.

Inspector Grae Anderson said around 10.42pm on Tuesday night emergency services responded to reports a person was stuck by a parachute to the side of a hotel on Albert Street.

"Fire and Emergency New Zealand were able to free the man, however the building suffered damage to the exterior and guests staying at the hotel had their evening disrupted due to the event.
