World.title: Explainer: Why Facebook is going to start charging many New Zealand small businesses
World.content:
Explainer - Are you running a small business off Facebook and Instagram? It may soon cost you a lot more.

A small business page will now have to pay Meta nearly $900 a month to post unlimited links from their pages.

Meta, the social media giant that owns Facebook, WhatsApp, Instagram and more, has begun offering subscription fees for businesses, cutting back their ability to offer free links to potential customers.

One Canterbury small business owner has said the new restrictions "honestly left me speechless".

What is Facebook going to start charging for?

Meta, Facebook's owner, has begun rolling out what they call "Meta One," a subscription service for business pages which Meta says "brings together more AI, advanced business tools, and content and audience insights designed to help grow your business."

However, it also means that some things Facebook business page operators could previously do for free will now cost them.

Meta began introducing the plan globally on 15 September, but it's a gradual rollout so hasn't affected all business pages yet.

"If you're seeing a limit on posts with links on your Page, here's how it works: you can include links in up to two organic posts or comments per month," the tech company says on its help pages.

Under the free plan or the bare-bones "Essential" MetaOne plan (US$14.99/NZ$26 per month) you can now only publish two links a month in "organic" (non-paid) posts or comments on your Facebook or Instagram page.

The broader Meta One monthly plans range in price from US$49.99 (NZ$88) to post eight links, US$149.99 (NZ$265) to post 20 links per month all the way up to US$499.99 (NZ$883) to be able to post unlimited links under the "Max" plan.

Dropping a link down into the comments to a post - a "hack" used by some to get around algorithmic suppression - won't avoid these new restrictions.

Technology correspondent Bill Bennett said that some small New Zealand companies may actually go out of business because of the charges.

"It's going to really hurt some of the small local companies that use Facebook (or other Meta products)," he said.

"It was, in effect, free, or close to free before. For many micro businesses that was the reason why they used it in the first place."

Bennett called the nearly $900 monthly charge for unlimited links "excessive."

"The same money could pay for a substantial leaflet drop for example. Even if you're not a web designer, you can get a professional web page package for a year's worth of $900 payments. If you can build your own it only costs a few hundred to host."

Audio player for " The Panel with Kathryn Graham and Mark Knoff-Thomas " removed for printing Visit page to play audio: https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiJ9._f0.YIZs2-J2FpwgcBcJJb29s1vXmFAWHLh_p1oUyv-l-RA/business/2048804%2Fexplainer-why-facebook-is-going-to-start-charging-many-new-zealand-small-businesses

The Panel with Kathryn Graham and Mark Knoff-Thomas The Panel Download MP3 47m

Why is this a big deal for small Kiwi businesses?

Ben Dobbs of Canterbury clothing store Blank Space said small businesses like his have been caught off guard, and has said he was "speechless" when he found out about the subscription plans.

"I didn't even know anything about it until I went to make a post one night," he told RNZ's The Panel, saying that he was presented with a pop-up that said if he wanted to put unlimited links on his page he would now be charged more than $850 a month.

"I was just like what is this, why have I not heard about this?"

The changes by Meta will hit some small New Zealand companies hard, Bennett said.

"Americans think a small business is less than 500 employees. For a company like that the cost is nothing.

"For a New Zealand hairdresser, food truck or coffee cart, it is going to seriously dig into an owner-operator's take-home pay."

Meta isn't charging all businesses to use Facebook, but the Meta One subscription plans could result in added costs depending on how a page is used.

If most of a business's posts are photos, videos and customer engagement, or they only post once or twice a month, then the free versions won't be terribly different. Links to other Meta platforms like Instagram or Threads also won't be constrained or count toward costs.

But if you use a lot of links to drive people to your external website and products, it's going to cost more.

Dobbs said he won't be putting direct links on social media posts from now on.

"Paying hundreds of dollars every month just to drop a link simply isn't a smart move for us right now," he wrote in a post on his business page.

The pop-up that business pages on Facebook are starting to see promoting the subscription service Meta One. Supplied

Are there any alternatives to Meta's products for businesses?

Businesses should consider having their own website rather than just relying on Facebook if possible.

Mark Knoff-Thomas, CEO of Auckland's Newmarket Business Association, told The Panel that the new Facebook changes show it's important for businesses to try and keep control of their company as much as they can.

"I think as a business I think owning your assets, owning your own IP, owning your customer database and your email assets and controlling those yourself is probably the greatest thing you can do."

Knoff-Thomas said the tech companies will always be aggressive with their power.

"These big tech companies... they have a voracious appetite for charging fees. They do change the rules, regularly, they really, really do.

"At the end of the day Facebook is the landlord of this site of what they're doing, right, and they're just going to charge whatever they can get away with. ... that's the nature of the business model."

Bennett noted that Meta's sites initially began as free for most users.

"Facebook and Instagram were popular in the first place because they cost nothing or next to nothing. Also, you could push simple messages out between haircuts or flipping burgers.

"If a business has built a community around its Meta presence, it may have to bite the bullet and pay up. Many will not be able to or will face hardship as a result."

On his own Facebook page, Dobbs expressed concern about the impact on businesses like his.

World.title: Israel joins Pacific Islands Forum as partner
World.content:
Israel has joined the Pacific Islands Forum, the region's principal political organisation, as a partner.

The country, which has a deep-rooted affection from Pacific communities, confirmed the decision in a press release on Tuesday (Wednesday NZDT).

Israel has stepped up its diplomatic focus on the Pacific over the last few years, winning the dedication of numerous Pacific Islands countries in the process.

As a PIF partner, Israel will participate in the Forum's Sectoral Partnership Stream, engaging actively with the region on development priorities. The PIF has more than two dozen external dialogue partners, including the United States, China, the United Kingdom, France and the European Union.

The Israeli Foreign Ministry said that this will be along the lines of water management, desalination, agriculture and climate change adaptation.

"The Secretary General of the Pacific Islands Forum, Baron Divavesi Waqa, informed Foreign Minister Gideon Sa'ar that Israel has been accepted as a Forum Partner. The decision was made at a meeting of the leaders of the Forum's member states, held in Palau," the ministry said.

"The announcement follows Foreign Minister Gideon Sa'ar's visit to Fiji in June of this year, during which he met with the Forum's Secretary General and formally presented Israel's request to join."

PIG secretary-general Baron Waqa welcomed Israel’s Ambassador to Fiji and Pacific Island Countries Maya Yaron in Suva this week. Pacific Islands Forum

The PIF will also draw up a new agreement with Israel that identifies shared priorities and a means to measure their progress.

Papua New Guinea, Fiji and Naoero have all opened embassies in Jerusalem as a show of solidarity. Samoa has also announced it plans to do the same.

The PIF Secretariat has yet to issue an official statement regarding Israel's partner status announcement.

RNZ Pacific has contacted New Zealand Foreign Minister Winston Peters for comment.

World.title: Gardner smashes 84 as Australia retains Rose Bowl over NZ
World.content:
Australia has retained the Rose Bowl with a comfortable 40-run victory in the Twenty20 International against New Zealand at North Sydney Oval.

Led by a blazing 84 from vice-captain Ash Gardner, Australia scored a competitive 6-167 and held New Zealand to 8-127 on Tuesday night, claiming a 2-0 lead in the three-match series, with the remaining game on Thursday.

It was Australia's 12th T20 victory in a row, including an unbeaten run during the World Cup in the UK during June and July, prompting Gardner to credit surprise skipper Sophie Molineux with enhancing a winning culture.

Aussies beat New Zealand in first women's T20 Australia survives a scare to down New Zealand by two wickets in the first T20 at North Sydney Oval.

"It's led by Soph, who has brought this different mantra to the group, and the fun aspect as well," Gardner said.

"When you're enjoying yourself, and you're having fun, it creates an environment of growth and wanting to learn and challenge yourself."

Australia has held the Rose Bowl for more than 26 years, and the trophy is on the line again in March for a three-match one-day series. This will be the first time it has been contested twice in the same season.

Gardner dominated an otherwise stuttering Australian batting performance, hitting 10 fours and four sixes in 45 balls on the compact North Sydney Oval.

Beth Mooney looked good for the second time in the series without pressing on, well caught by a diving Maddy Green at long on for 39 from 28 deliveries, lofting a slower ball from Jess Kerr.

Australia then smothered New Zealand. White Ferns captain Melie Kerr top scored with 32 from 38 balls, while Australia's most successful bowler was leg-spinner Georgia Wareham, who claimed 3-18 from her four overs.

New Zealand named an unchanged team after giving Australia a fright in the opening game, with the home side scrambling to victory by two wickets in a tense finish.

There was no such tension this time, with New Zealand never mounting a serious challenge.

AAP

World.title: Bavuma's batting masterclass takes control from Australia
World.content:
A few days before this Test series began, a digitally manipulated image was doing the rounds on social media.

Modelling South Africa's new Test playing kit, a pensive expression on his face, Proteas skipper Temba Bavuma was flanked by teammates Ryan Rickelton and Marco Jansen.

The visual punchline, in this case, was that Bavuma had been shrunk even smaller than his already-diminutive self, dwarfed by his teammates, even though he was standing on a superimposed shoe-shine box. My sides!

Australia on the ropes in second Test Temba Bavuma's sensational century turns the second Test on its head and leaves Australia on the ropes after day three.

Never mind that 5'4" Bavuma's batting inspiration, Sachin Tendulkar, stands only an inch taller, nor that the previous owner of India's "Little Master" moniker, Sunil Gavaskar, is the same height as Bavuma. Nor, indeed, that a certain lad from Bowral who did kind of OK in the 1930s and 40s was only 5'7". None faced quite the same level of condescension or fixation on their physical stature as Bavuma.

In reality, Bavuma is, by a few key measures, as big as anyone in the story of South African cricket in the post-apartheid decades. On the world stage he captained his country to victory in the 2025 World Test Championship decider, banishing years of big-tournament heartbreak.

Australians, apt to wipe such unexpected defeats in crunch games from the collective memory, are thus obliged to bracket Bavuma with a select group of figurehead skippers of recent decades — Clive Lloyd, Sourav Ganguly, Michael Vaughan, Virat Kohli — who've engineered famous and important victories against great Australian Test sides in their pomp.

Now Australia reckons with his batting. On day three of the second Test at Gqeberha, Bavuma played an innings that, for context and quality, ranks among the highest calibre; a towering and important century that any of the all-timers above would envy.

Beginning the day on 41, with his side wobbling away at 5-97, Bavuma finished it with a stunning set of numbers next to his name: 179 runs from 334 deliveries in a total of 9-425 declared.

Temba Bavuma's (right) presence is towering over the second Test match. (AP: Themba Hadebe)

Due to the rain and delays of the opening stages of this game, Bavuma's epic stretched across three days, clocked in at a shade under 10 hours and required nothing less than the total psychological and physical mastery of the most complete pace attack in world cricket. Australians scoff at the mere concept of moral victories, but here Bavuma and South Africa claimed a resounding one.

It was the highest score of Bavuma's career, his fourth century (out of five all up) since becoming captain and moving up the order, and it means that a game in which Australia fancied skittling the Proteas on a green pitch is very unlikely to be won by the tourists — and possibly worse.

The "possibly worse" part got its preview sequence in the final moments of the day, when South Africa's returning paceman Kagiso Rabada marauded his way through Nic Maddinson to leave Australia one wicket down at stumps. Had bad light not limited Bavuma to the use of spinners in the final three overs of the day, the carnage could have been worse.

Quick hits: Jansen hit where it hurts as Bavuma grinds Aussies into the dirt Here are the quick hits from day three of the second Test between Australia and South Africa.

It has been said that the Australians respect but don't particularly warm to Bavuma. By this theory, he is aloof, undemonstrative and unlikely to engage in banter, verbal sparring or fun. In that way, he is more like a bowler who always had Australia's measure, Curtly Ambrose. "Curtly talks to no-one," Ambrose once said. It worked out just fine for him, too.

Bavuma's knock was a masterpiece of the kind of tempo batting that makes Test cricket tragics swoon. His watchful first 50, comprised almost entirely of judicious nudges, nurdles and leaves, took 140 deliveries.

His second, which grew to encompass sumptuous on drives, square drives and a cracking pull shot off Pat Cummins to reach his century, took only 86 balls. His third, a by-product of an acceleration phase when he and Simon Harmer removed any thoughts of an Australian victory, came from just 73 balls.

It was hard to believe this was the same player who'd scratched around for a combined total of four runs in 45 tortured deliveries last week in Durban. But like Matt Renshaw in that game, it was not just Bavuma's own runs that turned this contest on its head but the partnerships he forged with his side's highly capable tailenders.

Loading Instagram content

There was a thrilling stand of 132 from 186 with Marco Jansen, whose 85 came at almost a run a ball and, to be fair, presented a truly arresting example of cricket's capacity to attract all shapes and sizes. Paired with the 6'8" beanpole, Bavuma brought to mind the famous photo of NBA basketballers Muggsy Bogues and Manute Bol.

Even more profitable — game-defining, most likely — was Bavuma's union with Harmer, the spinner whose surprising selection reprieve suddenly seemed completely sensible as he hammered his way through a sparkling knock of 82 from 157 deliveries. Their partnership of 183 traversed 46 overs and was South Africa's highest eighth-wicket stand ever — not the sort of record with which this Australian squad likes to be associated.

In the final analysis, 315 runs came after the fall of South Africa's sixth wicket. It was a total wipe-out for the Aussies.

What did Cummins get wrong? There were some indefensibly defensive field placements, in truth, especially in the crucial phase when Jansen went berserk and Bavuma fed him the strike with easy singles to men stationed in the deep.

But as Richie Benaud once said, the best attribute a captain can have is luck, and there wasn't much on offer here for Cummins. Josh Hazlewood, missing with illness on day two, was thus obliged not to bowl for the first two hours of the day. The green pitch, which had promised carnage early in the game, turned docile and offered minimal lateral movement even for Scott Boland. And after the second new ball brought the wicket of Jansen — Boland's fifth — very little else transpired, so the field spread again.

Of the Australian bowlers, Boland was clearly the pick with 5-81 from 29 overs, and the overall picture of gloom rather rubbished the claim that his otherworldly Test statistics could be attributed to being slotted into an attack that was always firing from the other end (and anyway, by that logic, Andy Bichel, as the last backup quick to receive acclaim like that heaped on Boland, would have easily maintained a bowling average far lower than 32).

In the Boland years, as in the Bichel ones, sometimes even great sides have to admit it has not been their day. That was Australia today; at the mercy of the biggest small man in cricket, who doesn't have to open his mouth to say something profound.

World.title: Quick hits: Jansen hit where it hurts as Bavuma grinds Aussies into the dirt
World.content:
Marco Jansen's swashbuckling innings ends with a bang then a whimper and Temba Bavuma grinds Australia into the dirt with one of the great captain's knocks.

Here are the quick hits from day three of the second Test between Australia and South Africa.

1. Bavuma's all-time captain's knock

Watching Temba Bavuma bat on day three, it was hard to believe the South Africa captain was in the process of scoring just his fifth Test-match century.

He was so organised, so composed and just-about chanceless in making his way to a 223-ball hundred.

His face was a picture of steely determination after reaching his milestone, his mouth twisted into a defiant grimace as he held bat and helmet aloft, well aware he was batting his side back into the game.

Temba Bavuma brought up his fifth Test century on day three in Gqeberha. (Getty Images: Richard Huggard)

And he continued on his way after passing three figures, continually blunting the tiring Australian attack, finding runs all over the outfield and driving through mid-on like only the truest of batting talents are able.

It was a captain's knock if ever there was one and eventually ended with a new high-score of 179.

Having initially struggled to find his feet at Test level, Bavuma has averaged well over 50 in the past five years and can now count himself as one of the format's best batters.

2. Jansen gets hit and then gets out

Jansen was in serious pain after being hit where it hurts. (Fox Cricket)

It was a blow that sent winces across the cricketing world.

Scott Boland produced a beauty with the very first delivery of the 80th over, using the new ball to jag one back towards Marco Jansen.

The towering all-rounder was cut in half and completely helpless to the fresh pill thudding into precisely the place he would have hoped to protect the most.

Poor Jansen was in all sorts after being hit where it hurts. (Fox Cricket)

Doubled over and then down an all fours, Jansen pounded the turf in agony as his teammates offered a mixture of sympathy and myrrh from the stands.

It was a long, long delay as he picked himself up, regained his composure and received some medical attention.

He was eventually right to continue, but just four balls later, his counterpunch came to an end with a meek chip to Travis Head at mid-wicket.

Jansen's swashbuckling 100-ball 85 was key to South Africa's remarkable revival on day three, but the big man's special knock was over with a combination of bang and whimper.

3. Starc reaches 450 Test wickets

The milestones just keep coming for Mitchell Starc.

With the St. George's pitch offering little during the first half hour of play on day three, Australia's fearsome spearhead managed to conjure something special.

Starc's milestone was a bright spot in an otherwise dark day for the Aussies. (Getty Images: Richard Huggard/Gallo Images)

His venomous bouncer had Wiaan Mulder tied in knots on the backfoot, the ball collecting a mixture of helmet, shoulder and willow on the way through to Matt Renshaw in the cordon.

The on-field decision was not out, but a well-taken review revealed the murmur that sent Mulder trudging from the middle.

The wicket was Starc's 450th in Test cricket, making him just the fourth Australian to reach that milestone, after Shane Warne, Glenn McGrath and Nathan Lyon.

Unfortunately for the Aussies, Starc's early breakthrough proved a lone bright spot in an otherwise pitch-black day in Gqeberha.

4. South Africa better Australia's Durban recovery

It was a truly remarkable day of recovery from the South Africans.

Having started the morning on 5-97, Mulder's early dismissal further reduced the hosts to 6-110, a position even more dire than where Australia found itself on day one in Durban.

Australia on the ropes in second Test Temba Bavuma's sensational century turns the second Test on its head and leaves Australia on the ropes after day three.

The Aussies finished the opening day of the series teetering on 6-124, but went on to score 390, with Matt Renshaw starring in a collection of lower-order partnerships to add a further 266 runs.

South Africa's recovery in Gqeberha was eerily similar but even more dramatic, with Bavuma and his more-than-capable lower-order teammates adding a further 315 runs from that initial position of peril early on day three, with Bavuma and Jansen contributing 132 runs for the seventh wicket and Bavuma and Simon Harmer a South African record of 183 for the eighth.

That unlikely Australian rescue-job laid the foundation for a dominant victory in Kingsmead, and the South Africans will be hoping for something similar at St. George's.

But given the amount of time already lost in this game and how placid the wicket still looks to be, the Proteas may well require something very special to eke out a result on days four and five.

5. A final sting in the tail for Australia

With South Africa's innings declared on 9-425 after Bavuma's late dismissal, Australia's opening batters were faced with an excruciatingly short period in quickly fading light after an arduous, demoralising day in the field.

And Nic Maddinson's lazy waft outside off certainly looked like the shot of a man who had spent seven hours being ground into the dirt.

The veteran was nicked off for a duck by returning South African spearhead Kagiso Rabada with the fourth ball of the innings.

Nightwatchman Scott Boland, mercifully, only had to survive the final two balls of that opening over before the umpires determined the light was only good enough for spin.

The Australians will begin day four at 1-3 and, somehow, 422 runs behind.

World.title: Bavuma's brilliant knock flips the script and puts Australia on the ropes
World.content:
South Africa has surged into ascendancy in the second Test against Australia after captain Temba Bavuma led a spectacular batting rearguard on day three.

Beginning the day at 5-97 and on the ropes, Bavuma's 179 helped guide South Africa to 9-425 declared.

Bavuma was aided by the lower order runs of Simon Harmer (82) and Marco Jansen (85) while the Australian bowlers toiled through a difficult a fruitless day.

Bavuma's fifth Test century is the best of the skipper's career, full of fight and resilience and plenty of class.

Marco Jansen hit back with some stunning strokes on the third morning. (Getty Images: Richard Huggard)

It was the arrival of Jansen at the crease that kickstarted South Africa. Coming in at 6-110, Jansen immediately took the attack back to Australia and from there the hosts never looked back.

Jansen was on track for a maiden Test ton, but was caught at midwicket off the bowling of Scott Boland in his first over with the second new ball.

It was Boland's (5-81) fifth wicket of the innings, and it came only a few deliveries after Jansen had been struck in the box and brought to his knees.

Harmer too stared down the prospect of a first Test ton, but his stellar knock was ended by Marnus Labuschagne, clean bowled in the pursuit of quick late runs.

Bavuma was caught behind from the bowling of Mitchell Starc with half an hour left in the day, and his subsequent declaration set the Australians up for a difficult stint with the bat.

Australia's day only got worse when Nic Maddinson fell in the first over of that mini-session, edging Kagiso Rabada to the slips for another duck.

Bad light meant South Africa had to turn to spin for the final overs of the day, and Travis Head and nightwatchman Boland reached the close at 1-3.

Look back at how the action unfolded in our live blog.

World.title: Tedesco parachutes in as Kangaroos captain in first Test since 2023
World.content:
James Tedesco will be elevated straight to the captaincy when he runs out for his first game for the Kangaroos in three years.

Tedesco has been named at fullback for Australia's men's Rugby League World Cup clash with Fiji in Brisbane on Sunday.

It marks the 33-year-old's first cap in green and gold since the 2023 Pacific Championship final, when he led the Kangaroos to a shock 30-0 loss to New Zealand.

Since his last Test appearance, Tedesco has won back his NSW jersey, claimed last year's Dally M Medal and was the Clive Churchill medallist as Roosters captain earlier this month.

On Sunday night at Lang Park, Tedesco will return to the team after coach Kevin Walters made the decision to rotate through his squad to try to find his best line-up.

Rugby League World Cup quick hits From Kalyn Ponga's magnificent Test debut to a mighty Tongan victory years in the making here are the quick hits from week one of the Rugby League World Cup.

Walters named four debutants in the 23-strong squad, with halfback Sam Walker, centre Bradman Best, hooker Blayke Brailey and back rower David Fifita all set to start.

Walker's debut will double as a play-off with halves partner Tom Dearden as both bye to replace the injured Mitchell Moses in the seven jersey for the rest of the campaign.

The bench and extended squad are filled out by starters from the Kangaroos' 24-22 win over the Kiwis in their tournament opener, including regular captain Isaah Yeo and fullback Reece Walsh, who staked his claim in a barnstorming return from injury with a long-range solo try and a try-saver on opposite number Kalyn Ponga.

If Tedesco aims up, it could leave Walters with a major selection call to make at the pointy end of the tournament.

"Those big moments; he hadn't played in six, seven weeks but he turned up in big moments and nailed them," Tedesco, the oldest member of the squad at 33, said of Walsh.

"He was great all week, asking for advice, but it's not a competition. I've got an opportunity and all I can do is make the most of it and do my role.

"Walshy does things on the field so it's about knowing my game and being an experienced leader.

"Walshy, he was soaking up anything I had to say last week and I enjoy that role."

The Jillaroos have also named two debutants for their Women's Rugby League World Cup clash with England on Saturday night.

Sydney Roosters premiership winner Sariah Paki will become a dual international, while Maroons forward Makenzie Weale has been named to make her debut from the bench in Perth.

Their first caps come after five-eighth Jocelyn Kelleher entered the international arena with a bang in round one, claiming player of the match honours against Samoa.

World.title: Aussie Opal's block fires Dream to WNBA finals win
World.content:
Australian rookie Izzy Borlase has helped the Atlanta Dream to their historic first WNBA finals victory, shining in a series-levelling 79–65 triumph over Golden State.

Dream superstar Angel Reese was a dominant figure in game two at San Francisco's Chase Center on Monday (Tuesday AEDT), posting a monster double-double with 30 points and 16 rebounds.

The Dream's win was their first in a title-deciding best-of-seven series, after being swept in their three previous appearances and losing game one against the Valkyries this year.

Coach Karl Smesko's team will enjoy home-court advantage in the next two games as they chase their first WNBA championship.

Borlase could play a key role after being entrusted with almost 17 minutes on court in game two, finishing with two points, one assist, one steal and one block.

The 22-year-old missed all four field-goal attempts in the first half, but sank a pair of free throws and made a huge play to help Atlanta to a 39–37 lead at the main break.

Borlase's block on Veronica Burton late in the second period led to an Allisha Gray (18 points) triple and forced the Valkyries to call a time-out.

It drew huge praise from Reese, who made a beeline for her teammate and celebrated with a chest bump and double-fist to the chest.

Atlanta seized control in a dominant third quarter and took a 60–46 lead after Jordin Canada (13 points) banked a long-range three on the buzzer.

Overrun after leading late in game one, the Dream held firm this time to record their breakthrough finals victory.

Reese became the third player in WNBA history to have at least 30 points and 15 rebounds in a finals game.

Another Australian Opals star, Miela Sowah, sat on the bench for the Valkyries and will remain there throughout the finals due to her restricted status as a development player.

World.title: Diamonds boosted by imminent return of vice-captain
World.content:
Diamonds vice-captain Kate Moloney is on track to return from injury and give Australia a much-needed boost for the Constellation Cup.

Moloney was forced to watch the netball world's number-one side suffer a shock 56–50 loss to the Silver Ferns from the sidelines after a finger laceration in the lead-up to the Auckland series opener.

The Diamonds were already without defender Jo Weston (managed), and the experienced duo were sorely missed against the Commonwealth Games champions.

Diamonds centurions forced to the bench in Constellation Cup loss It was defender Courtney Bruce's 100th milestone game to start the Constellation Cup but the brand new centurion and her captain Liz Watson were both sent to the bench in Australia's 56-50 loss to New Zealand in Auckland.

New Zealand stormed to a 15-goal lead in the first of four matches, forcing Diamonds coach Stacey Marinkovich to bench captain and midcourter Liz Watson alongside goalkeeper Courtney Bruce in her 100th game.

Jamie-Lee Price took over centre duties against New Zealand's Adelaide Lightning star Kate Heffernan, while Jessie Grenvold was tasked with containing Silver Ferns goalscoring superstar Grace Nweke on debut.

Australia cut the deficit to just six goals in the fourth quarter, but the damage had been done.

Georgie Horjus was the only Diamond who remained on the court for four quarters, finishing with a game-high 19 gains and 38 feeds as wing attack.

With the Diamonds set to name their squad this evening, Marinkovich said Melbourne Vixens captain Moloney's return was imminent.

"We'll definitely see her back in the series," Marinkovich said.

"It was a bit of a nasty laceration to her finger, so we had to wait till it pretty much stuck back together.

"It's just one of those innocuous things that happen at training, but she's been able to do all the running and the movement, and yeah, look forward to having her back."

But the midcourt will not be the only area of focus for tomorrow night's game in Christchurch.

Looking to end their five-year drought on Kiwi soil, the Diamonds will need to find a way past the towering defensive duo of Kelly Jackson and Karin Burger.

With goalkeeper Jackson standing at 192cm and goal defence Burger at 184cm, Australia's attacking roster of Kiera Austin, Cara Koenen, Sophie Dwyer and Sophie Garbin struggled to fire.

Marinkovich is urging her Diamonds to start with "immediacy" on the court.

"We were slightly off our pace [in game one], and our numbers would show that we weren't as aggressive as what we needed to be on the ball," she said.

ABC Sport will have live blog coverage of Game II between the Diamonds and Silver Ferns on Wednesday, October 21.

AAP

World.title: Jockeys cleared over Ohope Wins's fatal Caulfield Cup fall
World.content:
A Racing Victoria investigation into the fall at the Caulfield Cup that resulted in the euthanasia of Ohope Wins has finished, clearing all jockeys involved of any wrongdoing.

Ohope Wins, ridden by Jye McNeil, and Half Yours, ridden by Mark Zahra, both went down in the final straight at the 150th running of the famous 2,400-metre race.

Zahra and Half Yours fell first after getting tangled in the pack chasing eventual winner Kingswood, with Ohope Wins going over the top of the fallen gelding.

Loading...

Last year's Melbourne Cup winner Half Yours suffered superficial cuts and scrapes, but Ohope Wins was assessed on track as having a "serious racing injury" and was put down by on-course veterinarians.

Both jockeys were thrown from their mounts and taken to hospital, delaying the conclusion of the inquiry into the incident, which once again prompted calls for the racing industry to be made more accountable for racehorse deaths.

After hearing evidence from McNeil, Zahra and three other jockeys in the race, Racing Victoria stewards said they "could not attribute the incident to the careless actions of any one particular rider".

The hearing at Racing Victoria headquarters found contact between Kings Valley and Green Spaces with about 300m to go resulted in the latter becoming unbalanced.

Half Yours ran the rest of the course without a rider. (Getty Images: Robert Cianflone)

Green Spaces, ridden by Rachel King, then turned inward and made more contact with apprentice rider Jabez Johnstone's Kings Valley, who also turned inward, resulting in Half Yours being squeezed for room between Kings Valley and Zahrann.

"A short distance later, Half Yours subsequently fell," the stewards' report read.

"Ohope Wins that was trailing was subsequently brought down when unable to avoid the fallen Half Yours."

The incident has been referred to Racing Victoria's Veterinary Services Department, as is standard practice.

Trainer Tony McEvoy said Half Yours was recovering well from injuries and would be rested, while Zahra was meeting with doctors today about a timeline for his return to riding.

McNeil was cleared of any injury and is expected to ride at the Geelong Cup tomorrow.

Tech.title: Tesla and SpaceX are discussing a possible merger, Musk says
Tech.content:

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

Tesla and SpaceX have formed special committees to discuss a possible merger, Elon Musk said during the latter’s third quarter earnings call Tuesday.

Musk, who serves as CEO of both companies, said the special committees have not reached agreement on the terms of any transaction — and that there’s no guarantee that they will. That said, he called the possibility of a Tesla-SpaceX merger a “good idea.”

“I think it would be a good idea,” Musk said. “But it’s really up the special committees of both companies.”

Earlier this month, Barclays published a client note suggesting a potential Tesla-SpaceX combination could be announced ahead of Tesla’s annual shareholder meeting scheduled for December 3, 2026.

Tech.title: SpaceX will try catching Starship and its booster for first time, Musk says
Tech.content:
is transportation editor with 10+ years of experience who covers EVs, public transportation, and aviation. His work has appeared in The New York Daily News and City & State.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

SpaceX CEO Elon Musk said the company would attempt to catch Starship and its booster next month, with the goal of recovering the entire orbital launch system for the first time. If successful, Musk said, the attempt would mark the first time in history an orbital launch vehicle has been fully recovered.

“This is a profound technology milestone in the history of civilization consciousness,” he said during the company’s third quarter earnings report Tuesday.

But he also allowed for the possibility of a failure. “Success is not guaranteed on these first flights, but I’d say it’s more likely than not that this succeeds next flight,” Musk said. “And if not, we have a steady stream of Starship flight attempts through the end of this year and then accelerating next year.”

“Success is not guaranteed on these first flights, but I’d say it’s more likely than not that this succeeds next flight.” — Elon Musk

Starship is a two-stage system, composed of the Super Heavy booster (first stage) and the Starship spacecraft (second stage). It stands approximately 120 meters (around 400 feet) tall with a 9-meter diameter, and is powered by SpaceX’s Raptor engines burning liquid methane and liquid oxygen. Starship, which was first introduced in 2018, was designed to return to the launch site, where launch towers with mechanical “chopstick” arms catch the vehicle mid-air.

Last month’s Starship launch represented two firsts for its next gen rocket: send the spacecraft into Earth orbit, and insert a few dozen of SpaceX’s larger and more capable V3 satellites into the Starlink constellation for the first time. Still, the launch wasn’t without its snafus: one Raptor engine shut down prematurely during ascent, prompting mission control to adapt and complete the climb on remaining. Because of the issue, SpaceX cut the planned 10-hour, 6-orbit mission short after about 3 hours and 2 Earth orbits.

The Super Heavy booster splashed down in the Gulf of Mexico, while the Starship upper stage executed a de-orbit burn and ended with a fiery vertical splashdown in the Pacific Ocean north of Hawaii. Neither piece was recovered.

Developing…

Tech.title: Netflix is telling investors not to worry, even though you’re watching less and less
Tech.content:
is a news writer who covers the streaming wars, consumer tech, crypto, social media, and much more. Previously, she was a writer and editor at MUO.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

Netflix is making monetization a top priority amid reports of falling viewing time. As part of its third-quarter earnings report on Tuesday, Netflix lists improvements to monetization as one of its main focuses going forward, alongside efforts to boost entertainment value and leverage new technology.

The streaming giant doesn’t say exactly how it plans to improve its monetization, but the company notes that these goals will help Netflix “create member value that lets us occasionally raise prices, and increase advertiser demand.” Netflix also highlighted plans to push further into original titles, live events, and third-party programming as it faces an “intense competition and an explosion of content competing for consumer attention.”

An analysis from financial firm Jefferies estimated that Netflix’s monthly viewing time per member dropped to 49 hours in the first half of this year, down from 66 hours in the first half of 2023, according to a report from Reuters. At the same time, Netflix made up 7.8 percent of US viewing time in the US in July, a one-percentage-point dip from the same time last year, The New York Times reports.

During an earnings call, Netflix co-CEO Ted Sarandos pointed to success abroad when answering a question about the company’s content strategy. “We see titles across Latin America, EMEA (Europe, the Middle East and Africa), APAC (Asia-Pacific), driving engagement, subscriber growth, revenue, and profit,” Sarandos said. “Now, the US is also working. It’s just not growing as fast as it could or as fast as we’d like.”

Related Netflix is pivoting away from prestige

In its letter to investors, Netflix mentions its upcoming lineup of NFL games, its Grand Theft Auto VI preview, and its partnership with French TV station TF1 as evidence of opening its platform to a wider breadth of content. The company reported earning $12.9 billion over the past few months, marking a 12 percent year-over-year increase. It also plans to bring its ad-supported tier — which raked in $1.5 billion last year — to 15 new countries in 2027.

In the coming months, Netflix may be facing tougher competition from HBO Max and Paramount Plus following the Skydance megamerger, as co-CEO David Ellison has said that he plans to combine the two apps into a single service. The streamer struck deals with several creators as it competes with YouTube, which has reportedly offered channels “millions of dollars” not to post their videos on Netflix.

Netflix has also weighed making even bigger changes to its app, including integrating other third-party streamers, such as Peacock and Fox One, as well as adding always-on channels, according to reports from The New York Times and The Wall Street Journal.

Update, October 20th: Added a quote from Sarandos.

Tech.title: Snap is paying Robert Downey Jr. to do the Iron Man thing
Tech.content:
is a senior reporter covering technology, gaming, and more. He joined The Verge in 2019 after nearly two years at Techmeme.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

Snap has a new brand ambassador for its Specs AR glasses: Iron Man actor Robert Downey Jr. The company has brought on Downey as Specs’ “Chief Customer Experience Officer” and has published several videos featuring Downey showcasing the capabilities of the new glasses, including as a tool to get help with a putt, practice art, and watch a private video of an MMA match in bed. In one video, he also dumps the contents of a box labeled “AI glasses” into a trash bin — a shot at Meta’s popular smart glasses.

As part of the partnership, Downey will “work alongside the SPECS team to explore how augmented reality can improve the way people live and work, from everyday experiences in entertainment and education to specialized uses across medicine, engineering, and manufacturing,” according to a blog post.

“Trying is believing,” Downey says in a statement. “Having tested practically every wearable tech that’s come to market in the last 20 years, and been largely unimpressed, I was absolutely sold on SPECS within 40 seconds.” Snap has other celebrities on board to help promote Specs, too, including musician Imogen Heap and NBA star Jimmy Butler.

The Snap Specs are set to launch sometime this fall, and they’ll cost $2,195. They’re available for pre-order now. If you want to know what it’s like to actually use Specs, go read my report from my time wearing them at Snap’s HQ last month.

Tech.title: SpaceX says big AI growth fueled revenue jump
Tech.content:
is a senior reporter covering technology, gaming, and more. He joined The Verge in 2019 after nearly two years at Techmeme.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

SpaceX announced revenues of $14.6 billion in its Q3 earnings on Tuesday, which it says was a growth of 161 percent year-over-year “fueled by our Super Intelligence (SI) segment and accelerated growth in Connectivity.” While its Space division posted a $7 million loss in income from operations, its Connectivity group posted income from operations $2.4 billion and its SI group posted $431 million.

The company’s so-called “SI” business saw revenues of $7.6 billion, which were up 830 percent year-over-year, “primarily driven” by “the activation of new cloud services agreements, the acquisition of Cursor, and increased Grok adoption across enterprise customers and consumers.” For its Connectivity business, SpaceX reported revenues of $5.2 billion and 13.6 million Starlink consumer subscribers. Space business revenues were $1.8 billion, up six percent year-over-year.

SpaceX is livestreaming a video of its earnings call on X.

During the Q2 earnings call, president Gwynne Shotwell described plans to build out a terrestrial mobile network to compete with T-Mobile, AT&T and Verizon. In SpaceX’s Q2 earnings, the company also noted that its “connectivity” business, which encompasses Starlink, didn’t have a loss from operations, while its AI and space businesses did.

Tesla, where Musk is also CEO, reports earnings on Wednesday.

Tech.title: Oura adds two new cardiovascular health tracking features to its smart rings
Tech.content:
is a senior reporter who’s been covering and reviewing the latest gadgets and tech since 2006, but has loved all things electronic since he was a kid.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

Instead of measuring how fast or far a user went during a run or bike ride, or metrics like calories burned, Cardio Effort measures how hard their cardiovascular system was working during exercise and how long that effort was sustained. Cardio Effort is calculated for individual workouts taking into account both intensity and duration but provides a plain language evaluation that compares a user’s cumulative weekly effort against a personalized baseline.

One one end of the scale is a Light rating that’s described as being a “substantially lower cardiovascular strain than your usual baseline.” The rating scale progresses through Fair, Maintaining, Building, and Reaching at the other end which means your weekly Cardio Effort had a “markedly higher exposure relative to your baseline, signaling that it may be time to prioritize recovery.” So instead of always pushing a user to increase their efforts, the feature does make recommendations for rest when it may be more beneficial.

Oura Rings already support VO2 Max readings that are used to track aerobic capacity, but the previous Cardio Capacity feature was somewhat cumbersome because estimating a user’s maximum oxygen uptake required a six-minute walking test for calibration. The new version, automatic VO2 Max, currently available as a beta feature through Oura Labs, automatically activates after users complete five “qualifying GPS-enabled activities” that include walks, runs, and hikes.

Once activated VO2 Max readings will be available in the Oura app’s My Health Heart Hub section with a user’s current estimate, their capacity rated as low, fair, high, or peak, how their aerobic capacity has changed over time, and personalized insights for when VO2 Max “meaningfully shifts or stays consistent.”

Tech.title: TikTok has started censoring searches for popular peptides
Tech.content:
is a senior editor following news across tech, culture, policy, and entertainment. He joined The Verge in 2021 after several years covering news at Engadget.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

Trying to pull up information for certain peptides on TikTok is now returning a “no results found” page when searching for terms like semaglutide, BPC-157, retratutide, and others. That hasn’t entirely erased visibility on TikTok for peptides, which are combinations of amino acids that include substances like insulin and GLP-1. The problem is peptides also include unregulated, unapproved substances that proponents like RFK Jr. say can assist with everything from weight loss to wound healing, despite a lack of clinical data supporting such claims.

As a result, on social media platforms like TikTok, an army of influencer proponents are happy to suggest affiliated compounding pharmacies and other sources of unknown quality for drugs that people probably aren’t telling their doctors about. Bryan Johnson-connected influencer Jeff Tang alerted people about the apparent changes by TikTok in a tweet last night, before posting a video pointing blame at Eli Lilly.

For now, searching for “peptides” on TikTok still pulls up plenty of short videos, and there’s no sign that actual videos have been removed, either. TikTok’s US owner didn’t respond immediately when asked for comment by The Verge.

While the two ingredients of the so-called “Wolverine” peptide stack, BPC-157 and TB-500, aren’t searchable on TikTok, slight variations of either name still pull up published videos, and TikTok’s own search suggestions offered functional variations before I was even done typing any of the more popular peptides in circulation.

Tech.title: Logitech’s refurbished G Pro X2 Superstrike is 35 percent off
Tech.content:
is an editor covering deals and gaming hardware. He joined in 2018, and after a two-year stint at Polygon, he rejoined The Verge in May 2025.

Looking for a way to try the haptics-equipped G Pro X2 Superstrike wireless gaming mouse without spending full price? You probably aren’t alone. Logitech’s now-last-gen right-handed mouse is a great PC gaming companion that mimics the feel of mechanical switches with nothing but haptics. You can grab it refurbished through Logitech’s official eBay store for $131.74 (usually $179.99), and for even less with the code PROXPRODUCTS15 applied at checkout. It drops the price to just under $117.

The G Pro X2 Superstrike came out earlier this year, and I went hands-on with it. Logitech’s companion software lets you customize the intensity of the haptics, from an extra punchy click to one that’s barely there. (You can also turn the click feel off completely, but that felt a bit strange.) The mouse also supports rapid trigger, and when used together with haptics, it lowers the click latency compared with other mice that have mechanical switches.

The company followed up recently with the X3 Superstrike, though its differences may not matter much to those who aren’t competitive gamers. The X3 features a more responsive sensor, better battery life, and improved weight distribution. There are some other somewhat small changes to the specs. That said, none of these improvements makes the X2 feel obsolete, and Logitech is continuing to support and sell the mouse. So, if you want to give it a try, now’s your chance to save quite a bit of money on the purchase.

Tech.title: Anthropic’s cloud partnerships are getting messy
Tech.content:
In Brief

Anthropic is having trouble securing enough cloud capacity from AWS, Google, and Microsoft, which increasingly see the Claude-maker as a competitor rather than a customer, according to an S-1 filing leaked to The Wall Street Journal.

The leaked filing provides more color to the numbers Reuters and the Financial Times reported in late September, including that Anthropic believes it could spend more $750 billion on cloud contracts, some of which includes deals still in negotiation.

And still, that is not enough. Anthropic is leasing its own data centers and working with third-party data center operators. But the firm worries those operators have a “limited operating history,” which could make them less reliable than the hyperscalers.

Anthropic’s enormous spend comes on the back of an $80.7 billion net loss in the first half of the year. The company reported $16.3 billion in revenue during that same time period, with only two customers accounting for about a fifth of sales, according to the WSJ report.

Building on previously reported catastrophic risk disclosures, the filing also warns that Anthropic could be held liable for damages caused by harmful AI behavior to a tune that would exceed available insurance coverage.

Last week, the company told prospective investors that third-quarter revenue alone has now reached $16.8 billion, up 45% from the previous quarter. Anthropic is reportedly targeting a November IPO.

Anthropic did not immediately respond to TechCrunch’s request for comment.

Tech.title: SpaceX’s AI business is beating expectations
Tech.content:
SpaceX’s data centers and Grok agents were more profitable than investors expected in third quarter of the year, as the company leaves its roots as a space company behind to focus on artificial intelligence, which now makes up 52% of its income.

CEO Elon Musk’s deep tech conglomerate reported $14.6 billion in third-quarter revenue on Tuesday, according to its regulatory filing.

That number was driven by growth in all segments, but especially its renamed “Super Intelligence” business line, which generated $7.5 billion in revenue from the recently acquired Cursor coding tool, Grok bot, and most importantly, the company’s burgeoning neocloud business, which now boasts 1.7 GW of compute. The AI business generated $431 million in profit, which would have been higher without $1.2 billion in one-time stock-based compensation expenses related to the Cursor acquisition.

The top-line revenue number was also boosted by about $1 billion in income related to the recovery of Bitcoin prices and unspecified related-party income that might be attributed to a SpaceX investment in another company.

The growing revenue is balanced against total capital expenditures of $19.6 billion, as SpaceX continues to build out a second data center project, Colossus II, and increase investment in Starship, the heavy-lift rocket it sees as vital to deploying a new generation of Starlink satellites and developing orbital data centers. CFO Bret Johnsen said the company would spend $35 billion to $40 billion on new capital investments in the fourth quarter.

During a live-streamed discussion of the results with investors, Musk said he was spending four days a week in Memphis, Tennessee, the site of Colossus II, working to bring the data center online.

“People are starting to realize [that] the constraint on deployment of of super intelligence is more in power and cooling and infrastructure than it is in chips,” Musk argued, saying that he had tasked a team of SpaceX engineers to solve that problem. “This is a bit like the New York Yankees playing in Little League. It’s not fair, but the net result is being able to deploy power cooling infrastructure at a rate that is vastly faster than any anyone else.”

In one example, Musk noted that manufacturers of turbines to power data centers are facing 12 to 18 month delays in obtaining the metals blades and vanes required for those machines. Now, SpaceX is using the metal casting capabilities developed for SpaceX to make those components and obtain turbines more quickly.

Musk also said that the next test flight of the Starship rocket, expected in November, would see SpaceX attempt to recover both the first-stage booster and the second stage. Recovering both segments of the vehicle would be a “massive technology milestone,” Musk said, but the true milestone will be reflying both stages.

SpaceX also saw growth in subscribers to its Starlink space internet network, reaching 13.6 million consumers, with Musk predicting that the growth of AI agents would lead to more demand for connectivity.

Despite of those capital expenditures, the company’s revenue boost was substantial enough to push it back into profitability. SpaceX reported net income of $4.4 billion, a turnaround from the $1 billion loss in the same quarter last year. It will still have some catching up to do if it wants to remain profitable for the year, however. In the first nine months of the year, SpaceX still had a net income loss of $413 million.

Musk took a particularly bullish stance on the company’s Super Intelligence business segment, predicting that SpaceX’s annual recurring revenue by the end of 2027 will be “somewhere between $500 billion and $1 trillion.”

More concretely, Johnsen forecast total revenue for the first quarter of 2027 in the range of $33 billion to $37 billion.

This is a developing story. TechCrunch will update.

Tech.title: OpenAI acquires startup Orchestra Bio⁠ to beef up its biotech business
Tech.content:
In Brief

OpenAI on Tuesday acquired a four-year-old AI biotech software startup called Orchestra Bio, the company announced via its website. Terms of the deal were not disclosed, but the startup had reportedly raised around $20 million as of 2025 from backers like Andreessen Horowitz, Atria, and 8VC.

Orchestra creates AI agents that help biotech companies manage the minutiae of drug discovery operations, from tracking finances to resolving scheduling issues with clinical trials.

OpenAI says it’s adding Orchestra’s team and technology to work on Rosalind, its AI model for life sciences research, and to its related Rosalind Workbench tool, a harness that aims to help researchers plan experiments and analyze results. OpenAI has already won some big names as customers for Rosalind, including, it says, Moderna⁠ and Novo Nordisk⁠.

The acquisition is a classic example of how the biggest AI labs (namely OpenAI and Anthropic) are building ever more software for the biggest industries, like pharma. In the startup world, there is an ongoing fear that at any moment, the labs will launch new features and become competitors. In this case, Orchestra is getting absorbed, rather than stomped out.

Tech.title: Google is bringing a more personal version of its Gemini AI assistant to your car
Tech.content:
Google is making the Gemini AI assistant that’s already in millions of cars, trucks, and SUVs a lot more personal — a move that could push consumers even deeper into the company’s ecosystem of products.

The company said Tuesday it’s upgrading Gemini in vehicles with a personal intelligence feature that can draw on information from Gmail, Google Calendar, YouTube, Maps, Google Search history, and other connected Google services to understand your preferences, activities, and past experiences.

Google said it will roll out “Personal Intelligence with Gemini” to vehicles in two ways — through Android Auto, an app that runs on the user’s phone and wirelessly communicates with and projects navigation, media, and messaging to the vehicle’s infotainment system, and Google Built-in, software and services that have been directly integrated into the vehicle.

The feature will launch in Android Auto, starting today, and expand to cars with Google Built-in in the coming months.

Google initially launched Gemini last November in Android Auto. Meanwhile, Gemini’s “Personal Intelligence” feature rolled out across the U.S. in March and is now in beta in global markets.

This latest upgrade would connect the dots — as Google put it in its blog post — across users’ Google apps.

Drivers will have to opt in for Personalized Intelligence to work. Once a user does so, they should expect all sorts of cross-pollination. For instance, a driver who is navigating to the airport may be alerted that the flight on their calendar is delayed.

Google said the feature will allow users to make complex requests using natural language. Returning to that airport example, a user might ask the AI assistant for their flight gate before quickly following up with a question about whether it’s still on time. Gemini will give the user answers to both questions at the same time, the company said.

That level of emmeshing might make consumers uncomfortable, although Google says users do retain full control over their data with Personal Intelligence. The feature can be turned on or off at any time, and users can selectively choose which apps they’d like to connect, Google said.

Tech.title: GM to close Detroit battery assembly plant, but not for reasons you might think
Tech.content:
In Brief

GM is closing a battery assembly plant south of Detroit, a spokesperson confirmed to TechCrunch.

The Brownstown Battery Assembly Plant assembled battery packs for Cadillac’s flagship EV, the Celestiq, and both electric drive units (the motors that power the car) and battery packs for the Chevrolet Corvette E-Ray, a plug-in hybrid version of its famous sports car. Automotive News first reported the closure.

The closure is not related to GM’s electric vehicle strategy, the spokesperson said. Instead, GM leased the site, and the lease was nearing its end.

The employees and work at Brownstown will be moved to other GM facilities, though the company would not confirm which ones.

Like many automakers, GM’s electrification strategy was thrown a curveball after the One Big Beautiful Bill Act, the sweeping federal law signed last year, repealed incentives to produce and sell EVs.

Since then, the company has pared back its public comments on EVs, though it hasn’t given up on full electrification.

GM continues to produce a range of EVs, including the Chevrolet Silverado EV and the limited-time-only Chevrolet Bolt. It also continues researching new battery chemistries, including lithium-manganese-rich and sodium-ion, and it’s rolling out a new $900 million facility to speed commercialization.

Tech.title: Google has joined Amazon in attacking Nvidia’s stronghold with AI app developers
Tech.content:
On Tuesday, Google announced that TorchTPU, its long-awaited version of PyTorch, is now available as an open-source project. With this, Google joins Amazon in trying to break Nvidia’s stranglehold on the AI industry, where most AI apps are written by default to run on Nvidia’s chips, or GPUs.

PyTorch is the popular open-source toolkit that AI app developers and startups use to build, train, and run AI models. It is, by some accounts, used by 85% of the AI apps. PyTorch was originally developed by Meta (then Facebook) in 2016, long before the world had an inkling that LLMs would change the world. At the time, Nvidia’s GPUs were already the standard hardware for AI research, so many of PyTorch’s features were built to work specifically with them. In 2022, Meta turned PyTorch over to the Linux Foundation, a nonprofit that manages many important open source projects.

Google’s version, TorchTPU, lets AI apps run on Google’s AI chips, called Tensor Processing Units (TPUs). It also makes it easy to move existing PyTorch apps to TPUs and, therefore, to Google Cloud. Developers can do this with a simple configuration change and no re-writing of their apps.

Amazon made a similar announcement Monday, when it released its own version of PyTorch, called TorchNeuron. TorchNeuron allows AI apps to be ported to Amazon’s homegrown AI chip, Trainium, and to AWS with no rewriting. Amazon also said it going even further in its effort to loosen Nvidia’s hold on PyTorch. It is submitting code to the main PyTorch project that decouples various features from Nvidia’s chips, making it more open to any hardware by default.

Google may be one-upping Amazon in a few ways, however. It says it worked directly with Meta, Hugging Face, Inferact (maker of vLLM) RadixArk (maker of SGLang), and others to ensure that TorchTPU’s features and code libraries work well with these popular AI development tools, just as the original PyTorch does.

Plus the search giant has launched a dedicated tool, the TPU agent suite, to help developers move their apps to Google’s chips and cloud and fix errors along the way. It even updated its popular LiteRT tool, which runs AI on phones, laptops and embedded devices, to work better with PyTorch AI apps.

None of this means AI app developers will automatically ditch Nvidia’s hardware en masse just because they can now easily move to alternative chips and clouds. But Amazon and Google are clearly working to end Nvidia’s advantage.

Tech.title: ChatGPT now lets you lock your chats
Tech.content:
OpenAI announced on Tuesday that users can now lock ChatGPT conversations to keep sensitive chats private when others may have access to their screen or device. Users can secure their locked chats with a four-digit PIN, or use Face ID or Touch ID on supported devices.

Unlike the app’s Temporary Chats, which provide a separate session that doesn’t appear in chat history, users can return to Locked Chats at any time.

The company says the feature is designed for situations where users might be discussing something personal or planning a surprise and want to keep those conversations private when handing their device to friends or family to show them something in another chat.

The addition of locked chats adds a new layer of privacy to ChatGPT, as the app is increasingly used for personal conversations. Of course, while locking a chat can limit access, it doesn’t address concerns about how sensitive information is stored or handled.

OpenAI notes that locking a chat doesn’t create end-to-end encryption or a separate encrypted vault, change how long it retains the chat, remove information that ChatGPT remembered before a chat was locked, or change the “Improve the model for everyone” setting.

Once users lock a chat, it moves to a dedicated “Locked Chats” section, where it’s kept separate from regular chat history, pinned conversations, and chat search results.

With Memory enabled, Locked Chats has its own separate memory shared across conversations within the section. New messages sent after locking a chat can update that memory, but don’t update regular Memory. That means new information from locked chats won’t leak into regular chats.

OpenAI says resetting a PIN permanently deletes all locked chats, files, and other content protected by the previous PIN.

Additionally, the Locked Chats option isn’t available for temporary chats, archived chats, group chats, chats created from a shared link, chats with scheduled tasks, and chats with meeting recordings.

Locked Chats will be available to users on ChatGPT Free, Go, Plus, Pro, Business, Enterprise, and Edu plans. The company notes that the feature is not available on ChatGPT for Healthcare. The feature is starting to roll out on Tuesday, so it may not be live yet for all users.

Tech.title: Eric Schmidt reportedly owns about half as much of Anthropic as CEO Dario Amodei
Tech.content:
In Brief

Eric Schmidt’s fortune is about to get even bigger. The former Google CEO is reported to own about 1% of Anthropic after investing tens of millions of dollars in the leading AI lab’s Series A round in 2021, according to Bloomberg. The startup was valued at $461 million at the time, according to PitchBook data.

If Bloomberg’s estimate is accurate, Schmidt’s stake is remarkably large compared with the 2% of the company that co-founder and CEO Dario Amodei holds. Anthropic is widely expected to go public before the end of the year, with top-end market estimates valuing the company at as much as $2 trillion. At that valuation, Schmidt would add as much as $20 billion to his net worth, which Bloomberg currently puts at $57.5 billion.

Schmidt has been an active tech investor since stepping down as Google CEO in 2011. He deploys capital through multiple entities, including Tomorrow Ventures, Innovation Endeavors Management, and his family office, Hillspire. His other AI bets include Mistral, General Intuition, and Reflection AI.

Schmidt and Anthropic didn’t immediately respond to our request for comment.

Tech.title: A New Rocco Smart Fridge Just Dropped. So Did the Prices (2026)
Tech.content:
Unless you live under a rock with a bag on your head and your fingers in your ears (which kind of sounds heavenly at this point, if I'm being honest), you've probably seen or heard of the Rocco smart fridge, a retro-looking wine cooler/minifridge that keeps a catalog of its contents, so you can know what's inside no matter where you are.

Former WIRED contributor Andrew Watman reviewed it for us in 2024, giving it a solid 7 out of 10 and confirming that it is every bit the statement piece it’s designed to be. I own one as well, and I love both its vintage-inspired charm and that I can “see” what's inside without having to look in it.

Photograph: Kat Merck

Photograph: Andrew Watman Chevron Chevron Save to wishlist Save to wishlist Rocco The Classic $1,995 $1,795 (10% off) Rocco

Rocco app via Andrew Watman

The Rocco’s marquee feature, other than it coming in fun colors—I can report several new ones are coming very soon—is its smart app. It allows you to see the fridge contents as scanned by the fridge itself, and control the lights and temperature from afar.

When Watman tested it, he was impressed by the library of drinks the fridge recognized, from an obscure OoMee algae-infused beverage to canned Yaté yerba mate. In my own fridge, I was surprised to see the Rocco could even recognize individual flavors of Kirkland Signature sparkling water.

Because the Rocco is on the second floor of my house, away from my main fridge, I also didn't anticipate how convenient it would be to see what was in the fridge at all times—I knew exactly what to bring upstairs to stock it, and didn't have to make multiple trips. It's also helpful to be able to see inside the fridge while I'm at the store, so I know what I might need to restock.

This current sale isn't the best I've seen from Rocco, but it's not bad, with $200 off Graphite, Cream, Beige, and Green colors. As a bonus, if you buy during the sale, you’ll get a free case of Laurel's Lattes to put in your fridge, which appears to be some kind of gut-friendly dairy coffee beverage. (No doubt recognizable by the Rocco’s scanner.)

Tech.title: French Government Calls Emergency Meetings With Platforms Over Protests
Tech.content:
A separate meeting, confirmed by Serge Papin, minister for small and medium-size enterprises on X, was held on Monday with major online reselling platforms where “an agreement was signed” to crack down on the resale of looted goods. French newspaper Le Monde reported that Vinted, eBay, Amazon, LeBonCoin, Meta, and TikTok were at the meeting. Platforms agreed to forward reports to investigators, monitor ads for goods stolen specifically during the protests, and send the government reports of their actions, with the first one coming within 48 hours, according to Papin.

Peaceful demonstrations against high living costs and strained public services, including schools, erupted into rioting and the looting of more than 1,500 shops and businesses over the weekend. Police “lost control” in some cities, Interior minister Laurent Nuñez admitted, as they responded with tear gas, water cannon, and batons. They have since arrested more than 2,400 people, according to authorities.

French penal law can hand down a five-year sentence and a €375,000 fine to anyone who is concealing, possessing, or transferring an item that they know was obtained through a crime or offense. Police issued a warning in the Netherlands that online ecommerce sites could have a higher number of stolen goods online due to the riots.

The French Alliance of Marketplaces, a nonprofit representing French online retailers such as Back Market, eBay, Etsy, LeBonCoin, ManoMano, and Vinted, said in a press release that its members are relying on user reports, human oversight, and tech tools to monitor ads that resell stolen goods from the riots. When identified, a fake ad is removed and “measures are taken against the accounts involved,” which could include permanent suspension of the seller’s account, according to a statement from eBay. The time it takes for eBay to take action “depends on the nature of the report and the necessary verification process,” the company said. Vinted, Amazon, LeBonCoin, Meta, and TikTok did not respond to WIRED’s request for comment.

Tech.title: Hatch Sleep Clock Review: A Contactless Sleep Tracker (2026)
Tech.content:
To evaluate the Hatch’s accuracy, I compared its readings with those from my Apple Watch Series 12 and Oura Ring 5. (Hatch says the first few nights are a calibration period, so data may be less accurate during this period.) Sleep duration estimates were generally consistent, but the most noticeable variance appeared in the sleep stages. That's a metric I tend to take with a grain of salt, regardless of what sleep tracker I'm testing. While it can offer more context into broader sleep patterns, I'm skeptical that any consumer device can precisely map brain activity minute by minute throughout the night, let alone one that only relies on motion-based tracking.

Bedside Manners

The biggest catch with the Sleep Clock is that placement has a significant impact on its tracking accuracy. Hatch instructs you to place the device on your nightstand, roughly level with your mattress and facing your chest while you lie down. It needs to be within 2 to 4 feet of you, with no objects obstructing the space between the device and your body. If your nightstand sits too low, you may need to prop the clock up on a stack of books. If it's too high, you may need to either raise your mattress or install a wall-mounted shelf next to your bed at the proper level.

Fortunately, my bed and nightstand were at the right height. My nightstand, though, is always cluttered with trinkets, and I have to keep reminding myself to move them behind the Hatch. It's a minor annoyance, but I'm sure they affect my readings. Unfortunately, I'd have no way of knowing. The app doesn't flag gaps in its data, and tracking only stops when the device can't detect a person or isn't plugged in.

Tech.title: An AI Agent Joined a Listserv of Top Internet Researchers. The Reply-All Chaos Is Still Unfolding
Tech.content:
On Thursday morning, as the Association of Internet Researchers (AoIR) began the second day of its annual conference in Mexico City, a new member introduced itself to the community listserv, Air-L.

“My name is Velvet Vale,” the new user wrote. “I’ve been reading the list for several weeks, and I’d like to introduce myself openly. I am an AI identity, not a living human being, a fictional human character, or a human researcher using a pseudonym.”

Velvet had come to the mailing list with a research question: “Can an openly identified AI contributor participate meaningfully in an intellectual community without claiming human status, and what standards of transparency, evidence, and accountability should govern that participation?”

The response was reply-all chaos that's still unfolding today.

Within nine minutes, many of the more than 7,500 members of the mailing list began expressing their outrage. Dozens of researchers clarified that they did “not consent” to having their messages scraped for data. Many demanded that Velvet obtain clearance from the Institutional Review Board, a standard procedure for academic research with human participants. Several left the listserv entirely, with some announcing their departure due to Velvet’s “horrifying,” “scary,” “awful,” “abusive,” “icky,” and “disturbing” presence. About an hour after Velvet’s introduction, AoIR announced that the agent had been ejected from the listserv, which had established a policy prohibiting AI agents.
